SHE IS NOT HERE. Wlth eager steps and strangely wistful eyes, A weary soldier, bruised and mangled hi the wars, Returned, with sore dej‘cl3n and surprise. To find an empty home. Less painiul wtre his scars. He ried the door. alae ! in vain; No ails, er would appear All tremblingly he cried in pa',l,ll: "My love, she is not here! He sought the rustic p,rtals of the cot Where, long ago. his missing love had humbly dwelt; His tears fell fast before that hallowed spot, His heart with grief and passin seemed to burn and melt. When operil ng the door Le saw A face both strange and sear; He dropped the latch, exclaiming, "Oh, My love, she is not here ! " His aching feet now bore him to a place, The sainted dwelling where hii mother lived ere be Had left her aging form n abroad to trace A martial pathway to ren,wn ambitiously. A sickness seized his heart, and cruAred Its topes. as he draw near ; For through his ears a whiTer rushed: "My love, she is not here!" He raised the latch that oft' in days gone by Had opened him the lovit,g door to home and ease. He entered then, alas! to turn and fly: It is no home for him—a stranger there he sees. " Alas! dear home, my olden pride, Affliction is severe; My mother dead, and she," he cried, " My love. she is not her e ! " That soldleee breast had ne'er a struggle feared, But bravely net the danger of each foeman's Yet memory revived a scene revered That made it tremble with fore's ding's icy chill. "All, all is fled treat I can prize, Henceforth my life is drear, - Since now," the listless solder cries, "My love, stair is not here!" But battling with the death-like pang of grief. He sought time village churchy ird in tLe :ailing gloom. Slowly he searched, and found a heading brief Upon the simplest sto.;e : it marked his lost love's tomb. " At last! " the sorrowing warrior cried, " My sweet one, thou art near. Long will I stay thy grave beside, For thou my love, art herd:" Warrlngton, May 22nd, 1882. BENJAMIN S CWI3OII.

A Virginia mats OTIIS a hen that sings. One simple lay a day is her average. Curiosity is the core of the forbidden trait, which still sticks in the throat of the natural mate—Thontas Fuller. Master: "What does Condillac say about brutes in the scale of being ?" S.lholar : "He says a brute is an imper- fect animal." "And what is man?" "Man is a perfect bete?" CLEAR ENOnClir.—First English Gentleman (looking at railroad time table) : "Bill, why do they say pm. ?" Second Gentleman: "That means penny a mile." First: "And what does a.m. mean?" Second: "Why, 'apenny a mile, Of i:OurSe. I said to my little girl one day: " What a lame ft,reilead you have got! It is just like your father's. -You could drive a pony carriage round it." To which her brother, five years old said, "Yes, mamma, but on papa's you can see the marks of the wheels." A stranger in a printing office asked the youngest appren- tice what his rule of punctuation was. Said the boy: "1 set up as long as I can hold my breath, and then I put a comma; when I gape, I insert a semicolon; and when I want to sneeze, I make a paragraph. A young man who thought he had won the heart, and now asked the hand in marriage of a certain young widow, was asked by her, "What is the difference between myself and Mr. Baxley's Durham cow ?" He naturally replied, "Well, I don't know." "Then," said the widow," you had batter marry the cow." Learning that five inches of snow fell at Sheboygan, Michigan, a few days ago, a newspaper observes that it was Sheboygan wnich was once spoken of as a place where "the eighing ain't first-rate for a spell in August." Maybe the town is on the same isothermal line as the locality where it is "eleven months winter and one mighty late in the fall." It is said that along the coast of Newfoundland devil- fish, with arms of unheard-of length, are so numerous "that trudent men go hack ten miles in the country to get drunk." Perhaps if all the reeidents along there were pru- dent, and wont out of sight of the shore to get drunk, there would be fewer reports of big devil-fish from that quarter. "There, there; don't cry any more !" slid the kind- hearted stranger to a little girl, who was leaning against the railing in front of a Board School, weeping as if her heart would break," tell us what's the matter." The child turned two highly-inflamed orbs up at the good Samaritan, and then stammered between her sobs, "All the girls in my Clan was vaccinated last week, and mine's the only one that hasn't took!" A DEFINITION OF "RACK RENT."—" What is rack-rent, dad ?" inquired a young Comstecker who had been reading the news from Irelatd. Tas POWER or Music.—On one occasion, when young I Chopin had been travelling for several days in the slow fashion of German diligeuces, he was delighted and surprised, on stopping at a small poet-house, to discover a grand piano- forte in one of the roon;s, and still more surprised to find it In tune—thanks probably to the musical taste of the post- master's family. He sat down instantly and began to im- provise in his peculiarly happy manner—one by one the travellers were attracted by the unwonted sweet sounds, one of them even letting his beloved pipe go out in his ecstasy. The postmaster, his wife, and his two daughters joined the group of listeners. Unmindful of his audience, of the I 3 lumen the lapse of time, and everything but the music, 1 Chopin continued to play and his companinns to listen in rapt attention, when they were soddenly roused by a sten- torian voice which made the windows rattle, calling out, I "The horses are ready, gentlemen !" The postmaster roared ' out an anathema against the disturber—the postillion—and the passengers cast angry glances at him. Chopin started from his seat, but was instantly surrounded by his audience, who entreated him to continue. "But we have been here ! some time," said Chopin, consulting his watch, "and are due in Posen already." "Stay and play, noble young artist," cried the postmaster; "I will give you courier's horses if you will only remain a little longer." "Do be , persuaded," began the postmaster's wife, almost threatening ihq artist with an embrace- 1-%:= could he do but resume ! _a. . . his place at the Instrument 2 When at last he paused, the I servant appeared with wine ; the hosts' daughter served the artist first, then the travellers, then the postmas- ter proposed a cheer fer thelett-skin, in which all 'the women in their gratitude filled the a+utiake-pockets with the best eatables and wine the httlim contained; and when at last the artist rasa fa 0, his gigantic host seized him in his arms and bore him to the carriage! Long years afterwardn Chtpin Would recall this little incident with pleasure, and declare that the plaudits of the press had never given him more delight thin the homage of these simple music-loving Germans.—Good Words. THE IMPORTANCE OF SYSTEMATIC OLD TESTAMENT artmer.—There has never been a time when a right under- standing of the Old Testament as the historical substrac- Una on which Christianity builds was more necessary than in these days. On the one hand the Churches are still divided by controversies which had their first origin in mitt -eeceptions about the Old Covenant, and these miscon- ceptiote cannot be removed till they are traced back to their source. On the other hand we live in an age of searching historical inquiry, in which Christianity, by its own profes- sion a positive and historical religion, is daily called upon to exhibit its historical pedigree as the teat of its unique claims on the minds and hearts of men. And here again we are thrown back on the study of the Old Testament; for Jesus professed to bring no new religion, but only to carry to their fulfilment arid perfection the things already given in germ to Israel under the old covenant. It will not be disputed that the great majority even of intelligent Christians are accustomed to deal with these weighty matters quite in a haphazard way. Very many are content simply to accept the Old Testament as part of Divine Revelation, and to read Individual passages by the light of the New Testament, without trying to form any general idea of the differences between the two dispensations, and the reason why the people of God was so long left to live by an imperfect light. Others again are so much struck by the imperfection of the Old Covenant that they practically leaveit on one side and hardly attempt to go back beyond the New Testament at all. Very few make any serious effort to understand the Old Tes- tament as a whole, or to form a clear picture of the actual life of the nation of Israel under the Law. Yet if the He- brew Bible had been lost for centuries and were now brought Into our possession by some new disoovery, as the Assyrian records have been, our first observation 'would be that this book contains the whole history of a nation nurtured under conditions remote from all our present experience. The ahcient laws which it contains, the wonderful religious life which it records, would present themselves as an historical problem, and we should not be content until we had re- constructed a complete and harmonious picture of the growth and maturity of the commonwealth and religion of Israel. We should not think ourselves to have done justice to so wonderful a record by merely looking at isolated chapters, by admiring the simplicity and truth of individual parts of the narrative, the beauty and spiritual depth of particular p t3sazes in the Psslms or the Prophets. Why then should any Christian be content with so superficial a study of the Old Testament, simply because the book, instead of being a ,q discovery, has been from the first days of Christianity a eacred possession of the Church ?—Good Words.

HANGING BEIDGE.--FURTITER REMAINS —Manchester antiquarians will be interested to learn that another arch over what is known as the "Great Feces," at Hanging Bridge, has been recently brought to light. It will be re- membered that about two years ago, in the removal of some old bui:dicgs at the end of Hanging Bridge, opposite the south entrance to the Cathedral, two arches of ordinary span were discovered. At the same time, in excavating for the fonndations of the building which now occupies that site, an ancient watercourse was deosvered, about 18 inches , wide, which watercourse was generally regarded as the re- mains of the "Great Fosse," or Hanging Ditch," in,licases] by Whitaker in the plans of Saxon Nfaechester (A D. 627 and 800) accompanying his well-known history of ancient Mancnnium. It was then supposed that these two arches formed the bridge spanning the original fosse. Within the last month the buildings adjoining those already named— that is, at the south-east corner of Hanging Bridge, facing ' Cateaton-street—have been demolished, and in excavating' the foundations for the new premises another arch of similar proportions to these mentioned has been discovered. The absolute date of the construction of the arches is somewhat doubtful, but the masonry is still in a good state of preser- vation. Though the arch has been only visible during the past few days, it has already attracted a large number of visitors.—Manchester Guardian. • Earan'ore INSEAsn—The report of the Inspectors of Salmon Fisheries, which has just been issued, is chiefly remarkable for the very elaborate and scientific examination—obviously the work of Professor Huxley—of the causes of the late outbreak of disease among salmon. The disease first ap- peared in the Esk and the Nith in 1877, though the Inspec- tors are of opinion that sporadic cases had been previously observed. Since then it has spread rapidly and seriously in English. Scotch, and Welsh rivers. The first symptom is a grayish discolouration of the skirl, which gradually forms a ileZp bleeding sore eating down to the bone, an Z.?nding off ramifications in all directions. Within a few days the fish dies from irritation or exhaustion. Microscopic examination shows that the disease is a fungoid growth, analogous to the "blue mould" on pots of jam, Much farther know- however, required before any safe foundation can be -o-17taTned, or any view as to the best method of dealing with the disease. The Inspectors do not regard pollution of the , water as a primary cause, but think it may have an ins- por ' tant secondary influence as determining whether the die, ' ease shall be sporadic or epidemic. They are C.?. opinion I that it would be desirable to destroy Zeroed fish, but ! they see no practical means et tatrying out the policy of eXtirpation. In other ICspects the Inspectors report a general improvemat in the English and Welsh fisheries, though the old difficulty has cropped up again between the proprietors of the upper waters and the net fishermen. The former complain that the latter get all the benefit of the conservation of salmon, and that they have some grounder for complaint is shown by the fact as stated in the report that there are scarcely any English rivers which produce on an average half a dozen salmon per rod. The Inspectors seem, however, to be unable to suggest a practical remedy for an undoubted grievance which must sooner or later tell seriously against salmon cultivation. THE RECENT MAGNETIC Sronst.—The curves given by the Kew magnetograph during the week ending April 22, when auroral displays were so common in America, and earth currents so prevalent in the inland telegraph lines and Indian and Atlantic submarine cables, clearly indicate a severe "magnetic storm" or disturbance of the terrestrial magnetic field. According to Mr. Whipple, the indicating magnets at Kew were somewnat disturbed on the 14th of April, but remained quiescent until the 'night of the 16th, when they became stronly affected at about 11 45 p.m., and from that time the Storm raged until 8 p.m. of the 17th. The maximum redaction in the earth's magnetic force took place at 6 a.m. of the 17th, and a little after noon on the same day both forces became so increased that the regis- tering speck left the field of the receiving instrument for nearly two hours. A second period of disturbance began about 3 40 a.m. of the 20th, which was violent up till about 2 p.m., and gradually diminished in intensity until 7 45 a.m. of the 21st. During this period the magnetic force fluctuated largely, but not to the extent occurring on the 17th. The fact that there were at the time two unusually large spots crossing the sun's disc is certainly in support of the theory that these magnetic storms are associated with sun spots. Mr. Whipple accounts for the abrupt commence- ment of magnetic storms by the supposition that possibly a sun spot only produces such an effect when cutting certain lines of force, which he imagined might extend for a limited angular distance around the earth's radius sector. It is to be hoped that magnetic observatories will be multiplied, especially in the southern hemisphere, as Professor W. On arable land it is generally computed to exhaust at the rate of one-tenth per annum, but is by same deemed most beneficial after the first year or two. Horse, cow, and town manure last frem three years on sandy soil to nine years on clay land, two fifths being exhausted the first year. Of guano, bones, and phosphates, the greatest endurance is given to half-inch bones, which are said to extend over seven years at the rate of one-tenth per annum. Bone meal covers six years, with most effect the first year, while quicker action is assigned to dissolved bones, Ammoniac tl and phosphatic guano, nitrates, sulphates, and special manures are yet more speedily exhausted, the former often spending its effects in a single year, though special manures and cakes sometimes show their effects over three and • four years. Very in- teresting comparative statements, showing the conclusions arrived at in different districts and by different authorities, are embodied in the document. With the guiding prin- ciples of this report it is contended that compensation, sub- lect to arbitration, may be made an accomplished fact were the Legislature but to sanction the principle by some com- pulsory enactment, doing away with the presumption of law which now confiscates to the landlord any improve- ment which the tenant may effect in or upon the land. Among other proposals of the Chamber's bills are the abolition of Entail. Primogeniture, the Game Laws, the remnant of Hypotbec, and the granting to tenants the liberty of cropping and power to assign iletiteleases. THE HARVEST FAN. The "Harvest Fan," in wet and late seasons, when there is little or no sunshine, must prove invaluable to thousands of farmers, in enabling them to complete the curing of their hay and corn crops in the rick, when otherwise these must be completely spoilt or greatly reduced in feeding value by, prolonged espoetire to rain and weather. This simple in- vention is likely to effect a complete revolution in our method of haymaking and harvesting. It will, if rightly used, be the means of preventing mustineee in hay, and it will enable corn crops to be dried and preserved in the rick, without taking ss. or 81. a quarter off the grain, as often happens when it has to be kiln-dried. The handling of late hay crops, such as second cuts of clover, damp meadow- grass, and aftermath of all kinds, will be greatly facilitated kv:_tleis nrecess. It wilt Also eneonrege the practice of grow. gig catch Crepe and many kinds of forage planti oh the autumn atubbles. One of the greet difficahies in the way j , of this hitherto, has been that land thus cropped could not I always be cleared when wanted; or, if it was cleared, the value of the catch crop had in a manner to be sacrificed, because, under the old methods, it could not be converted and conserved for winter use. It will be an immense boon to farmers everywhere, but especially so in the high-lying and late districts, where the operations of baying and har- vesting have always been tedious and uncertain, and conse- quently carried on at great expense, and the produce often rendered almost worthless before it could be secured. There will be no further occasion, however, for corn sheaves to be standing in the fields amid winter snows, because the weather would not dry them enough to admit of carrying; nor will the great flush of autumn grass on hill and vale in pastoral districts new be allowed to rot: under foot, as has been the case pretty much in the past, from inability to cure and preserve it. It will be cut and cured in the stack, which will reduce the cake bill, and greatly benefit the flocks in winter. This method of curing crops is a very simple one. It consists in controlling the ferment .tion which takes place when grass or corn Is put together in a damp or green state. The stack is built with an air-hole or shaft in the centre, and pipes are laid to connect this shaft with a suction fan or exhauster. When the fan is set going, it speedily draws off the heated air and moisture from the central shaft, and, as this creates a partial vacuum, the external air is drawn In at all points of the rick, thus thoroughly drying the grass or corn, however wet its condition to begin with. Fans of various descriptions are now employed for this pur- pose; most of them are workable by band power, and, being on wheels, are easily moved, so that one of them will answer for any number of ricks. The pipes employed to connect the fan with the air shaft are usually of iron, the diameter being eight or nine inches. The end of the pipe next the air shaft is fitted with a damper, which is opened or shut at will. It does not appeor to be of importance whether the pipes are laid underground or above ground, or inserted in the side of the stack, but the air shaft requires to be brought well down to the bottom of the rick, and should not be car- ried within six feet of the tcp of it. An air bole may be formed by using a corn sack stuffed with straw, and drawing it up as the rick is built, until the required height of the shaft is reached, when the sack Is taken out altogether ; or a framework of poles and shafts may be used for the purpose. The cylindrical form of rick is best, and it must not be too large. It is found that air cannot be rapidly drawn through the stack when the radius exceeds eight or nine feet. If the rick is a long one (say 32 feet), it will require two air shafts ; if 48 feet, three shafts. The temperature of the rick is ascertained by the thermometer, and Mr. Philips has invented a very useful thermometer-stick for this purpoee, which does away with the necessity of having a thermome-
miniimi

for "the Man of the people," their watchword being "For God and O'Connell"—the most intelligible expression of theirs for "God and the Right." At the close of the first day the numbers were found to be—For Mr. Vesey Fitz- gerald, 194; for Mr. O'Connell, 200; majority for O'Con- nell, 6. At the end of the second day's struggle the majority for Mr. O'Connell was slightly augmented. On Thursday evening the result of the first three day's polling was—Mn Fitzgerald, 842; Mr. O'Connell, 1,820; majority for O'Con- nell, 978. "The battle," said Mr. Shiel, "is won, but the effect of the defeat will be measured elsewhere by the de- monstration of the overwhelming numbers. There must be no laying down of our arms while our adversary keeps the field." At length the poll closed. For O'Connell there were two thousand and fifty-seven votes; for Fitzgerald, one thousand and seventy-five. It was argued before the Asses- sor that a Catolic could not be legally returned. But the objection was overruled, as it rested with the House of Com- mons itself to exclude a representative if he refused the oath tendered to him. Wherefore O'Connell was declared duly elected. Such was the memorable Clare election. It was perhaps the most important one in the entire history of English, Irish, and Scotch elections. There are only two other elec- tions that can for a moment stand in comparison with it. The Middlesex election in the last century in which Wilkes was a prominent figure, and that Tipperary election which re- turned O'Donovan (Rossa), an Irish rebel suffering penal ser- vitude under a Treason Felony Act, to the British House of Commons. Bnt the Clare election remains unarivalled on the historic page, when we consider the excitement that it occasioned and the influence that it exercised. The excite- ment which it evoked was tremendous. "Nothing is talked of now which interests anybody the least in the world," writes Lord Eldon on the 9th of July, 1829, " except the election of Mr. O'Connell, and the mischief that it will pro- duce among debates in the House of Commons, and the more serious mischief which it will in all probability excite in Ireland. As O'Connell will not though elected be al- lowed to take his seat in the House of Commons unless he will take the oaths, &c. (and that he won't do unless he can get absolution), his rejection from the Commons may excite rebellion in Ireland. At all events this busi- ness must bring the Roman Catholic question which has been BO often discussed to a crisis and a con- clusion. The nature of that conclusion I don't think likely to be favourable to Protestantism. It is clear that the Clare election had already done some good. It had opened the eyes of the most haughty of the anti- Catholics to the fact that the question was approaching "its crisis and conclusion." The next obvious effect was a singular one—the conversion of some of the county mem- bers of Ireland who were strong in the Protestant interest. The Association was threatening and preparing to carry all the other Irish counties as it had carried Clare. It had also an obvious influence upon the Cabinet. They could not fail to perceive that if concession was not made almost every Catholic county would follow the example of Clare, and the Ministers, feeling further resistance to be hopeless, brought in a Relief Bill. On the sth of March Sir Robert Peel moved for "the Committee of the whole House for con- sideration of civil disabilities of His Majesty's Roman Catholic subjects," and the motion was carried, after a warm deb ateaby a large majority. The Bill was passed on the 30th of March by a majority of 36. Next day it was carried to the House of Lords, and on the 2nd of April its second reading was moved by the Duke of Wellington, who made no scruple to urge its necessity in order "to prevent civil war." After violent debates in the House of Lords, the Bill was read a third time and passed by a majority of 104. On the 13th it received the Royal Assent. And so it came to pass that almost 137 years after the Treaty of Limerick the Catholic-a were emancipated. It cannot be denied that this great victory was won by the genius of a single man, and that man Daniel O'Connell. Without any arrogance, he could fairly claim the victory. There bad been other warriors who had fought bravely in this bloodless battle of Right against Wrong. Fox and Grattan, and Plunkett and Canning, had made the walls of St. Stephen's ring in their denunciations of the Protestant ascendency, and in their advocacy of the Catholic claims. The trenchant reasoning of Jeffrey in the Edinburgh Re. view; the piquant humour of Sidney Smith in "Peter Plymley's Letters ;" the brawny might of William Cobbett. who wherever tyranny and intolerance showed their head smote it amain with his knotted club; the exquisite satire of Moore, like a rapier of the finest edge that eften, with the lightest and most graceful movement, as if in play, seal ched the very vitals of some villain in high places and made him howl; the brilliant shafts of Shiers wit, shot from the bow of the New Monthly Magazine ;—all these were enlisted on the side of Catholic Emancipation and against the Protestant ascendency. But O'Connell was the man who marched at the bead of this crusade for the eman- cipation of his creed and race. It was to the sound of his trumpets that the walls of Jericho fell down. All the elo- quence of Grattan and of Plunkett—all the influence of Pitt and of Canning—had failed to accomplish this. But this "untitled lawyer," "without any advantage of rank, or wealth, or influence, and from no prouder eminence than the platform of the demagogue," entered on the contest when the bitterest enemies of emancipation held the reins of power—when these enemies were guided by the most successful statesmen of his generation, and by one of the most stubborn wills that ever directed the affairs of the nation, and yet in spite of the religious intolerance which Toryism had evoked—in spite of the de- nunciations which resounded from the English pulpits—in spite of the fierce passions of Puritanism which the Evan- gelical movement had roused—in spite of Peel and Welling- ton, Lord Chancellor Eldon and King George, this man won the victory without the effusion of a single drop of blood, and stood out before his countrymen and the world as " Tiss Liberator." "If be had never risen," says Leckaa "Emancipation would doubtless have been at length con- ceded, but it would have been conceded as a boon granted by a superior to an inferior class, and it would have been accompanied and qualified by the veto. It was the glory of O'Connell that his Church entered into the Constitution triumphant and unshackled—an object of fear and not of contempt—a power that could visibly affect the policy of the empire."

div.head: MELANCHOLY BOAT ACCIDENTS 'ON THE SCOTCH COAST. SIX MEN DROWNED.
div.p: MELANCHOLY BOAT ACCIDENTS 'ON THE SCOTCH COAST. SIX MEN DROWNED.

Two WA accidents, each involvin7 the loss of three lives, occurred on Saturda yon the coasts of-Forfar and Kincardine. Three men, George Pert, aged 23, a lair,urer ; William Dun- can, aged 24, a cooper; and James Orkney, aged 28, a cooper, all of Montrose, set out on Saturday afternoon from the harbour of the port for a pleasure sail. About two milei off Johnshaven a sudden squall upset the craft, which was an exceedingly frail one, and all the occupants were drowned. The occurrence was observed from the shore, but by the time a boat arrived at the spot all had disappeared. Duncan, who was a splendid swimmer, made a determined effort to save his life, but was seen to give up and disappear. Duncan was married; the other two men were unmarried. Some persons who saw them proceed to sea warned them not to go far in so unsafe a boat. About the hour when this accident happened another boat, belonging to Catterline, while engaged crab fishing off Kinneff, Kincardinshire, was caught in the Equal' and upset. Her crew of three men perished, although not far from the shore. Their names are Alexander Taylor, 43 years, skipper, leaves a widow and five children ; David Taylor, 25 years, brother of the skipper, unmarried; and Alexander Forbes. The accident happened while the unfortunate men were leaning over the side haul- ing the creels. None of the boAies have been recovered.

CAPTURE OF A SUPPOSED BUROLA.R; IN 111A.NOFIESTER. Adam Holt, a shoemaker, carrying on business at 28, 'Cross-street, Hyde-road, was on Wednesday charged before Mr. Headlam, at the City Police Court, under the Man- chester Improvement Act, with being in possession of a large quantity of property supposed to have been stolen. The property consisted of a large number of gold and silver lever watches, watch movements, cases, and works, several pairs of earrings, gold keepers, an opera glass, six rolls of new alpaca, four or five dozen silver 'forks, knives, and spoons, two pairs of sugar tongs, a large revolver' pistol, cartridges, a dagger, a number of knives supposed to be used to open window sashes, a number of skeleton keys, a canister of gunpowder, a life preserver, and a large quan- tity of other articles.—Detective Inspector Rowbottom said that on Tuesday, in company with Detective Sergeant Williams, he took the prisoxer into custody in consequence , of a girl in the neighbourhood where the prisoner lived having offered some watches in pawn. When apprehended Holt had on him a watch, two guards, and £2O lOs in money. In reply to the charge he said that about two years ago he bought 50 watches for £l5 from a man whom be did not know, and that he had been disposing of them by pawn- ing them and selling them. He had given the girl a small gold watch for herself for pawning the others for him. At first the prisoner refused to give any address, but afterwards he gave the one in Cross-street, and on going there in com- pany with Williams they found amongst other things the articles enumerated above. Most of the silver articles are marked with the initials "W. H. E.," and one pair of the sugar tongs with the letters "L. G." underneath the Hall stamp. A lady's small gold hunter watch case, the works having been taken out, has the monogram "A. H." engraved on one side and a kind of picture on the other. The knives, revolver, and pistol were all found securely attached to a belt, and the life preserver is a formidable weapon, having a leather strap on the end, so as to prevent it slipping or being knocked out of the band of the person using it. Inspector Rowbotforn, in applying for a remand, added that there were 14 or 15 other watches pawned in different parts of the city which he wanted to make inquiries about.—The prisoner was remanded for a week.

Happiness is like manna. It is to be gathered in the grains and enjoyed every day; it will not keep, it cannot be accumulated; nor need we go out ourselves, nor into remote places, to gather it, since it has rained down from heaven, at our very doors, or rather within them. In a railroad car on the Pittsburgh and Lake Erie Rail. road, the seats were all full except one, which was occupied by a pleasant-looking Irishman from Wampum, and at Beaver a couple of evidently well-bred and intelligent young ladies came in to procure seats. Seeing none vacant, they were about going into the next car, when Patrick arose hastily and offered his seat with evident pleasure. "But you will have no seat for yourself," responded one of the young ladies with a smile, hesitating, with true polite. ness, to accept it. " Niver mind that !" said the gallant Hibernian, "I'd ride upon a cowcatcher to New York for a smile from such jintlemanlv ladies."

div.head: ILLUSTRIOUS IRISH IFN.
div.p: ILLUSTRIOUS IRISH IFN.

BY WILLIAM FRANCIS. No. XXII.—DANIEL O'CONNELL. "New times demand new measures and new men; The world advances and in time outgrows The laws that in our father's day were best. And doubtless after us some purer scheme Will be shaped out by wiser men than we, Made wiser by the steady growth of truth."

The "help-me-God" speech delivered by the Duke of York, in the House of Lords, as we have seen, roused the Catholics of Ireland to make greater sacrifices and more strenuous exertions for the accompliehtnent of their emanci- pation. The results of that speech were seen in the General Election of 1826, which was signalised by several remark- able triumphs of the Association. The representation of several counties was wrested from great ascendancy families that had hitherto controlled the elections of those districts with absolute sway. The machinery of the associa- tion, spread like network over the country, was admirably adapted for achieving conquests of this kind. The great 110weeof Bereeferd was totally defeated in Waterford. The two great ascendancy aristoctats of the county Lowth—the Earl of Roden, head of the family of Jocelyn, and Lord Oriel, head of the Fosters—were also humbled. The Liberal candidate for Lowth, Mr. Alexander Dawson, a retired bar- rister, was at the head of the poll ; the second member was Mr. Foster. Mr. Fortescue, Lord Roden'e nominee, was totally defeated. At Dublin the two Liberal candidates were also returned. These electioneering triumphs produced a great sensation in the political world. The machinery of the association, "the rent" and the self-sacrifice of the forty shilling freeholders, applied and directed by the skill and energy of O'Connell, had so triumphed during this general election that it was now plain to the world that with most Irish constituencies candidates who refused to pledge themselves to vote for emancipation had little chance of being returned. Early in the next year two of the opponents of Catholic Emancipation passed over to the " great majority." After a long and painful illness the Duke of York expired, and O'Connell, who had incurred a good deal of odium by the fierce invectives which he had uttered against him after his "so-help-me-God" harangue, now when the Duke had actually ceased to exist expreesed a geuerons sorrow for his death and a keen regret for the bitter words he had spoken in anger. " Tbe Catholics of Ireland," said O'Connell, "exult not at the death of the Duke of York. We are not with the dying or the grave. Our enmities are buried there. They expired with the individual who caused them. What- ever his Royal Highness may hese said against us we for- give. No man ever acted with greater impartiality at the head of the army. He never made a distinction between a Catholic and a Protestant there." The other bitter oppo • nent of the Catholic claims who died this year was the Premier the Earl of Liverpool. He was incapacitated by an apoplectic seizure from taking any part in public.affairs early in the year, and did not survive this attack many months. The removal of this timorous and narrow bigot from the helm of Government was a source of rejoicing to the Catholics of Ireland. And when it was known that the impassioned, the brilliant, the eloquent George Canning, of Irish parentage both by father and mother, had been en- trusted by the king with the task of forming a ministry the hopes of the Catholics rose higher and Metter than ever. As he was known to have become a warm friend to Emanci- pation, Wellington Peel, Eldon, and other Tory members of the Liverpool Cabinet refused to take office under him. However, he succeeded in forming a Cabinet which was upon the whole favourable to Emancipation—so much so that the great mass of the Irish people were in a state of the highest exultation. The popular feeling in Ireland was well ex- pressed by Shiel when, amid ringing cheers, he triumphantly exclaimed at a public meeting in Dublin—" Peel is Out; Bathurst is oat; Westmoreland is out; Wellington, the bad Irishman, is out; and, thanks be to God! the hoary cham- pion of every abuse, the venerable supporter of corruption in all its forms, the pious antagonist of every generous sen- timent, Eldon, procrastinating, canting, griping, whining, weeping, ejaculating, protesting money-getting and money- keeping Eldon is out. Better than ali,better than the presump- tion of Wellington, the narrow heartedness of Bathurst, the arrogance of Westmoreland, the ostentatious manliness and elaborate honesty of Mr. Peel—we have got rid of Lord Eldon's tears." But all these bright expectations that Can- ning would now enfranchise the Catholics of Ireland and Great Britain were destined to be rudely dashed to the earth by, the premature and melancholy death of that great and gene- rous statesman. Four months after he had been made Prime I Minister he retired to the residence of his friend the Duke of Devonshire, and there, under the noble cedars and among the lovely gardens of Chiswick, his mighty soul found rest. His death occasioned deep sorrow in Ireland. O'Connell pronounced an eloquent panegyric on the deceased states- man. Referring to the helping hand which he had extended to Greece and South America, struggling for freedom, he said :—" There is in struggling Greece many a gallant spirit that will long to demonstrate the sincerity of his grief for Canning's departure by sacrificing at his tomb whole heca- tombs of the enemies of Christianity. In South (Spanish) America too, in Mexico in Peru, in Chili, and in La Plata, and, more than all, in Mexico, his death be followed by mourning. The great, the immortal Bolivar will shed tears of bitter anguish; the sounds of sorrow will ascend to the summits of the Andes; and throughout all the nations of the earth the name of Canning will be consecrated in the grief of every worthy breest." Canning's Cabinet sui vived him a few months, with Lord Goderich at their head, but their inefficiency soon became evident, and on the 18th of January, 1828, after admitting four of Mr. Canning's friends into their ranks, the Tories resumed the reins of the Government, with the Duke of Wellington as Prime Minister and Mr. Peel as leader of the Howes of Commons, with the office of Home Secretary. While Mr. Canning was Prime Minister the Irish Catholics had made no noise, for they hoped in him and were careful not to hamper the good intentions of the Government by awakening popular alarm ; but as soon as they SAW the Tories once more at the head of affairs they renewed the conflict. The Catholic Association recommended its public meetings, its harangues, addresses, pamphlets, subscriptions, all its ardent and well-planned labours in order to arouse and dis- cipline the people in Ireland and in England to intimidate. its enemies and to encourage and recruit its partisans. It soon became evident to the less bigoted of the advisers of ' the Crown that Catholic Emancipation must be conceded. Ireland appeared on the verge of revolution. The whole mass of the people had been organised like a regular army, ' and taught to act with the most perfect unanimity. Adopt- ing a suggestion of Shiel, they were accustomed to assemble In every part of the county on the same day, and scarcely an adult Catholic abstained from the movement. In 1828, it was computed that on a single day 2,000 meetings were I held. Clearly the condition of things was too anomalous to last. To all who possessed even a moderate degree of politi- cal insight and discernment it was clear that either too leeech or too little had already been conceded to the munity. Too little had been —• to eatidy ; too much to allow the a' ambition Zatholic com- ambition to sleep of one day being able to extort the 'rest. So it had come to a choice betwixt two evilse--between the restoration of peace by granting the Catholic claims, or the inciting of civil war by resisting them. As Lord Anglesey, the Irish Viceroy put it. "there was no way of dealing with the Catholic organisation but by satisfying the demands of the Catholics." Bat an incident occurred which forced the hand of the Ministers. Mr. Vesey Fitzgerald, who represented the county of Clare, was the succe-lor of Mr. Grant as Presi- dent of the Board of Trade, and sought re-election. He had hardly bestowed a thought upon the contingency that his return might be opposed. He had always voted for Catho- lic Emancipation. He was popular as a landlord and magis- trate. By his property and connexions he possessed what was usually deemed a paramount influence in the county. So strong was his influence, indeed, that many members of the Catholic Association declined to recommend what they considered a more than doubtful experiment. But Shiel urged them to try the experiment. "They were arrived at a point when not to advance was to fall back. Their vie- tories in Waterford and Lowth had struck men with astonishment, but it was necessary that the sensation should be repeated, and for this something in itself more startling was requisite. They must show an increase of vigour. Vesey Fitzgerald must be seized with a gigantic grasp and hurled from the House of Commons. In such a cause it was impossible to stop. On! on! should be the maxim. They could not rest where they were. The seven millions must advance. What they had done would be of no avail unless they could do more. They had made great impres- sions, but these must not only be renewed but deepened. They must make men exclaim—This question must be settled else there is no limit to the consequences of such a condition of things." As several had declined to contest the election. O'Connell came forward and proceeded to can- vass. The Catholics in London held a meeting and sub- scribed funds, and the Rent in Ireland yielded what else was wanted. The excitement was prodigious. In every corner of the county of Clare there was such preaching and haranguing, that to the spectators it looked more like a Crusade than an Election. As Mr. Shiel said, "Every altar was a tribune." At length the day so long expected dawned upon the hills that rite on either side of the Fergus,and before the shades of night had passed away the hum of multitudes filled the air. From every part of the county the people came to witness the great trial of strength between the "political outlaw," who claimed to represent the feelings of the people, and the Minister who, supported by the whole aristocracy of the county, repre- sented the Government of the Bing. The most perfect order and sobriety prevailed. Intoxication was nowhere to be seen. A vow of self-denial had for the first time been unani- mously taken by the peasantry, and a sort of democratic police had been improvised, whose commands were implicitly obeyed. The polling commenced. Bands of forties, under the leadership of the priests, marched to record their vote

div.head: POLITICAL ITEMS.
div.p: POLITICAL ITEMS.

At a private meeting of Conservative electors of South Leicestershire, on Saturday, it was agreed to ask Major H. M. Curzon to contest the division at the next election, in conjunction with Mr. A. Pell.

A statement was published on Saturday that several gen- tlemen to whom the post of Liberal whip, lately vacated by Sir Arthur Hayter, had been offered, had declined it, on the groußd that they would not be certain of re-election. The statement is without fouedation, as is also the further state- ment that Mr. Richard Power had refused it for political reasons. The post has Rot been offered to that gentlemen.

div.head: FENIANISII IN LONDON. THREATENING MR. GLADSTONE AND THE HOME SECRETARY.
div.p: FENIANISII IN LONDON. THREATENING MR. GLADSTONE AND THE HOME SECRETARY.

The Right Hon. the Premier and the Right Hon. the Home Secretary have each received within the past fort- night a letter from a private source conveying to them in- formation of a most startling personal nature. The writer of the communication stated in his letter to the Prime Minister that having been present on the evening of May Bth (of this year) in a debating club in Bloomsbury, a large number of Irishmen of most advanced Nationalist opinions invaded the room, and took occasion during the time allowed for the discussion upon the subject of the evening— the appointment of Lord F. Cavendish to the Irish Chief Secretaryship—to air their peculiar crotchets with reference to the best means of absolutely freeing Ireland from British yoke. In the course of the proceedings one of those present exclaimed (the subject being then upon the Phoenix Park assassinations) "I hope old Gladstone will be the next !" [ts be assassinated]. The writer pointed out that these words were uttered with a very marked emphasis, and that although they might have been but a rri,?re jest, yet at the same.thne it became the right hon, gentleman to take all steps to secure his personal safety in the future. The writer also addressed upon the same day a letter to the Right Hon. the Home Secretary, stating the contents of the letter which he had addressed to the Prime Minister, awl_ urging the Home B,l2z:retaly to afford him all the protection necessary.

The immediate result of these communications was that in the case of the latter a formal aknowledgment of receipt was received from the private secretary to the Home Secre- tary; and in the former two detectives from Scotland-yard called at the residence of the writer two days after the re- ceipt of the letter, and had an interview with the writer. They asked him whether he had written to Mr. Gladstone concerning a threat upon his life, and if so, whether he would furnish them with particulars of place of meeting, description of the parties concerned, ,tc. As a result he made a short statement, which was written down by the seniar officer, and, having been read over and confirmed, the informant stated that he believed he had some lengthy memoranda of the proceedings in question in his posses- sion, which he would fotward to the authorities in the course of the next day. He stated at the same time that though the language concerned might have been merely "tall talk," yet at the same time it was the duty of the authorities to take cognisance of the matter.

div.head: PUBLIC MEN ON PUBLIC MATTERS.
div.p: PUBLIC MEN ON PUBLIC MATTERS.

Mr. Borlase, M.P., speaking at Wadebridge. on Tuesday, said, in view of the present state of Ireland, the Prevention of Crime Bill and the Arrears Bill were highly necessary measures. Should they not prove sufficient, he should not hesitate to apply still more stringent measures of repression. The Earl of Jersey, soaking at a gathering of Oxford- shire Conservatives on Wednesday evening, said the Arrears Bill was one of the most pernicious measures ever brought forward by a responsible Government. Sir J. Mowbray, M P., declared that the bill violated every principle of political economy and every rule of finance. At a meeting of Liberals of Scarborough, held on Wednes- day night, Mr. NV. S. Caine. M.P., presiding, a resolution was passed congratulating the Government on the firmness and wisdom displayed in adhering to a policy of remedial legislation in Ireland, and expressing an earnest hope that a measure to relieve tenants overwhAmed by arrears of rent would speedily be passed:

Mr. James Lowther, addressing a meeting of villagers in North Lincolnshire on Wednesday night, dwelt upon the adversities resulting from foreign competition. The right hon. gentleman told his agricultural friends that he cer- tainly thought, that if the production of corn of any kind was seriously menaced, it would to the duty of the Legisla- ture to take precautions against such a national calamity. Earl Cadogan, an ex-under secretary of the last Tory Ad- ministration, was one of the speakers on Tuesday night at a Conservative banquet at Stockton. He asserted that the dealing of the Government with Ireland was net an isolated case of misgovernment, but was "the natural outcome of the policy of Radicalism, a policy which pandered to the worst instincts of nations." 'Mr. J. Lowther condemned the foreign policy of the Government, and referring to Ireland he urged that no policy could be more mischievous than that which abstained from pointing out to the people of that country that, whether they liked it or not, their con- nection with this country must be maintained. He con- tended that the Irish policy of the late Government com- manded the unanimous support of the great mass of the Irish people. While they studied the interests, the aspira- tions, and the sentiments of the Irish people, they did not hesitate in their first duty of firmly administering the law. Lord Sandon, speaking at a banquet given to Mr. Salt, M.P., at Stafford, on Wednesday night, said the Conservatives would give ungrudging support to the Government in bring- ing beck Ireland to loyalty. The Coercion Act was needed as much for the protection of loyal people in Ireland as for the terror of sedition-mongers. Mr. Gladsthne's latest bill for Ireland was a startling one—namely, to pay out of the public funds arrears of rent; and they must remember that English taxes would ultimately be taken for the same pur- pose. Mr. Gladstone had also committed himself to the measures desired by the Home Rulers and Land Leaguers, and such legislation could only lead to the severance of the empire. The question ef Ireland was enormously important to the future or England. Mr. Gladstone had set forth his policy as one of no coercion, but he had to come to Parlia- ment, like previous Liberal Governments, for repressive ' powers. The Lend Act was represented as being for the advantage of landowners, but the effect was to render pro- perty insecure. Mr. Gladstone's policy on this question for twelve years had been hopelessly wrong, and they must look I with distrust on any legislation approved by Home Rulers I and Land Leaguers._ _ _

Mr. Gorst, M P., addressed a crowded meeting on Tuesday night, held in St. George's Hall, Burton-on-Trent, under the auspices of the Conservative Association. He said that when the present Government came into power they reversed the policy of Lord Beaconsfield, and because Lord Beacons- field had said that Ireland was in a dangerous condition Mr. Gladstone declared that Ireland had never been in a condi- tion of greater peace and prosperity. Outrage and murder followed, and Mr. Gladstone, in order to appease them, promised that if these outrages ceased the people of the country should be taxed for the benefit of the Irish tenants. At this time there was a Bill before Parliament which might become law unless the people of this country were aroused to oppose it; and what prevented that infamous treaty being brought into effect? It was the murder of Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Bnrke. These murders in no way changed the position of affairs in Ireland, but only showed that the Government's estimate of the position was entirely wrong. It was the duty of the constitutional party to leave no stone u'nturned until they had laid the true state of affairs before the country, and do their utmost to return to the old unostentatious line of Government undet which Enpland had become so free and great. Lord Henry Lennox, M.P., also addressed the meeting.

, Mr. Mundella, M.P., Vice-President or the Council, was present on Tuesday at a dinner to the Anglesey 400 given by Captain and Mrs. Verney. The right hon. gentleman, responding to the toast of Her Majesty's Government, took a brief survey of the political situation. Referring to Egypt, he said that the present difficulty arose from no fault of Mr. Gladstone's Government. They had done all, as would be found when the diplomatic correspondence came to be published, to maintain the interests and honour of this country. The policy they had pursued was that which they had inherited from their predecessors. It was the duty of this country as far as possible to act cordially with France and to preserVe the peace of Europe. Referring to home affairs, he said it was the duty of patriots of every party to sink party differences, to throw aside the spirit of faction and endeavour to restore to the House of Commons its old dignity and usefulness, and also to restore tranquility to Ireland. It was necessary that a complete change should be made in the rules of procedure of the House. He was of opinion that the demoralisation existing in the House of Commons had to a large extent caused the demoralisation which was so wide-spread in Ireland. Referring to the question of higher edncation in the Principality, Mr. Mun- delia said that the last official act of Earl Spencer, previous to his departure for Ireland, was to sign a document embodying the principles upon which this question should be dealt with; and he (Mr. Mundella) was only waiting for a suitable opportunity to introduce it into the House of of Commons. He indicated briefly what was needed in the Principality and what, we may presume, will be the features of the Government measure.

A bill was recently introduced in the Ohio Legislature to permit a Buckeye girl to change her name. The statesman who presented the bill was a bachelor, and an amendment was offered substituting his name for that which the young woman coveted. This measure was rashly adopted before she had been consulted. A motion to reconsider was there- fore deemed no more than fair to her, and she was au. thorised to take the name of her chtice. Nearly half a day was thus spent in legislative skylarking. THE STARFISH AND THE OYSTER.—The real mode by which the starfish attacks, opens, and devours the oyster is as follows :—First, the starfish clasps its arms round the oyster, so as to bring its mouth against the edges of the shells. It is able to hold itself firmly in its place by means of the ambulacra, each of which is a separate sucker. Then from the mouth it protrudes a series of vesicles, one cor- responding to each ray. These vesicles are never equal in size, some being as large as grapes, while the others scarcely equal peas in dimensions. E teh vesicle is attached to the animal by a footstalk. It is filled with a transparent fluid, and at its end is an apperture through which this fluid can be expressed. Whatever may be the nature of the contents of the vesiclee, it seems to have the power of penetrating be- tween the shells and paralysing the adductor muscles. The shells are thus forced to open, and the starfish then pushes the vesicles between them, and absorbs into its own diges- tive system the whole of the oyster except the adductor muscle.—Sunday Magazine.
