the Times says the negotiations between the Special Com- missioners and the members of the Burmese Embassy pro- ceed at Simla but slowly. The Indian Government, it is understood, requires that all trade monopolies, with the ex- ception of those on timber, earth, oil, and precious stones, shall be abolished for ever; that the Resident shall be en- titled to be received with all the marks of respect customary among Western nations; that his safety shall be guaranteed; and that all possible facilities shall be given to trade by a reduction of the obstructive Burmese duties, and byZa per- mission to open up new trade routes. The especial require- ment of the Burmese is permission to import arms and munitions of war; and to facilitate the effectual carrying out of the mutual obligation and agreements they propose the re- establishment of a Resident at Mandalay, and the resump- tion generally of amicable diplomatic relations. THE CROPS IN THE UNITED STATES.—Crop pruspects in the United States continue favourable, and the season is now so far advanced that an abundant harvest appears to be certain. According to the latest reports, the yield of cotton is confidently expected to exceed last year's crop, and may approximate the latgest known. The cold of May killed vermin, which might otherwise have injured winter wheat, and gave vigour to the straw, so that, though there is no increase in the area of the wheat crop, the yield is expected to be larger than that of ISBI. In Texas, the harvest has commenced; in the majority of the Southern States in will begie in June; and in the Northern latitudes it will not be later than July. Spring wheat is a full crop, and promises to surpass last year's but it is a fortnight late. Considering the effect of an abundant harvest has upon national industry and prosperity, better days in the United States should not be far distant. AWFUL BKRBARITY.—Many stories of ferocious barbarity have come from Burmah since King Thebo began to rule at Mandalay, but none more revolting than that of the murder of a young queen to satisfy the vindictive jealousy of a rival. Thebo, although called king and blamed for the massacres that have taken place, is less the ruler of Burmah than the Chief Queen Soopayahlat, and recently, when Soopayahlat was indisposed, the king had the temerity to favour a new queen. When Soopayahlat recovered, however, she gave the king no peace until he consented that the new queen should be beaten with rods, and no sooner was consent given than this fiendish woman had her victim brought forth and beaten to death in her presence. Then, to prevent the story getting abroad, she cast into prison every one who knew of the crime. So terrible is the terrorism at Mandalay that it is described as a city of the dead, and every man stands in fear of his neighbour. AFFAIRS IN ZULULAND. John Dunn is on exceedingly unsatisfactory terms with his subordinate chiefs. The Pietermaritzburg correspondent of the Daily News, in a telegram sent off on Monday, says that Dunn having summoned his chiefs to assemble, they refused, but named a day when they were going to meet the British Resident, and told him to be present if he had any- thing to say to them. A lrrge meeting: of chiefs and head- men has been held in Dunn's district to consider the action to be taken against him. "The situation is highly critical, and 93110 US bloodshed might occur at any moment," though the correspondent believes the Zulus will be slow to begin.

PROPOSED REFORMS IN RUSSIA. Advices received at Berlin from St. Petersburg state that , the Emperor being desirous of entering upon a policy of conciliation has determined to organise a series of reforms. To this end commissions have been appointed to inquire into the expediency of developing a system of local institutions, the question of central institutions, and the share to be granted to the people in the administration of the country. Count Louis Melikoff is placed at the bead of these three commissions. An Imperial manifesto will shortly be issued, declaring that His Majesty desires to celebrate the day of his coronation by the granting of reforms. The Emperor has, however, postponed the ceremony till May next year, on account of the impossibility of completing the necessary preparations before that date. THE HERZEGOVINA REVOLT. The Vienna journals announce that the Austrian head- quarters at Ragusa are about to be broken up, the Crivoscian movement being considered as finally crushed." The grants for the necessiry expenses of the army in Bosnia and the Herzegovina have been passed by the Hungarian Parlia- ment after severe opposition. The Pesth correspondent of the Standard says that after a debate which occupied eleven days the Lower House sanctioned the grant which has been agreed to by the Hungarian Delegation in the last extraor- din try session for the suppression of the insurrection, and both the Opposition parties had moved a resolution in favour of the evacuation of Bosnia. " The debates," he says, "have been very passionate, and in the course of the discussions the party of independence frequently insulted not only the Government and the majority, but also the House of Haps- burg and the Austrian army in the most disgraceful manner. 'The party in question intends during the summer to stir up the passions of the Magyar population against the occupation of Bosnia, and, if possible, to force the Austrian troops to evacuate it.' THE ALLEGED MASSA.CRE OF 200 GIRLS. A correspondent of the West African Reporter, writing from Cape Coast Castle on the Bth April, stttes that little importance is to be attached to the denial of Prince Ansah of the reported massacre of 200 girls by the King of Ashan- tee. "Prince Ansah," the writer says, "it is welt known is an Ashantee by birth and a prince of the Royal blood, and it is impossible that he should be expected to give the true version of a case which he knew very well would reflect dis- credit on himself and country. We have no reason to doubt the truthfulness of the whole matter as it stands against that Moodthirsty monarch; and Sir Samuel Rowe, in inquiring into the truthfulness of it, ought to have tried to gain his information from other sources than from people who were ' in every way connected with the King. It is to be hoped that Captain Lonsdal›, in his present visit, has been • authorised to inquire fully into this matter."

div.head: EGYPTIAN QUESTION. SERIOUS COMPLICATIONS: INTERVENTION VECESSARY.
div.p: THE EGYPTIAN QUESTION. SERIOUS COMPLICATIONS: INTERVENTION VECESSARY.

The representatives of England and France presented, on Thursday week, an ultimatum to the Ministry a Cairo de- manding the temporary exile of Ourabi Pasha and the re- tirement of two of his colleagues, under pain of interven- tion by force of arms. On Friday the Ministers sent in their resignation to the Khedive, at the same time protesting that he had by admitting the intervention of the Western Powers infringed the sovereign rights of the Sultan. The Khedive sent for Cherif Pasha, the former Premier, and 1 steps were taken to form a Government, but the military party showed no inclination to submit. On Saturday they held a meeting, and resolved to demand of the Khedive the retention of Ourabi Pasha as War Minister, and the final rejection of the Anglo-French ultimatum. Tewfik refused to give way, and summoned the heads of the ecclesiastical and military establishments to his presence. He informed them of his intention to follow the advice given by the Powers, whereupon the Ulemas and officers " precipitately " quitted his presence, and subsequently sent in an ultimatum of their own, but stopped short of decreeing the deposition of their Sovereign. Great excitement prevailed on Sunday at Cairo and Alexandria. In the latter city, the European residents were told that their embarkation would, if neces- sary, be protected by the guns of the combined fleet, but no immediate danger Yens apprehended. It would be impossible, of course, for the fleet to prevent mischief being done if the garrison were to give way to an impulse of fanaticism. The Khedive also assumed by proclamation supreme command of the troops. The following official statement was issued on Sunday evening :—" At five o'clock to-day all the Ulemas of El Azhar University, the whole Chamber of Notables, numerous Arabic notabilities, and a body of native merchants came to the Palace to pray the Khedive to take back Ourabi Pasha as Minister of War,because the army insisted on that course, and menaced them if the Khedive should insist on refusing ,to reinstate him. In consequence of the reiterated entrea- ties of these representatives of the people, the Khedive de- sirous of the maintenance of order and tranquility in the country, has acceded to their prayer by reinstating Ourabi Pasha as Minister of War." Before being restored to power Ourabi Pasha gave assurances to the diplomat!c agents of Germany, Austria, Italy, and Russia, who declared that they held him responsible for public security. The assurance which Ourabi gave to the Consuls has up to the present been fulfilled; but amongst European resi- dents in Egypt panic prevails, and the Christian population generally is either leaving the country altogether or moving to Alexandria, where the. warships ensure them a certain amount of protection. Ourabi, who is master of the situa- tion, is said to be spreading a statement to the effect that Hallo) Pasha has been nominated Khedive by the Sultan. His subardinates, too, are busily engaged in compelling peo- ple to sign a petition to the Sultan praying for the reinstate- ment of the late Ministry, the withdrawal of the ultimatum and of the fleet, the recall of the English and French diplomatic agents, and the deposition of the Khedive in favour of an Egyptian Prince. The Powers are moving, if not with inconsiderable speed at least in coucert and with decision. Neither England nor France threatens to intervene in. Egypt; both are resolved to maintain the sovereign rights of the Sultan and the authority of the Khedive. The Porte wishes to intervene in Egypt, and the Powers are willing that it should do so in a form which they strictly define—namely, by making a declaration in favour of the Khedive, stating that in dismiss- ing his Ministers and following th e advice of the Powers he did not act contrary to the Sultan's wishes, and summoning Ourabi Pasha and other military leaders to Cohstantinople. This is not at all what the Porte desired; its wish was to in- tervene in Egypt, but not from Constantinople. The repre- sentatives of Germany, Austria Russia, and Italy, however, recommended acceptance of the Anglo-French demands ; and if Turkish intervention is to take place it 1 must be within the limits the Powers prescribe. Meanwhile the combined squadrons at Alexandria are to be strengthened. We have as yet no definite information as to the course which the Sultan has resolved to take, but it is said that the Porte is opposed to the despatch of Turkish ships to Alexandria so long as the combined squadrons remain in Egyptian waters. The reports from Cairo repre- sent the Khedive as being in imminent danger from the revolted soldiery if he continues firm in his present course The correspondent of the Times at Cairo, telegraphing on Wednesday, warns the Powers that "no time is to be lost in employing measures for saving the life of the Khedive, compared to which danger to public order here is of small importance. There is no Englishman nor Frenchman here who does not regard the present position of affairs as a national disgrace. The expectation that the simple presence of the fleets would be likely to produce any effect creates amazetnent, and a fear that a similar dangerous blunder may be made with regard to the Turkish mission."
A poor woman who has been driven insane by the Plmeilix Park murders was on Wednesday admitted into a Dublin lunatic asylum.

div.head: EXAMINER _SATURDAY, JUNE 3, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER _SATURDAY, JUNE 3, 1882.
ISCELLANEOUS.

Sir Charles Legard has returned 15 per cent of the half- year's rents to his tenants on the Ganton and other estates. A woman named Murray died on Monday, in Glasgow, from injuries inflicted by her Eon. She had refused him money for drink. At a meeting held at Truro, on Tuesday, it was reported that the subscriptions towards the new Cornish Cathedral amounted to over £50,000, about :£41,000 of which has been

paid. An official contradiction is given to the statement which has been published to the effect that a marriage has been arranged between Princess Beatrice and Prince William of Hesse. • At Arbroath, on Monday, William Tomlins, captain Salva- tion Army, was fined 403., and George Topping 205., for a breach of the peace by holding a procession. Two men who molested the Salvationists were fined 20s. and 30s. respec- tively. Mr. John George Shepbard, of Campsey Ash, Suffolk, died somewhat sullenly at his London residence, Eaton- place. early on Sunday morning. The deceased gentleman was deputy-lieutenant and J.P. of the county of Suffolk, and served as foreman of the jury in the celebrated Tichborne trial. Two young girls were drowned in the Lea, on Monday afternoon, through the capsizing of a boat. Our laws, which require that a cab driver shall be licensed, at present permit any incompetent man or boy to take out a number of per- sons on to deep water, with the strong probability of a fatal result, as in this case. The Right Hon. John David Fitzgerald, one of the justices of the Queen's Bench Division in Ireland, has been appointed Lord of Appeal in ordinary. Lord Fitzgerald has been Solicitor General and Attorney General for Ireland, and was raised to the judicial bench 22 years ago. Judgement was given on Tuesday at Hull in the Board of Trade inquiry concerning the loss of the Dundee steamer White Sea by collision with the Alfgar. The Court decided that the White Sea was in fault, and its master's certificate- was suspended for three months, a mate's certificate being granted him meantime because of his excellent character. I Thomas Taylor was charged before the Clitheroe magis- trates on Monday with having committed a violent assault on a policeman. On Saturday night the prisoner was fighting with another man. A policeman interfered, where- upon the prisoner violently attacked the constable and kicked him savagely. The officer sustained serious injury. Taylor was sentenced to six months' imprisonment with hard labour. Sir Wilfred Lawson, M.P., writes to a gentleman in Arbroath :—" These frequent outrages on the Salvation Army are most disgraceful. Ido not see what is to be done to improve matters as long as the riotous portion of the com- munity are virtually protected by the authorities instead of being checked by them. We must hope that public opinion may ere long compel those who ought to keep the peace to take a more creditable course." At the Salford Police Court, on Monday, a young man named William Gannon was committed for trial for stab- bing Mary Doyle, with whom he was keeping company. On Saturday they went for a walk and quarrelled, and he pushed her into a passage and abused her very severely. She screamed, and then he knocked her down and cut her throat with a pocket-knife A surgeon stated that she had had a narrow escape of her life. A bank engine, which was assisting a heavily laden ex- cursion train up an incline from Oswestry to Ellesmere shortly after noon on Monday, left the rails and was dragged for about half a mile, tearing up the chairs, sleepers, and permanent way very badly. The driver and stoker were thrown off, and the passengers in the last carriage of the excursion train were much shaken, but no serious injuries were sustained, and the traffic was little delayei: At Seaforth, on Tuesday, the memorial stone was laid of a new Congregational school, which is intended to be used also as a chapel until the congregation is strong enough to erect a church. That the pres:nt building can now be put up at a cost of £1,500 is indicative of the progress that has been made during the four years that have elapsed since a chapel was opened in Seatorth under the auspices of the Waterloo Congregational Chapel. The foundation stone was laid by Mr. Lee, M.P. SAD ACCIDENT TO SCHOOL CHILDREN.—A sad accident occurred at Accrington on Monday afternoon. The Baptist scholars were marching in Trocession to a field, and were followed by a horse and cart laden with forms for the use of the scholars. When in a narrow lane the horse took fright, and two children in the rear of the procession were knocked down. One of them, a girl named Ashworth, had the calf of her leg taken off, and the other, a boy named Wadworth, had his shoulder dislocated. The girl was dangerously injured. Severalothers had a narrow escape. The accident naturally created intense excitement. THE LATH MR. MACDONALD, M.P.—The Press Associa- tion understands that the movement for the erection of a memorial to the late Mr. A. Macdonald, M.P., has been tar- dily responded to throughout the country, the chief cause ascribed being the circulation of a report that Mr. Mac- donald had left a sum of £50,000, besides large areas of land. The former statement is denied by the Miners' National Union, and it is stated that all the land he possessed con- sisted of a few acres at WellLall, his residence in Scotland. A series of cases of brutal assaults on women were before the Manchester and Salford magistrates on Tuesday. At the City Police Court there were three such cases, and in two of them the wives of the prisoners were the victims. Two of the prisoners were remanded, and the third was sen- tenced to six months' imprisonment with bard labour. The Salford Stipendiary also sent a man to gaol for six months for kicking his wife on the head, face, and body; and the Salford police on Tuesday apprehended another man on a charge of wounding his wife by cutting her throat. His Excellency, Mr. Spencer Walpole, the newly ap- pointed Governor of the Isle of Man, paid a visit to Peel on Monday. Ho was received by a large crowd and the high bfiliff at the railway station, and a procession was formed to the school which was presented to the town by the Cloth workers' Company of London. An address was bere pre- sented to his Excellency, to which he made a suitable reply. The Governor then witnessed a practice by the recket brigade, after which he went over the ancient castle and the harbour works in progress. THE COLLIERY ACCIDENT IN WARWICKSHIRE.—The number of deathe from the recent disaster at Baxterley Colliery, Warwickshire' . has now been augmented to 31, the latest victim being Mr. Barker, manager of the colliery, who was one of the ill-fated exploring party. Much importance was attached to the evidence Barker was likely to. give as to the cause of the explosion. The nine colliers and eleven horses that were in the workings when the explosion oc- curred are still entombed. They have now been in the pit nearly a month, and although the fire is hell wed to be nearly out, it is feared some weeks will elapse before further attempts can be made to recover the bodies. The relief fund has reached between £3,000 and £4,000. GROUSE rROSPECTS.—It is a long time yet until the 12th of August, but already reports are coming from the Scotch moors as to the condition of grouse, and, unfortunately, they are not of a satisfactory kind. Unmistakeable signs of disease, it is said have shown themselves, especially in the counties of Perth, Inverness, and Ross; and, considering the very mild winter that we have had, there is much perplexity as to what can be the cause of the mysterious -ailment. On previous occasions it has been attributed to excessive frost and excessive wet, but this season there has been neither the one nor the other, and yet the disease is there, and is as inexplicable as pink-eye in horses or the malady that attacks salme.n. SUNDAY SCHOOL PROCESSION AT MANCHESTER. The Whitsuntide procession of Sunday schools connected with the Church of England in Manchester took place on Mon- day, and, favoured by beautiful weather, proved very suc- cessful. The scholars assembled in Albert Square between half-past eight and half-past nine. The muster has never probably been so large. It was estimated that over 20,000 children and teachers were present. Upon a balcony in front of the Mayor's Parlour, in the presence of the schools, an address was presented to Mr. Alderman W. Booth, the treasurer, whose connection with the procession dates back for half a century. Subsequently the children sang two stanzas of the National Anthem, led by the band of Cheet- ham Hospital. and then left the square in precessional order. Leaving by Princess-street, the procession went along Mosley-street, Market-street, and Market Place to Old Millgate. From this point a number of the schools went to the Cathedral, where a special service was held, others pro- ceeding to their resptctive districts. THE ROTHERHAM MURDER Cs.—The Rotherham police have obtained an important witness, whose evidence will form another link in the chain of evidence already secured against the men now in custody. The man's name is Charles Nuttall, of Awkley, near Doncaster. He was for- merly a farmer, and on the night of the murder returned from York market with several beasts, having a large sum' of money in his pockets. Just before the murder he had been in company with Whittaker, and says that the men whom he supposes were the murderers followed him some distance. Oee of the cattle ran up a by lane, and on follow- ing it he came to an inn, where he put up for the night. Some time after two or three men came in, one being about 17 years of age, but they left rather speedily on seeing Nuttall. The latter has a most distinct recollection of these circumstances, and affirms that be could now swear to the men if he were to see them. He has seen one of the men on more than one occasion and the man has alvays got away as soon as possible.—Seedham and Siddell were further re- manded on Monday. Seedbam has made a confession incul- pating Siddell and two other men since dead. Mut-name OF A TRAMP.—Amidst Whitsuntide festivities the town of Wareham, in Dorset, was on Monday thrown into a state of great excitement by the report of a man having been murdered in the public thoroughfare in broad daylight. It appears that two persons named Dennis Riley and Henry Wright, have been in the company of each other for the past fortnight, getting their living by hawking and sinng songs about the recent assassinations in Ireland. On Monday they visited Corfe Castle, having travelled from Wareham, where they stayed Saturday and Sunday. Having sung through the streets they were proceeding to Swanage, but, when going out of the town, they quarrelled, and Wright was beard to say that be would do for his companion by and by. He then gave Riley one or two heavy blows, knocking him do en, and Riley remained on the ground some time. Wright went on for a short distance, and then waited for his mate. On the deceased getting up to him he asked for his share of the money, and the deceased, who was the worse for liquor, would not give up any. Wright then proceeded to a wall, and took off a stone of about 141 b. weightand returned. As Riley was lying down, with his hand under his face, Wright proceeded to strike him on the back of the head. literally beating it to pieces. Wright was afterwards' secured by two persons who were near, and handed over to the police. The deceased died within ten minutes of the in- juries being inflicted,

The Royal University of Ireland has at last obtained a habitation, the Senate having purchased the stone-built por- tion of the Dublin Exhibition Palace. There has been a contest at Handsworth, near Birrning- ham, on the question of school board or no sch.ol board, and the negative was resolved on by 1,200 votes to 754. The Cambridge University Union on Tuesday night passed a resolution by 102 votes to 68 "that the present Government no longer deserves the confidence of the country." The York Chamber of Agriculture at their last meeting passed a resolution approving of Mr. Ckaplin's bill to com- pensate tenants for unexhausted improvements, with certain modifications. A considerable portion of thelnfantry Barracks at Penally, near Tenby, at present occupied by the 23rd Royal Welsh Fusiliers, has been destroyed by fire. The cause of the fire is unknown. At a meeting held in the Dublin Mansion House on Saturday, it was agreed, to meet the views of the promoters of the proposed industrial exhibition, to unveil the O'Con- nell monument and open the exhibition the same day—the 15th of August next. At Bridport, on Saturday, Henry Alfred, seed farmer, Fishpond Bottom, Dorset, was committed for trial on a charge of the manslaughter of Levi Bridle, his tenant, with whom he quarrelled respecting some land, and struck him with a large stick, and, it is alleged, caused his death. The members of the Curates' Alliance have resolved to " boycott " the sale of advowsons wherever such a course may be practicable. At a meeting on Saturday the members placed on record their "grave sense of the injuty to religion caused by the traffic in sacred trusts." A large quantity of Roman coins has been discovered near the Ham Hill Quarries, Yeovil, by a labourer who was ex- cavating. The coins are in a good state of preservation, and date from A.D. 81 to 182. The spot where the dis- covery was made was at one time a Roman camp of observa- tion, and overlooks Sedgmoor. Captain Schwensen, commander of the Hamburg liner Westphalia, has just completed his three hundredth voyage across the Atlantic, and on his arrival at Plymouth be was presented, on behalf of a number of bankers and merchants of London, with a memorial of so rare an event in the dangerous profession he follows. An alarming accident occurred on Saturday on the Wrex- ham, Mold, and Connah's Quay Railway. In descending an incline a train acquired a terrific speed. The enginemen and guard jutnped off, and all escaped except the driver, who had his head badly cut. The train ultimately ran against an embankment, and the waggons were overturned. The Bishopric of Newcastle has been sc nferred upon the Rev. Ernest Wilberftorce' Canon of Winchester, and Sub- Almoner to the Qthen. Mr. Wilberforce, who is a son of the late Bishop Wilberforce, held before his appointment to the Canonry of Winchester the living of Seafcrth, near Liverpool, to which he was presented by Mr. Gladstone. As Mr. Justice Bowen and his wife were the other after- neon driving in a carriage and pair from their residence at Warninglio, near Hayward's Heath, Brighton, to Cuckfield, one of the horses became restive, and the carriage pole snapped. The carriage itself ran upon the footpath and was nearly overturned. The horse was then secured, and Mr. and Mrs. Bowen escaped with a slight shaking. The authorities have received information warranting the adoption of stringent precautions to guard the vast powder magazine at Purfleet, probably the largest storehouse of the kind in the world. Troops were sent to the spot as soon as the hint was given that mischief was intended, and they remain vigilantly on the alert. No one believes that it would be possible to carry out a design of blowing up the magazine, but the authorities do not intend to leave anything to chance in so serious a matter.

A meeting of delegates of the Democratic Federation from all parts of the kingdom was held at Westminster, on Wed- nesday, Mr. Hyndman presiding. A resolution was proposed to add to the programme the establishment of a British republic. Considerable opposition, however, was raised, and ultimately an amendment in favour of the abolition of the House of Lords was carried by a majority of three. Disestablishment of the Church was also added to the pro- gramme. Sir H. Brand was one of the guests of the Crystal Palace Company at a banquet on Saturday in celebration of the splendid Electrical Light Exhibition. The Speaker, in returning thanks for a toast in honour of the House of Com- mons, said there had never been a house more disposed to do justice to Ireland, "notwithstanding the trials imposed upon it by the enemies of order." Sir W. Thomson said that what his native country wanted was the spread of varied forms of industry, "and he saw one patch of blue sky in the com- mencement of the first electrical railway in the United King- dom of Great Britain and Ireland at Portrusb." SHOCKING DEATH OF A "STEEPLE JACK."—A Leicester "Steeple Jack," named William Daybel, has just met with a shocking death. On Monday he excited general attention by giving the Prince and Princess of Wales a demonstrative welcome from the top of St. Mark's Church. The following evening he was illuminating one of the high devices on the Belgrave Gate when he slipped, and, failing to catch the piping to save himself, fell head forward on the pavement beneath. His skull was terribly fractured, and he died at the Infirmary on Wednesday. In Holy Trinity Church, Windsor, a handsome window has been placed as a memorial of the escape of Her Majesty from assassination. The central panel consists of a queenly female figure, crowned, sitting upon a throne, and holding a sceptre and wreath, while an angel is shielding her from Death, who, bearing in one hand a lighted torch, clutches with the other a sword, which is breaking to pieces. The inscription is, "To the glory of God and in grateful corn- memoration of the merciful deliverance of Her Gracious Majesty Queen Victoria on the 2nd March, 1882." STEEL FROM STAFFORDSHIRE IRON.—On Wednesday, it was made known on 'Change in Wolverhampton that the new Basic-Bessemer process of making steel had proved successful with common Staffordshire iron as the material. A committee of ironmasters, assisted by Mr. Thomas, one of the inventors, has conducted the experiments with striking success. A bar of the steel, one Inch broad by half an inch thick, was rolled, and then put under a heavy sledge hammer and doubled up, vet without breaking. Another portion was broken and reweided, and was then bent in the weld, but it manifested no indication of friction. THE Dux ECHT OUTRAGE.—According to an Aberdeen correspondent, there is not a word of truth in the rumour circulated by some of Saturday's papers that the desecrators of the vault at Dun Echt had returned the body of the late Earl to the place from which it was stolen, that the whole mystery had been revealed, and that certain parties who had not hitherto been suspected were implicated in the outrage. The absurdity of the report is the more evident from the fact that, since the removal of the body was discovered, the place has been under the sttictest watch by day and night, and it would be impossible to replace the remains in the vault.

SALVATION ARMY EXTREMES.-011 Saturday, the Mayoi of Salisbury was waited upon by a captain of the loca branch of the Salvation Army, who sctually upbraided his worship for not haying been present at his harangues in the square on Friday,- to personally protect him from the violence of the mob. The officer remarked that his blood would be upon his head, and interposed vigorous ejacula- tions to the Deity. Whatever the consequences, he said he should carry out the instructions of " General " Booth. His worship who conceived himself insulted, has with the advice of the magistracy, decided to call attention to an advice prohibiting the processions, and it that is disobeyed, to proceed summarily. The magistrates are, it is stated, arged to this step by the inhabitants. POURING OIL ON TROUBLED WATERS.—The River Tyne Commissioners are about to erect in connection with the harbour .work, now being carried out at Tynernouth a num- ber of oil tanks, so that oil can, when necessary, be used to prevent the sea breaking against the North Pier at the en- trance to the river. The successful experiment recently made with this agency for subduing the violence of the waves has led to the adoption of this arrangement. Some interest- ing experiments have been made at Dungeness Point as to the effect of throwing oil upon the waters. The result was that round the boat a considerable stretch of still water was produced, against which the breaking wasyes are said to have fallen dead, and passed by in a harmless roll. ROYAL VISIT TO YArtmotyree—On Wednesday, the new 'Town Hall in Yarmouth was opened by the Prince of Wales. The streets were decorated and thronged with people. The Prince was received at the hall by the Mayor, and presented with a silver key, with which he unlocked the door. An ad- dress was then presented, to which his Royal Highness briefly responded. Luncheon followed, at which the Prince was supported hy the Mayor and Earl of Aylesford, and, after the usual loyal toasts, the proceedings terminated. Sub- sequently the Prince left for Shaddinefield amidst enthusi- astic popular demonstrations. It was understood that during the afternoon he would drive over to Somerleyton Hall, the residence of Sir J. Crossley, and in the evening attend the pet formance of the Gaiety Company at the Aquarium. PROGRESS AT READING.—A new Town Hall, Free Library, Reading Room, and School of Science and Art, costing about £60,000, were opened at Reading on Wednee- day, by Mr. Walter, M.P., who delivered ah inaugural ad- dress, referring pat ticularly to the importance of public libraries and science and art classes. He declared himself satisfied now they had a building worthy of the reception of works of art, that private gifts would sueplement their efforts in increasing its attractions, and in thus raising the moral and social condition of the people. At the luncheon, Mr. Shaw Lefevre, M.P., responded for the Houses of Par- liament, saying when the House of Commons had strangled the bores and smothered obstruction it would be able to carry on its work successfully. DREADFUL MURDER AT FULITA3L—A party, consisting of a woman named Line Keyson Sykes, of Fulham, a man named Wells, who occasionally, if not usually, resided at the same house as Mrs. Sykes, and another man named Frederick Carlisle, went to Epsom on Friday, and at night returned to the house at Fulham, where the men while drinking whisky and water seem to have quarrelled about the woman, and to settle matters they went out into the back garden and had a very rough fight. The police were sent for, but the men ma-de up their difference, and both were left in the house. Later in the evening however, they quarrelled again,and just as a policeman got to the door, Carlisle staggered down the steps and fell into his arms, declaring that Wells, who was at the door, had "stabbed him this time." In a few minutes Carlisle died, and it was found that he had been twice stabbed in the back. Wells, of course, was arrested, and on the house being searched a carving knife with bloed upon it was found. Nothing is known as to the character or position of any of these persons; but Mrs. Sykes, who says she is living apart from her husband, states that she has known the prisoner for sixteen or eighteen months, and that he introduced Carlisle to her. The house is described as a very quiet one.

Thursday being the third anniversey of the Prince Im- perial's death, a solemn mars was celebrated at Chiselharst in the presence of the Empre3s Eugenie. The marriage of Margaret, the second daughter of Sir Stafford Northcote, with Mr. Frederick Shelly, of Shobrooke Park, Crediton, took place on Thursdayaat Upton Pvne. A collier, named Gratton, was on Thursday, at i'unstall, sentenced to 21 days' hard labour for smoking in a gaseous seam in the Chell Colliery, North Staffordshire, in which only safety lamp lights are allowed. It was shown that the prisoner lighted his pipe by sucking the light .through the gauze of his lamp. Thera was a serious fight in Manchester on Thursday night between some soldiers of the 103rd Regiment and the police. The latter were called upon to remove the soldiers from a tramcar. They resisted, and a desperate struggle ensued. Finally, two soldiers were carried to the police station. A Stockholm telegram says :—The poor-house in the small town of Oesthammar has been set on fire by lightning and burnt to the ground. Out of 52 inmates, 20 perished in the flames. Before closing their session at Chester on 'Wednesday, the National Order of the Sons of Temperance passed a resolution in which a hope was expressed that the Premier would deal with the licensing laws in the spirit of the local option resolution twice affirmed by the House of Commons. An extraordinary story comes from Shetland of an en- counter which a crew of a fishing beat are reported to have had with a sea monster, said to be about 150 feet in length and which was supposed to be a species of giant cuttle fish or octopus. Replying to a resolution from Limerick, asking him to allow the erection of huts for evicted tenants on the Clon- curry estate, the Lord-Lieutenant writes :—" Proceedings were taken to prevent the erection, as the huts were intended for intimidation. An appeal from the magistrates is now pending, and must take its course." Writing to the Dublin Express, Colonel King Harman denounces the Irish members who, calling themselves Con- servatives on the hustings, flock into the Radical lobbies,l and says it is only right and honest that those members who prefer to vote with the Radicals, or who are afraid to vote with the Conservatives for fear of losing their seats, should take their places in the House with those whose principles they endorse. Mr. John Bright, lord rector of Glasgow University, has offered a prize of 25 guenias for the best essay on "The Influence on the Italian Republic on the Civilisation of Europe." The Glasgow University students of the last three sessions will be entitled to participate in the cone- petition. The returns of metropolitan pauperism issued on Wednes- day morning show that during the second week of May 49,581 indoor and 39,662 outdoor paupers were relieved, making a total of 89,243, against 89,059 in the correspon- ding week of last year, 86,278 in 1880, and 83,448 in 1879. The number of vagrants relieved was 839. The Mayor of Cardiff, accompanied by Sir E. J. Reed, M.P., on Wednesday, declared the new Free Library build- ing open. The Cost of erection has been £9OOO. Among the contributors to the Art Gallery was the late Mr. Menelaus, whose gifts represented a monetary value of £lO,OOO, while Sir E. R. Reed, M.P., has given a picture worth £lOOO. The Hartley magistrases, on Wednesday, committed a man named Hicleton to gaol for two months, with an additional six months in default of finding sureties, for ill-treating his wife. The prisoner had literally starved his wife till she became fearfully emaciated, and after beating her a few days ago he kicked her with his heavy clogs and turned her out of doors. He had previously sold all his household furni- ture, excepting a cradle and an old bed. The Alhambra Music Hall at Sheffield was destroyed by fire on Thursday morning. It broke out shortly before four o'clock, and in spite of the utmost exertions of the fire brigade the flames could not be extinguished till the whole of the building was destroyed, together with two shops on the ground floor. The damage amounts to many thousand pounds. The origin of the fire is unknown. The hall was used nightly. On Tuesday, the wife of a Jew, named Rossesson, who has taken up his abode in Accrington, returned from Poland, bringing with her two boxes of cigars as a present for her husband. The man did not smoke the cigars, but was found hawking them on Wednesday, and Was brought before the magistrates on Thursday morning for selling them without a license. Oct the applicatioa of the Inland Revenue Officer, the defendant was discharged, for proceedings to be taken by summons. Margaret Hogarth, barmaid to a Liverpool publican, was taxed on Wednesday with dishonesty by her employer who threatened to call in a policeman. The girl, however, pro- tested her innocence, but she was shortly afterwards missed from the bar. Search was made and she was found in her bedroom on her knees with a terrible gash in her throat, evidently inflicted with a large' carving knife which lay by her side. She was taken to the hospital and her wounds were attended to, but she is in a critical condition. The Blackburn borough magistrates on Thursday com- mitted Thomas Dean, labourer, to prison for three months for deserting his wife and four children on May 6, 1881 The prisoner eloped with a married woman, who had only been con6ned a week previously, and his family became chargeable to the union, and received thirteen guineas in relief. The bench, characterising it as a very shameful case of desertion and immorality, refused to allow a settle- ment. The will (dated March 2, 187) of Sir Pierre Louis Napo- leon Cavagnari, K.C.8., C. 5.1., who died on September 3 last, at Cabul, has been proved in London by Dame Mercy Emma Cevagnari, the widow and sole executrix, to whom he leaves all his estate and effects. The personal estate in British India exceeds Rs, 50,000, and in this country amounts to about £3so.—lllastrated Loudon Yews. . From New York comes the following telegram :—The threatened strike of the iron and steel workers commenced on Wednesday in Pennsylvania. Twenty-six mills were shut. The movement is spreading to Ohio, West Virginia, Missouri, and Kentucky. At present fully 50,000 men are out of employment, more than 18,000 being on strike in the Pittsburg district alone. Both manufacturers and workmen have taken up a firm attitude, and it is expected that the struggle will be a long one. The Skye land agitation is again assuming a serious aspect, following the Glendale tenants' action in forcibly removing stock from Watterstein Hill, grazing and occupy- ing it with their sheep. An attempted ejectment and deforcement is reported from Loch Carron. Two crofters were served with removal summonses by an officer, two assistant police, sergeant and constable. One crofter de- clined to leave. His effects, were, however, removed. An excited multitude, including a hundred men accompanied by a piper, collected and attacked the officers, compelling them to retire. The effects were replaced, and after vainly waiting for the officers to return with reinforcements the crowd dispersed. A telegram from Paris, on Thursday, says:—The French Government has made a proposal, which has been ac- cepted by England, for the assemblage of a Conference of Ambassadors at Constantinople upon the Egyptian question. It is expected that the invitations to the Powers will be despatched to-day, and that the Conference will meet very shortly. A telegram from Cairo also on Thursday states : The proposal for a conference of Ambassadors at Constanti- nople causes great consternation among the European popu- lace, being regarded as an indication of delay in the final settlement of the Ee;vptian question. The native papers El Alava and El 21fahraussa have been suspended for one month by order of Ourabi Pasha, on the ground of having publialled articles endangering the maintenance of public tranquility. THREATENING THE DUKE OF WESTMINSTER.—A corres- pondent telegraphs that some excitement has been caused in Cheshire by a report that since his return to London the Duke of Westminster has been the recipient of a threatening letter. Letters have also been received by several of his grace's servants, advising them to leave the employment at once, as at a recent meeting of a secret brotherhood it was ' resolved, on a certain date, to blow up Grosvenor House. Although little importance is attached to the anonymous missives, the authorities are on the alert, and it has been considered advisable to take precautions. The affair, how- ever, is regarded more in the light of an attempt to boycott his grace than to do serious injury. The receipt of such letters by so excellent and well-disposed a nobleman as the Duke of Westminster has given rise to a great deal of dis- content and alarm in the minds of other residents in the. West-end of London. NEW COUNTY SESSIONS COURT FOR LIVERPOOL.—The Earl of Derby on Thursday laid the foundation stone of a new County Sessions Court in Liverpool, and he took ad • vantage of the occasion to make an interesting speech on the subject of county administration. His Lordship said he did not believe that there was any desire for the abolition of the unpaid magistracy; but though he himself was a lay chairman of quarter sessions, he had long entertained con- siderable doubt whether matters would not be on a better footing if that office was filled by a professional lawyer, and—speaking for Lancashire—if one such appointment could be made to serve for the entire county. He should also be in favour of transferring to this legal chairman a portion of the business now dealt with at assizes. As to the administrative local business now devolving upon the quarter sessions court, he thought they might make up their minds before long to hand over, if not the whole, at least the greater part of it to some body chosen upon the representa- tive and elective principle. Such a reform was founded upon a sound principle; but he must at the same time assert his belief that the magistrates had no reason to fear ' comparison with their successors in regard to the purity, the economy, or the efficincy of county ad miuistration. VISIT OF THE PRINCE AND PRINCESS OF WALES TO LEICESTER.—The Prince and Princess of Wales visited Leicester, on Monday, and opened the New Abbey Park, laid out by the Corporation at a cost of nearly £40,000, near the ruins of the ancient abbey. Their Royal Highnesses were received with great cordiality, the decorations of the town were of the most lavish kind, and there was great cheering all along the route from the railway station to the park. The Freemasons took the opportunity to present the Prince of Wales with an address, to which Hi 3 Royal High- ness made an appropriate reply. After the arrival at the park the Princess of %Vales planted a tree, and shortly after- wards the Prince was presented by the Mayor, on behalf of the Corporation, with a gold key, as a souvenir of the day's proceedings. At the luncheon which followed the Prince of Wales spoke of the "magnificent and enthusiastic" reception which lie and the Princess had met with. He should not fail, he said, to tell the Queen when next he saw her of the "enthusiastic welcome" they had received, and of the ' loyalty of the inhabitants of Leicester to Her Majesty and to her family. The Lord Chancellor of England was pre- sent, and responded to the toast of "The Houses of Lords and Commons."

Cow,iderable excitement prevailed in Leicester on Tues- day morning, owing to a rumour gaining,- currency that a plot had been made to assassinate the Prince ef Wales on the previous day white passing through the town. The only ground for the report was the ravings of a drunken Irish- man, who had gone about the town proclaiming that an attempt would be made to assassinate their Royal High- nesses. This was reported to the police, who endeavoured to find the man. As usual, special detectives accompanied the Royal train, and precautions were issued to the police to be very watchful. It Wined out that whilst passing into Granby-street there was a great rush cf spectators, which attracted the attention of their Royal Highnesses, and when near the Post Office a man dashed through the crowd and through the cavalry escort, stopped the Royal carriage, and held out his hand to shake hands with the Princess of Wales. Her Royal Highness pushed the man away with her parasol. Detective-Inspector Mardlin rushed forward and seized the man, and sent him to the police station in charge of two officers. He gave the name of Charles Walkerdine, aged 30, shoe welter, living in New Bridge-st., Leicester, and he was brought up at the police court on Tuesday, charged with being drunk and disorderly. It appeared that he had been drinking, and whilst under its influence foolishly made a bet that he wuuld shake hands with the Princess, and hence his extremely strange conduct. He pleaded guilty to the charge of being drunk and disor- derly, and said he was extremely sorry. The magistrates cautioned him as to his conduct, and sent him to gaol for seven days without the option of a fine. It was noticed at the time that Walkerdine's conduct causol their Royal Highnesses some alarm, but the Princess soon recovered from the momentary nervousness which the unpleasant incident must have caused her. The deepest regret is felt in the town at the occurrence. The man who spread the report of the plot to assassinate their Royal Highnesses has not yet been found.

div.head: FUNERAL OF LORD JUSTICE I[OLKER.
div.p: FUNERAL OF LORD JUSTICE I[OLKER.

The remains of Sir John Holker were buried on Tuesday at Lytham Parish Church. The wish of the deceased judge that the funeral should be of a private and simple charac- ter was fully respected. Comparatively few persons were present, no hearse or mourning coaches were used, and the ceremony was of the briefest and plainest character, The only persons invited were relatives, a few intimate friends, and the members of the bar who acted under Sir John whilst he held the office of Attorney-General. The barristers and others not included in this narrow circle who attended did so voluntarily, from a desire to show their respect for the memory of the deceised gentleman. The body, enclosed in an oak coffin, with brass mountings, arrived at Lytham from London on Monday night, and was taken at once to the church, where it remained until the funeral. The coffin bore the following simple inscription :—" John Holker; born 24th March, 1828; died May 24th, 1882." The mourners and friends assembled about noon at the Clifton Arms Hotel, and walked in procession to the church, arriving there about one o'clock. The mourners were Mr. S. Holker (brother), the Rev.. J. R. Walker, Mr. C. Walker, Mr. Samuel Walker, Colonel 0. 0. Walker, Mr. R. Walker, Mr.. Edtnund Mr. J. J. Wilson, the Rev. Philip Graham, Mr. T. H. Jor- dan, Mr. W. Parker, Mr. E. Jordan, Colonel Hales Wilkie, Mr. C. J. Coleman, Mr. Hugh Cowie, Mr. W. Harper' Mr. T. Spencer (London), Mr. A. V. Dicey, Mr. Herbert Swift, and Mr. Mallinson (Manchester). The Conservative Club, , Preston, was represented by Mr. Alderman W. P. Park (chairman), Mr. R. Fazakerly (secretary), and a number of members. The Working Men's Conservative Club, Preston, sent a deputation consisting of Mr. J. Long (president), Mr. E. Clarkson (secretary), and others. The members of the two clubs present numbered about 250. The Bury Conservative Asso- ciation was represented by Mr. Oram, and the Manchester Law Clerks' Friendly Society by Mr. B. R. Davis, president, Mr. James Owen, secretary, Mr. J. R. Moss, and other mem- bers. The late Lord Justice at the time of his death was not only one of the patrons of the society, but was the largest subscriber to its funds. Mr. J. St. John Wheelhouse was present on behalf of the benchers of Gray's Inn. Mr. W. H. Higgin, Q.C., was unable to attend owing to indis- position, and letters were received at the Preston Conserva- live Club on Tuesday from Mr. C. Raikes, M.P., and Mr. F. Ecroyd, M.P., expressing regret that they could not be present. The route to the church was lined with spectators, and a number of persons had gathered round the gates and in the churchyard. The officiating clergy were the Rev. H. B. Hawkins, vicar, and the Rev. W. R. Pitn, curate. No hymn was sung either in the church or at the graveside, the proceedings being confined to the reading of the burial ser- vice, including the usual psalm and lesson. The grave is one in which Mrs. Holker, mother of the late judge, who died in 1868, is buried. It was Sir John's desire that his re- mains should be interred beside those of his mother, to whom he was very much attached. Lady Holker, who had attended service in the church at noon, was in the vestry during the .funeral. Her Ladyship had placed a beautiful wreath upon the coffin, and wreaths had also been sent by the Misses Anne and Mary Burton (London), Mr. att'si Mr,s, J. Wilson (London), &c.

div.head: LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT KNOWSLEY.
div.p: LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT KNOWSLEY.
ALLEGED PLOT TO ASSASSINATE
THE PRINCE OF WALES,
SPEECHES BY MR. E. K. MUSPRATT AND MR. W. E. BRIGGS, M.P.

Liverpool Liberals turned the bank holiday to practical as well as pleasurable advantage by paying a political pil- grimage to Knowsley. A monstre picnic was organised by the united clubs of the party—the Liverpool Reform, the Junior Reform, and the City Reform Clubs—and the pic- turesque park was placed at their disposal with a hearty willingness by the Earl of Derby. A similar gathering on a smaller scale was held last year, under the auspices of the City Reform Club, and the enthusiasm with which the members greeted the proposal to include the three social organisations in this 'year's excursion ensured its success from the beginning. li.lauy thousand Liberals from the city and from the county found their way to the ancestral seat of the Stan leys. Special trains were run at frequentintervalsto Huyton and Prescot by the London and North-Western Railway, and crowded omnibuses end waggonettes conveyed those who preferred a drive through country lanes. That these were by no means few was abundantly evident, for the traffic by the Prescot road was SO heavy that the highway presented a scene as animated as the road to Aintree on the Grand National day. Amongst those who contributed to the vehicular procession were the members of the Edgehill Reform Club, who drove from their headquarters in special omnibuses. Pleasure and politics were happily mingled in the day's programme. The burning questions of the day wee discussed by fluent speakers from an improvised plat- form, and whilst these were attracting a very large and at- tentive amdience several thousand spectators were watching with keen interest an athletic festival in another part of the park. The younger, and perhaps more portion of the pleasure party engaged in dancing, •' Kiss-in- the-ring," and other amusements, whilst the more gravely disposed roamed at leisure through the shady woods of Knowsley, where the shelter of the fresh foliage proved a refreshing retreat from tbe rays of the summer sun. The entire organisation of the gathering, including the catering arrangements, was most satisfactorily carried out by a com- mittee of the clubs.

THE SPORTS. The athletic festival was most successful in every way. The programme was a long and interisting one, the" events," both open and confined, were well contested, and the whole of the arrangements proved most complete. The prizes, which were exposed in front of the grand stand, were very valuable, and consisted of a number of articles of silver plate, clocks, dressing cases, 6:..c. Annexed is the prize list :- 150 Yards Flat Race (handicap), confined to the members of the clubs.-1. J. Butcher, Junior Reform ; 2, A. Levy, Junior Reform; 3, W. Marriott, City Reform. - . One-mile &cycle Race (handicap.), confined to the mem- bers of the clubs.-1, C. W. Haves, City Reform- 2, A. W. Willmer, Junior Reform; 3, Ernest Barendt, Junior Reform. One-mile Flat Race (handicap), confined to the members of the club.-1. R. Hoystead, City Reform ; 9, W. Mar- riott, City Reform; 3, S. Reynolds, City Reform. 120 Yards Flat Racee(handicap).-1, N. S. Woodyatt, Liverpool ; 2, G. Savage, Cressington ; 3, G. F. Bar‘. • ora Fairfield. Two Mile Bicycle Race (handicap).-1, C. W. Haves' Liverpool; 2, T. H. Overton, Liverpool ; 3, W. H. Hough' Castleton. 220-yards Flat Race (handicap) for Youths under 18.- 1, D. A. Harding, Whines; 2, J H. P. Montford, stoke ; 3, A. J. Pennington, Stoke ; 4. J. J. Hartley, St. Helens' • 5, T. Constantine, Old Swan; 6, .1. Norman, Liverpool. (Protests were lodged against the three thee on account of age.) Half-mile Flat Race (handicap) confined to members of the clubs.-1, W. Marriott, City Reform ; 2, A. ' Levy Junior Reform; 3, R. Hoystead, City -Reform. ' Two-mile Walking Race (handicap).-1, H. Dobson, Liverpool; ; 2. W. Howard, Bromborough e 3, R. Howard, Thornton Hough. Quarter-mile Flat Race (handicap). -7 1, G. Savage, Cressington ; 2, J. Adams, Aigburth ; 3, N. G. Woodyatt, Liverpool. One-mile Flat Race (handicap). 1, W. J. Nancarrow, Liverpool; 2. T. Crellin, Liverpoel ; 3. J. Wright, Widnes. Half-mile Flat Race (handicap).-1, G. Savage, Garston ; 2, J. Adams, Aigburth ; 3, W. Peters, Liverpool. At the termination of the sports. the prizes were delivered to the successful competitors by Mrs. E. K. Muspratt. THE POLITICAL MEETING. During the afternoon a political meeting was held on the ground near the enclosure for the athletic sports. The speakers stood upon a waegon, and there was an immense gathering of listeners. Mr. E. K. Muepratt occupied the chair, and supporting him were Mr. 'W. E. Briggs, M.P., Colonel Pilkington (the mayor of St. Helens), and many others. Mr. James M‘Comb (honorary secretary of the general committee), read the following letter of apology for absence from Lord Derby :-"Feirhill, Tunbridge, April 27, 1882. Sir,-In answer to your letter of the 25th, I will with plea- sure give my name as a patron to the proposed meeting on Whit Monday. My personal attendance is, I regret to say, impossible, for I have already, and for some time past, been engaged to take part in a public gathering which is to be held in Stanley Park on the Fame day, and abeut the time TRADE NOTES, when, I presume, your meeting will come off.-I wish von END OF THE NORTH WALES COLLIERS' STRIKE.-The all success, and remain your obedient servant, DERBY." Mr. 11PComb also stated that letters of apology had been re- strike of colliers in North Wales, which has lasted nearly seven weeks, against a reduction of 5 per cent. in wages, ceived from the following members of Parliament :-Messrs. W. Rathbone, John Roberts, W. S. Caine, S. Williamson, has at length collapsed. Five collieries are now working, H. Broadhuret, T. Burt, P. Rvlands, Sir W. ACCIDENT AT BANK QUAY STA.TION.—A man named William Thomas Mitchell, 22 years of age, a brakeman, residing at 24, Galborne-street, met with an accident on , Monday last at Bank Quay goods siding. He was backing some wagons ort to the brake of a special train, which was being got ready, previous to a start being made for Crewe. As be was coupling the brake to the wagons his foot slipped* over a lump of coal which threw him on his knee.and before he could recover hinisAf the wagon passed over his left leg, smashing it to pieces. He was immediately conveyed to the Infirmary, where it was found neces.e3ry to amputate the in- jured limb.

div.head: WHITSUNTIDE FESTIVITIES.
div.p: WHITSUNTIDE FESTIVITIES.
RUNCORN.

This year the lovers of the great annual holiday which is given to theworking classes of this district were favoured with Queen's weather. From first to last the most inveterate grumbler would have found it hard to give an unfavourable opinion upon it. Each day the atmosphere was of that sunny charac er which lends light and life to everything. The stream of visitors from the Lancashire side of the Mersey was as uninterrupted as upon similar occasions in years past. The London and North-Western ran several trips to the town, and the streets were filled with holiday- makers, many of whom appeared to be totally at a loss what to do with themselves, and ultimately took refuge from the very powerful rays of the sun in some inviting public-house. At the Parish Church, on Sunday, the ringers celebrated the advent of Whitsuntide by filling the air with the sweet music of church bells. Special hymns were also sung at the trious services. A spirit of progress appears to have over- shadowed Bethesda Congregational Chapel of late, and the church and congregation seem to be getting out of the old grooves into ways which are certainly distinguished by con- siderable variety and attractiveness. On Sunday, the special hymns of the Manchester Simday School Union were sung by the children and choir, and a collection made in aid of the school funds.

Early on Monday morning, the entire town was astir, and before nine o'clock the streets were full of people. Bands paraded the various streets, tilling the glorious atmosphere with pleasant sounds; flags fluttered from nearly every public building; the ships in the docks were covered with bunting ; and during the day the river was alive with small boats, filled with happy pleasure seekers. Devonshire- square was, as usual, the great centre to which the crowds flocked, in order to witness the processions of the various Friendly Societies, who are very powerfully represented in the town, numbering between 3,000 and 4,000. Five lodges put in an appearance, and shortly after ten o'clock the members of the Shepherds' Tent, of Runcorn, No. 777, made a start, in full regalia, which was of the usual effec- tive character. The Northwich Volunteer brass band headed the procession. Next came the Runcorn's Pride Lodge of Oddfellows, No. 368, preceded by the Swinton brass band. Then the Lily of the Valley Lodge number- ing 80 members, led up by the Wincham brass band. The Duke of Edinburgh Lodge of Oddfellows (70 adults), was preceded by the Runcorn Volunteer brass band, and followed by a large number of juvenile member. The Duke's Club, which was established in 1790, was represented by more than 100 members, who wore the badges of the Order. They were beaded by the Whines Star of Temperance brass band, and walked to the vicarage, where they were pleasantly received by the Rev. Canon Barclay, who afterwards delivered a sermon to them at the Parish Church, from the text—"l have shown you all things, how that so labouring ye ought to support the weak, and to reMember the words of the Lord Jesus, how He said, It is more blessed to give than to receive.' " The preacher urged the members to cultivate habits of thrift and temperance. He hoped that they would continue to help each other in the hour of sickness and bereavement, as they had done so nobly in the past. Mr. Johnson pre- sided at the organ, and Psalms 25 and 26, to the chants of Aldrich and Elvey, were sung by a full choir. The usual procession of Sunday school scholars, which is always a great attraction to visitors, took place in the after- noon. The number in the procession was estimated at nearly 5,000, and the ronte, which w, guarded by the local polico, Was lined with Spectators. The Parish aura scholars assembled in Church-street, and were strengthened by a numerous contingent from the Newtown Mission school. The younger children connected with the latter school were placed in a large cart, which had been generously lent by Mr. Stanway, of Shaw-street. The two schools numbered 700, and they first of all walked to the Vicarage, after which they adjourned to Beacon Hill, where they had what our American cousins call" a right good time of it." The scholars belongngto Holy Trinity Church, and those of what is locally known as the Ragged School, proceeded to a field belonging to Mr. Horsefield, in Canal-street.
Mr. Ford, farni. er,•lent his field at Higher Runcorn to the Dissenters, vrho walked to the spot in the foll4wing order :

Mr. Shaw's Mersey Mission children paraded the streets, headed by their well-known drum and ,tite bind, and after- Avards adjourned to the Duke's Field for refreshments, after which they spent the time in various games. St. Edward's Roman Catholic school mustered at Mill Brow, and marched to flatten, prec. ded by their drum and fife band. We understand that some "fellows of the baser sort" broke through the ranks in Halton-road, And broke one of the flag staffs and damaged the flag. On Superin- tendent Williamson hearing of this, he despatched several constables, with orders that they should attend the proces- sion for the rest of the day. i The members of the Salvation Army (671 h corps) had a grand field day. The bill announcing the proceedings was a perfect curiosity, and several gentlemen of position in the town have paid for the privilege of obtaining a copy. It began with the question " Holloa ! What's up, Jack ?" It then went on to say, "The Salvation Army are going in for ' a Salvation feed. Let us go in for a feed with them. Open fire on Jumbo's territory, at half-past live in the morning. A tnonstre open air procession in the afternoon. Meeting in Devonshire-square at 1-30 to shoot the devil ! Tea will .be provided at 4-30. Tickets, 3d. each. Come in crowds. Meet again in Devonshire-tquare at six o'clock, when some IWoolwich infants will bombard Jumbo's territory. Inside the. Foresters •Hall at 7-30, the Brick-lane thief, from Lon- don. Sister Sutton (from Alvanley Green) ; als.) the ! man who went up the chimney instead of going to bed ! And the Right Hon. Father Matthews will address the meeting. There will be a solo played on the instruments of torture, the whole winding up with one of the best days that has been spent in Runcorn. Captain Fireway Gibbs and Mate."
WIDNES

This town presented a most peaceful appearance on Whit- Monday. The tall chimneys Were nearly smokeless, and the air was, comparatively, pure, and bathed in sunshine, which gave even the ugliest piles, for which Widnes is somewhat famous.a golden glory. Many of the weather prophets looked with solemn visages on the few fleecy clouds to he seen in the early part of the day, and predicted rain, but their vaticinations proved, like many of those telegraphed by their American brethren, utterly false. The shops and counting houses were all closed, and thousands left by train for fresh fields and pastures new. The promenade was th e chief centre of attraction for the excursionists who visittd the town, and hero the children of a lauer growth gave themselves up to studying the h2anties of the flowing tide, or the pretty Parish Church of Run- corn, from whose tower the sweet bells sent forth their joyous peal at the early part of the day. The great bridge, which is such a triumph of engineering. skill, was inspected inall its majestic proportions; the plea- sure boats which covered the jiver, were a never-ending source of interest to the minds of our country cousins, who thronged Widnes with their wives, and those who were " still nearer to them thin all other." A few travelling shows and merry-go-rounds had found a home near the promenade, and these were very well patronised by the children. Hundreds of Widnesians crossed the bridge to Runcorn, for the purpose of witnessing the processions, walking to Norton Priory, or taking the train for the pretty resorts to be found near Helshy and Froilsharn. Several excursion trains stattr.l :an the London and North-Western station, which was alive with traffic during the day. The Widnes Catholics proceeded by trip to Blackpool at 6-45 on Monday morning, the total number in the train being 650. They visited the Winter Gardens, Itaikes Hall, the Aquarium and the other attractions, and commenced their return • journey at 9-15, arriving at Widnes at 11-20. There was

the customary yearly trip to Belle Vue, from the London and North-Western station, ani it was patronised by about 300 people. The Central station presented a very lively scene most of the day. At seven o'clock, the Star of Wid- nes Sick and Burial Society's trip which numbered about 700 excursionists, left for Matlock and Chatsworth. The return journey was commenced from Rowsley station at 8-35, and the train reached Widnes shot tly after eleven.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

IThe number of visitors to Frodsham on Bank holiday was quite up to the average, and, favoured with beautiful weather, a very pleasant day was spent, there not being so much as a passing shower to mar the enjoyment. In place of ferns, with which the excursionists usually adorn them- selves, the oak trees had to pay tribute to the Royal Oak Day. The obstructions in the main street were as numerous as on previous occasions, and we may here correct a misprint which occurred in our last issue, and state that the memorial presented to the Marquis of Cholmondeley in the matter, was in similar terms to the memorial presented to the West Eddiebury Highway Board. That the obstructions are a dangerous nuisance was clearly shown on Monday, when a conveyance came to grief through the horse taking fright at the harsh music produced by a barrel organ, and but for timely assistance we should have had to record a serious acei- dent. The country attractionsaround Frodsham are so well known,and have been so often described, that we may briefly say the hills were as largely patronised as heretofore, and tlfe extensive view from the summit of the Overton and Beacon Hills was ample repayment for the trouble, or, shall ' we say, the pleasure of scrambling up. The friendly socie- ties mustered in good force and attended Divine service at I the school-room in Overton, the service being conducted by the vicar, who gave a short but practical address which was exceedingly appropriate. The bands with the respective clubs afterwards discoursed sweet music at the vicarage,and the clubs afterwards paid a visit to Mrs. Haves, Mr. Wright, and other places in the town. The grounds at Castle Park (the seat of E. A. Wright, Esq.) were again thrown open to the public and were visited by crowds of admirers of the beautiful in nature, the umbrageous shade and cool retreats affording every opportunity fcrr the whispering of sweet noth- ings and a renewal of the toast- -Think to me only with thine eyes, And I will pledge with mine." The annual treat provided by Mr. Wright was a source of keen enjoyment on Monday, and we heard but one opinion as to the taste and excellent arrangement displayed in the management. The conservatory was much admired, the stage in the centre having the appearance of a large bouquet. The flower garden had been planted out for the summer, and the American ground was well worth a visit, as the choice rhododendrons were in full bloom, indeed the tine botanical apechnens cannot fail to interest all who may have even the slightest Linnean taste. A glance at the position of the friendly societies which took part in the festivities may not be out of place in con- cluding this notice.—Court Independence, No. 410 of Ancient Foresters. The number of members in this club is 275, and the sum of £257 123. 6d. has been expended in sick pay during the past year, and £4O 103. for funerals, the total amount of the funds being £2,408 9s. 81— 1 Emblem of Hope Lodge, No. 516 of the Grand United Order of Oddfellows. The number on the rolls is 136, and £43 103. has been paid to sick members and £l9 for funerals, the total amount of money invested and in the treasurer's hands being £1,031 63. 101-I—Modern Druids' Society: Maiden Queen Lodge. This club musters M members, and the sick pay during the year amounted to £lO9 17s. 61. and I fune.rals £37 103., while the fiinds in hand were £335 93. 1 9L-1. PitESCOT. . . I

Whit-Monday was us-h ered in at Preseot. most aespici- ously, Riving pleasure seekers early promise of a beautiful day. From an early hour the railway station was crowded with passengers arriving and departing. Business was entirely suspended on Monday, all the iradesmens' establish- ments being closed. Crowded trains arriving hourly 4lis- charged their numerous freight safely, under the watchful sot veillance of Mr. Davies, station master, assisted by an increased staff of porters. The high road from Liverpool, St. Elelens, and Warrington was alive with vehicles of all descriptions, from the humble whitechapel to the more wa- ter:6ons "tandem." The tram cars from St. Helens came in largely for the day's takings, each being crammed. Of course, the centre of attraction was Lord Derby's seat— Knowsley—which never assumed so charming a garb as to- day. Far as the eye could reach field after field of grassy verdure met the gaze, and must have proved peculiarly re- freshing to city denizens present in such large numbers. Other visitors preferred the verdant glades around and drove through PrescA at a rate which on any other occasion would have Come under the category of "furious." The majority of the passengers alighting from the station at Prescot made their way by the new street leading from Station-road up Park-street into Eccleston-street, and thence to the park by Derby-street entrance. Busses ran from Liverpool every half hour at the rate of is per pacsenger, bringing' large loads of p tssengers. What might have resulted in serious injuries to many people was averted by the prompitude of the guard and driver of a heavily laden bus.. The two front wheels were found to be giving way under the great weight above, and this, added to the steep- ness of the thoroughfare (Derby-street) through which they were passing, increased the danger which however was fortunately averted by the passengers all descending and finishing the rest of the journey on foot. The day continued beautifully tine, thereby conducing greatly to the enjoy- ment of the visitors. Those departing by rail in the evening for Liverpool were not very agreeably surprised to learn 1 that they would have to walk to Hnyton, two miles distant, and there take the ttain. One hoisterons individual at Prescat station, on being informed of this, promptly replied that he. "shod do nowt o'th snort as walk to Iluyton." The porter ercpired what he meant doing, on which the other answered, " Well, aw reckon aw con ride Oleer for twopence hawpenny, connot aw ?" a query to which the railway , representative certainly could not object to say "Yen-."

div.head: WARRINGTON
div.p: WARRINGTON

Liitie business was done in Warrington on Whit-Monday, and the townspeople seemed determined to make the most of their first summer holiday. In this they were greatly aided by the weather, which was most propitious, and from an early hour the streets were crowded with persons in holiday attire making their way to the railway stations. The plat- forms were crowded all day, ant hundreds of Warringtonians went to join in the festivities at Frodsham or to spend the day on the hills at Overton and Helsby; and not a few went further on to see the sights of the historic city of Chester, and enjoy the pleasures of a row on the delightful Dee. For others the recently created city of Liverpool, and the pretty and popular resorts across the Mersey, had their attractions, while large numbers were drawn in the opposite direction by the fascinations of the city of cotton and its environs. Places nearer town, such as Runcorn, Lymm, Le., were also visited by numbers of holiday makers. Besides those who left town by rail, many people drove to their destinations by road. A goodly number of the members of the Blue Ribbon Army assembled opposite St. Paul's Church in the morning anti proceeded in waggonettes to Heatley, where they spent a pleasant day with the members of the Oughtringten Branch of the Church of England Temperance society. Similar means of locomotion were employed by the Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel Bible Class, who journeyed as far as Helsby, and others went by 'bus to Stockley Wood, Stretton, where a sale of work was held in connection with Whitley Wesleyan Chapel. There was a great demand upon the resources of the local cab proprietors, and heavily laden vehicles of every kind and description left Warrington dur- ing the day for the various places of pleasure in the neigh- bourhood. Bicyclists, too, were numerous, and those who could not afford the cost of any of these modes of travelling, or had no desire to do so, went in all directions on "Shank's pony" to see nature's summer splendours. Thoee who from choice or obligation stayed in town, found enjoyment in sauntering through the Park and admiring its enjoyment and foliage adornments, while numbers rambled through the fields and lanes in the vicinity, and to others boating on the river was a source of pleasure. The day was greatly enjoyed, and the excursionists conducted themselves in a very orderly and creditable manner.
