div.head: FASHIONABLE MARRIAGE AT RUNCORN, •
div.p: FASHIONABLE MARRIAGE AT RUNCORN, •

If there is anything in the saying " Happy is the bride whom the sun shines on," Miss Annie Shaw, of the High- lands, Runcorn, elder daughter of Mr. Robert Shaw, alkali manufacturer, Widnes, must have been supremely happy on Tuesday, when she was married to Mr. Walter Frederick Panlihurst, of Reed Court, Rochester, and Upper Baker- street, Regent's Park, London, gentleman. The sun shohe with great brilliance and power, and the lovely weather doubtless contributed in some measure to the large atten- dance of friends and neighbours, who assembled at St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel for the purpose of witnessing the ceremony. The body of the pretty chapel was crowded with members of both sexes,—although, as a matter of course, the ladies predominated,—and the gallery was well filled, and this arose mainly from the circumstance that the day was a holiday, and also that this was#he most fashionable wedding that has been celebrated in Runcorn for a long time. Soon after eleven o'clock, the hour fixed for the marriage, the wedding party began to arrive, and at a quarter past the bride entered the edifice with her father, and attended by her six bridesmaids, Miss Ella Shaw (sister of the bride), Miss Thiirese Paskhurst (sister of the bridegroom), Miss E. Davies, Miss Bella Guthrie, Miss Fohnstone, and Miss Ada Shaw (sister of the bride). They were immediately joined by the bridegroom, who had previously entered the, building, accompanied by his brother, Mr. Torn Pankhurst, as best man, and Mr. Newton Davies, , Halton; Mr. W. C. Cross, Chester; Mr. J. S. Eccles, St. Helens; and Mr. W. Marsh, St. Helens; and the ceremony 1 commenced with the singing of the hymn "The voice that breathed o'er Eden. The officiating minister was the Rev. 1 Dr. Osborne, president of the Wesleyan Conference; and he was assisted by the Rev. J. Nowell, superintendent of the 1 Runcorn circuit; and the Rev. A. Sargent, of Chester. At the conclusion of the service, which was read by Dr. Osborne, another hymn, " Saviour let thy sanction rest On the union witnessed now," was sung, and the party retired to the vestry to sign the register. On the completion of this important part of the ceremony Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst played the Wedding March on the organ, and the party proceeded to the carriages in waiting and drove for the Highlands amid the good wishes of the spectators. The front of the chapel was gay with bunting, and the steps to the entrance were covered with scarlet cloth. The bride was attired in an ivory white satin petticoat bodice, and train of broche satin, trimmed with orange blossom and lace, and she wore a wreath of orange blossom and myrtle. The bridesmaids' dresses ware of nun's cloth in can de nie, trimmed with lace, chenille silk pointed bodices, with cream silk sashes. They also wore cream Langtry bonnets with roses and streamers, fastened with gold horse shoe brooches (presents of the Liidegroom) and I culled muffs trimmed with lace, and roses to match. Break- 1 tast was served at the Highlands, and the guests included ' Mr. H. S. Hall, J.P., and Mrs. Hall ; Mrs. Davies, Halton ; Mr. Alfred Davies, Mr. and Mrs. Speakman, the Rev. G. I Hack, the Rev. J. Bateman, Miss France, of Wigan ; Mies Scott, of London; Mr. W. Eccles, St. Helens; Miss Ada Speakman, Dr. and Mrs. Robinson, Mrs. Nowell, Mrs. Pankhurst, Mrs. Kershaw, Saddleworth ; Miss M, Guthrie, Aberdeen ; Mr. C. H. Lewin, and Mr. Herbert I Marsh. At 3-30 the newly-wedded min drove from Higher Rencorn to Frodshare. where they joined the Liverpool I train and proceeded to Peninienmaavr, at which place they j will spend a portion of their honeymeon, and then proceed to Norway.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

This Board held tlkir fortnightly meeting on Tuesday afternoon, at llutron Workhouse, under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Barclay. There were also present—the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, Messrs. G. S. Hazle- hurst, C. Rigby, T. Norman, J. Smith, J. Stokes. J. W. Baguley, C. Mountleld, James Weir, John Weir, J. Challoner, G. Whitlow, J. Mclntyre, P. Percival, W. Jack- son, J. Catnpkin, Joshua Midvood, H. Stringer, E. A. Wallington, Henry Linaker (clerk), and W. 11. Linaker (deputy clerk).
TIIE MA'SYER OF TILE WORKHOUSE AND THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT HOARD.

A communication was read from the Local Government Board, acknowledging the receipt of a letter from the clerk, dated the 11th inst., in which he informed them that Mr. R. Junes, the Master of the workhouse, had at present six children living with hint in the building, of whom the eldest was 20 years of age. The Board directed the clerk's attention to the fact that when, in 1857, the Poor Law Board assented to the residence in the workhouse of three children belonging to the master, the eldest had not then attained the age of five years. The Local Government Boald exp7ees,d their regret that so irregular an arrange- ment as that now brought to their notice, should have been allowed to exist, and to state that in accordance with an I, invariable rule which they had laid down upon the subject,l the male children of the master, aged respectively 14, 15, 17, and 20 years, should at once be provided for elsewhere than in the workhouse. As regarded the female, aged 19 years, it appeared to the Local 'Government Board that her presence in the establishment on Saturday and Sunday must be calculated to diminish discipline ; the workhouse being intended primarily for the pauper inmates, and the reqoisite staff of officers, and they would be obliged if the Guardians would give their consideration to the question from this paintof view. The Lac 11 Government Board added that theywould be prepared to assent to the residence in the house of the boy aged 12 years, until he reached the age of 14, provided a suitable repayment were made in respect of his maintenance. They also wished to know what sum it was proposed should be repaid in respect of such child. A MEMBER s dd he was not aware that any complaint bad been made by the L )cal Government Board Inspector in respect to Mr. Joues's children. Mr. NORMAN strongly deprecated the action taken by the Local Government Board in the matter, and said that most people liked to have their children at home with them—he did for one. After a little further conversation on the sub- ject, he moved that the contract entered into by Mr. Jones be adhered-to. Timis resolution was seconded by the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner. _ _ _ _ _
...... _ Mr. RIGBY considered the action of the London Board a great piece of impertinence. The CHAIRMAN: We do not come here merely to register the decrees of the Local Government Board.
The motion was unanimouAly agreed to. MR. NORMAN ON HIS VICTORY.

The CLERK read a communic diem of which the following s a copy :—" Local Government Bard, Whitehall, 25 May„ 1882. Sir,—l am directed by the Local Governmenr Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 18th inst. enclosing a copy of your ce-tificate of the Guardians elected for the Runcorn Union for the current year, and to state that the Board proposed to issue an order authorising the special election of three Guardians for the township of Runcorn, in conseqoenca of their having been a failure to , nominate the proper number of Guardians for the township at the last annual election. Tarn, sir, your obedient servant, W. RorroN." Mr. NORMAN (jubilantly) : Hear, hear, gentlemen r Have they sent the (Prier, Mr. Linaker ? The CLERK : It has not corn, but it will do so. (Laugh- . ter.) In answer to Mr. John Weir, the CLERK stated that any general expenses of advertising, &c.,would fall upon the Union. hut if there was a contest, the cost would have to be borne by the Runcorn township. The CrtAtimot said that as this was a special matter, be might. perhaps, be permitted to ask the Clerk what time was allowed for the sending in of nomination,z. The CLERK : The whole of thse matters will be fixed by the Local Government Board in their order.
Ttw CHAIRMAN: And also the mode to be adopted for avo'ding a enntest ?

The CLERK: Everything. The CnetnmAs said that, of course, thcse various matters would ty- dealt wlth in the advertist•ment. The CLERK: Yes. THE REPRESENTA.TION OF APPLETON. The DEPUTY CLERK read a cononunicition tranfimitted

by the Local Government Board for the consideration of the Guardians, being the copy of an application from the rate- payers of the township of Appleton for the election of an additional guardian. The London Board observed that be- fore considering any proposal which should have the effect of increasing the total number of guardians for the union, they wished to draw the attention of the Runcorn Board to 1 I the provision contained in the statute 31 and 32 Vic., can. 122, sec. 61, which enabled the Board to add any parish im the union the population of which did not exceed 000, and 1 the annual value of which did not exceed the average rate- able value of the parishes in the same union, to some ad- joining- parish of the union for the purpose of the election of guardians. This proposal might be taken advantage of by the Runcorn Board, and they wished to ask what course tee Guardians proposed to pursue under the circumstances. Mr. Nonnt,ter considered that the gentleman who was inure particularly affected by the communication now under the consideration of the Board than any one else ought to have been present._ _
The CLERK explained that perhaps the guardian referred to did not know that such a communication was to be laid before the meeting._

After one or tweobservations of no general public interest, Mr. NORMAN moved a resolution to the effect that Appleton was fairly entitled to the privilege of having another guardian, but the Board did not see their way to deprive any other township in the union of its direct representati-ic. Mr. GEORGE WHITLOW snondeci the motion, which was. passed nem dis.

div.head: MR TIPPING ON lIIS DEFENCE.
div.p: MR TIPPING ON lIIS DEFENCE.

The DEPUTY CLERK read a letter from the Local 6,-,vcro- ment Board; enclosing copy of a correspondence which taken place between Mr. W. Tipping, assistant overseer for the parish of Walton Inferior, Walton Superior, and Hatton, on the subject of reports made by the District Auditor, after his audit of that officer's accounts for the half•year endin,?; Michaelmas last; and stating that the London Board would be glad to receive the observations of the Guardians. Mr. RIGBY satirically asked if there was any other com- munication to be read that day from the Local Government Board.
On the proposition of Mr. NORMAN, a committee was ap- pointed to consider the correspondence, and report to the next Board meeting.
WORKHOESE SEWAGE.

A meeting of the whole Board in committee had been held that morning, and the minutes were read by the Deputy Clerk. The subject to be considered was the best means of dealing with the sewage from the workhouse. A report, ' prepared by the Clerk, was read, tracing the history of the complaint of nuiance caused by sewage flowing from the workhouse, and also the action taken by the Guardians thereon, from 1880 up to the present time. All reports, plans, and documents relating to the matter were produced. An ad jeurnment was made to the sewage outfall, in order to enable the Guardians to inspect the present tank, and on re- turning to the Board-room, after some conversation, it was proposed by Mr. Peter Percival, seconded by Mr. J. Stoke:, and resolved—" That the sewage be carried from the present tank across the field, by pipes, into an adjoining field, oa to which the sewage could b 3 turned, and that the agent to the Aston Estate be communicated with, in order to ascertair on what terms the field can be leased."
It was resolved that the consideration of the report be adjourned to the next Board meeting, and that Mr. Jones be asked to make a plan, to be submitted to the Aston Estate authoritits.
The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: THURSDAY—Before Mr. Wm. &mks.
div.p: THURSDAY—Before Mr. Wm. &mks.

A SON CHARGED WITH STEALING A VALUABLE 11ORSL.— A young man named Albert Peck, respectably dreseed, was charged with stealing a bay gelding, value £4O, and a bridle, the property of his father, Mr. James Peck.—Prosecutor said he was a livery stable-keeper in Bridge-street, and the prisoner was his son, and 17 years of age. On the 18th Feb-nary, the young man left home, and absconded with a sum of money. He believed that the prisoner then went to sea with a schooner. At about half past eleven, on the night of the 29th ult., he went into the stable, and saw there seven horses, one of which was a hired one. He locked tht etahle, but left the window open owing to it being a hot night. At twenty minutes to five o'clock on the following morning, he again visited the stable. He found the door of the place, the door of the saddle room, and one of the gates of the yard open. He missed a bay gelding worth £4O. The bridle now produced belonged to him, and was safe in the saddle-room, on Monday night. About half-past nine on Monday night, he saw the prisoner in the stable yard,and, as he was interfer- ing with the men in the execution of their duty, he put him out. The missing horse was brought home again at about six o'clock, on the evening of the 30th ult., by a milk boy, in the employ of Mr. Bagley, of Stockham. He did not give the prisoner power to take the horse, which was so tired when it came home that it could not stand to eat. He lost the service of the animal during Whitsuntide, owing to his son's conduct.—Prisoner, in reply to Mr. Johnson, deputy magistrates' clerk, said he had no question to ask his father. —Mr. G. B. Yarwood, farmer, of Dutton, about six and a half miles from Runcorn, said that on Tuesday morning, about a quarter past six, the prisoner came to his place, and asked hi ai if he was buying any horses at present. He said "Yes," and prisoner replied ,that he had one to sell which was a fast goer. He knew the young man as being the son of last witness, and from his description of the horse he knew it. Prisoner next asked him if he would go to an adjoining farm kept by Mr. Bradburn' for the purpose of examining the animal. He told him he had not time to do so, and. he had better bring it round for his inspection. Prisoner went in the direction of Bradburn's farm, and brought the horse with him, at about seven o'clock. His suspicions were ex- cited that the young man had no right with it, and he asked , him what sum he wanted for it. Prisoner replied " I think it ought to make £10." He then asked the prisoner to pot the horee in the stable, and he gave it. a feed, as it -looked 51 if it had " been knocked about." The young man com- plained of being unwell, and be gave him a glass of beer. Prisoner next remarked that if he did not wish to buy. the animal be would go on to the Twine) Top, which is a public-house near, and try to sell it. He told the prisoner that he was going that way in his trap, and if he wouid rather ride lie could do so. Prisoner made no reply, but again complained of being unwell, and he advised him to lie down and have a rest. Ile (witness) went away about two hours and a half, and on returning he saw the stolen horse in the possession of a Northwich man, near the workhouse. He asked him what he was doing with- it, on which he said, "Am I wrong? " He replied, " I should think you are wrong; give him to me." The man replied, "I have been thinking all the time that I had no !right with it." He gave the man sixpence and took the ' horse from him, on which he remarked that "it was hard for him to have to walk for nothing, as he had been promised half a crown and some food when he got back to Runcorn." On afterwards seeing the young man Peck, he said his father was selling the horse because he had too many, and was not busy at present.-P.C. Bossons said that on Tuesday night he apprehended the prisoner at the Navigation Inn. On telling him to come along with him, the young man said, "But the horse has come back, hasn't it?" He told him this was correct, but he had better be very careful what he I said, as he was charged with stealing the animal and a bridle. Plisoner, in reply, said "I wanted to see my brother's grave at Hill Cliff, and I took the horse to ride upon. They cau- -1 not do anything at me, becauee I never offered it for sale, or anything; but I petit up, gave it a feed, and afterwards sent it home by a man." Hill Cliff was not anywhere near Mr. Yarwood's farm.—Mr. Yarwood was then put in the box, and said that Hill Cliff was six miles from his house. If the prisoner had gone to Hill Cliff and then to his (witness's) farm, he would have had to travel about thirteen miles.— In reply to the usual charge, the prisoner said he was in drink at the time, and when he became sober he sent the horse home again. He had been abused on the night before taking the animal by his father and Peter Brereton. He thought he would- have a ride out. (Laughter.'—The prisoner was committed to linutsfori sessions for trial. _
