div.p: • Meitero to the gdttor. BAD BEHAVIOUR. would suggest that it would be to the advantage of those robble-de-hoys, or should I say ignoramuses, who occupied the room above the greengrocer's shop in High- street, on Monday afternoon last (whilst the scholars were walking), to cultivate their manners and behaviour a little more rather than to make use of the disgusting language awl insulting remarks which were overheard and afterwards commented upon by persons passing. Strangers thought them scarcely compos menus, but the writer declares it to be the result of light literature. Alas! what a boon a free lending library would be to such. A VISITOR. Runcorn, May 31st.

A FERRY BOAT WANTED. Sir,—l was considerably surprised,aswell as disappointed, to find that on Tuesday afternoon last, about half-past three o'clock, there was no ferry boat plying between Runcorn and Widnes. There were four or five pleasure boats, or what may be termed river gigs, sailing about, but these did not come within hearing distance or probably I might have been able to have gone across. I waited, however, at the ferry upwards of half-an-hour, thinking the men had gone into the town to get some provisions or refreshment; and whilst there I should think about 20 or 30 persons arrived, only to be disappointed. At this season of the year there are numerous sports on the Widnes side of the river, and people who have children too big to be carried, and yet too little to walk far, do not wish to have the trouble of climb- ing up the steps and across he bridge, when they can reach their destination by one-third of the distance. I think the interests of the public should be studied a little on such occasions. ONE WHO WAS DISAPPIONTED. Runcorn, May 31st.

WARRINGTON ANNUAL HOLIDAI. Sir,—' am afraid that greater unanimity of feeling will no prevail upon this subject until juster and more correct views are entertained and expressed upon it. I greatly fear that the course Mr. Morris took at the meeting of the iron- workers, over which he presided' has only tended to com- plicate the matter, and to engender and perpetuate pre- judices which, holding the position he did, it should have been his study to allay and eradicate. He very em- phatically tried to impress upon the meeting that he krows I how to manage workingmen and women, a knowledge which, he says, Sunday school teachers are but little acquainted with. If workingmen can be managed by "gammon" possibly he may be proficient in the art of management. When a person like Mr. Morris stands before a number of his men, and asks for their consideration on the plea that he is a "Warringtonian "—a plea more than once urged by him—to me it borders somewhat on the ludicrous. As a workingman I prefer honest manliness on the part of those who give me the benefit of their opinions, or tender me their advice. And I believe that is the senti- ment of the mass of my fellow-workine,rmen. Mr. Morris professes a warm regard for Sunday school teachers. It may be so; but it is clear to me that he entertains very erroneous ideas of the nature of their work, and the relation in which they stand to the working-classes. It must be borne in mind that for the most part Sunday school teachers are workingmen. But Mr. Morris put this question to the meeting, "To whom do the children belong who meet and walk and attend the Sunday schools, but to the working- men " The applause with which the sentiment was re- ceived convinced me that the men understood it, as it was perhaps intended that they should understand it, that in sending their children to the Sunday school, the working- men were placing the teachers under an obligation to them and that as they thus sent their chiidern to these schools they bad a right to dicate to the teachers the time and circumstances under which those teachers should minister to the gratification of the children of those men. Now, Mr. Morris must know that there was a considerable number present at that meeting who are not heads of families; and it is equally certain that a still larger number trouble themselves very little indeed whether their children go to a Sunday school or not. But supposing they did, who are the parties placed under an obligation—the Sunday school teacher, or the parent who sends his children to the Sun- day school? Every man of common sense knows it is the parent. The Sunday school teacher does the work which the parent, in too many instances, neglects to do. It is this very neglect on the part of parents that necessitated the formation of Sunday schools, and still renders their existence essential. If the working classes did their duty to their children, and gave them suitable scriptural instruction—as they by the claims of natural affection ought to do—Sun- day schools, in their original form would not be needed. If Mr. Morris and the men who applauded his fallacious and misleading sentiment are not aware of the fact, I would wish them to note that the teachers—male and female— who voluntarily and gratuitously take charge of the religious education of these workingmen's children do so not merely at the sacrifice of the pleasantest hours of each Sabbath-day, but at the cost of much mental and physical energy, to say nothing of the monetary outlay, for, as a rule, the funds necessary for the support of these institutions come largely from the pockets of those who labour in them. If Mr. Morris on any future occasion takes a prominent part in any public matter, let him try and be fair towards all, and not by " soft-sawder " on the one aide„ or inuendo and sophistry on the other, seek to gain his paint. There is always a day of reckoning; and in this case it may not be far distant. As to the holiday itself, I think it would be better, if it is thought needful that the national holiday should be supplemented by a local one, that some constituted authority—say the Town Council, instructed by public sentiment, not of one or two sections of the community, but of the whole, should set apart the day, and not leave to the chid magistrate for the time being the invidious task of deciding. And the day thus fixed, it would be open for the Sunday schools, the benefit clubs, and trade societies, on other similar organisations to avail themselves of it or not for demonstration purposes; but to put a stop to all business in the town at the bidding of a limited number of men because they want to see some horses run is a scandal on common sense. May 29th 1882. WILHELM,

div.head: WANTED, AN. IRISH POLICY.
div.p: WANTED, AN. IRISH POLICY.

Sir,—A solution of the Irish question does not appear on the programme of Parliamentary certainties. For, however admirable may be the extra energy imported into Mr. Glad- stone's treatment of the question since the still unfathomed mystery of the Phcenix Park transpired, no one acquainted with the nature and justness of Irish grievances can place much faith in the Gospel comprehended in either the Pre- vention of Crime Bill, or the Arrears of Rent Bill. Both these measures represent one-sided legislation —too long a trait in England's administration of Irish affairs—and, in the writer's opinion, are so far from being remedial in rela- tion to the evils which permeate Irish society, that they must eventually operate deleteriously where a more saga- cious and anticipatory policy would result in permanent good. We have no desire that a Parliament at this stage of our national progress should legalise anything imperfect, anything likely to confront us at a later period as a source of complaint or recrimination. We are reaping quite suf- ficient annoyance already from laws raising a rich crop of disturbances and outrages on the soil of Ireland. The har- vest is attributable to bed legislation in the past, either to matured wickedness in design, or a great falling short of justice in the Irish policies of previous governments. Ire- land has been what the Daily Telegraph aptly designates a see-saw, and on it party tactics have oscillated to the dis- comfort and barren mal-appropriation of Irish interests. Toying with Ireland must cease or eventuate in repeated rebellion among a people provoked to it by the unfair strata- gems of partizan-statesmanship. History has abundantly proved that Ireland is averse to being played with; and common-sense, if not history, should teach our statesmen what, as "men of light and leading" they ought to know, that neither coercion, as in the Prevention of Crime Bill, nor a gift of rent, as in the Arrears of Rent Bill, will abolish the Irish difficulty. Of coercion little need be said; its most recent application is condemnatory in its results, with- out marching back to remoter times, when intrigue and personal influences subjected Ireland to the most baneful species of political subordination, making her the prey of dishonest though aspiring crown agents, whose machina- tions excited revolts that had to be quelled by English troops, thus introducing coercion under circumstances that make us blush for our ancestors. With the suspension of the Habeas Corpus—a step damaging to the prestige of a j softy glorying in its defence of liberty sentiments-- innocent men throughout Ireland have been kept under arrest. No doubt to-day, if the prison cells of Ireland were opened, a nice story of tyrranous wrongs would din the ears of the I suspect law authorities. Again "armed intervention" has been tried, to be registered as a huge failure. Pouring the military into the country is one of our traditional methods of "settling the Irssh." Unfortunately it neither pays nor succeeds, and is not complimentary to the martial pride of our solders, who feel: as they deserve, worthy of more honorable service than dummy parade before recalcitrant mobs, with " heart-breaking " humiliation restrained from responding with dignity to the sallies of brick-bats that greet them when on patrol. Coercion is no remedy. Time after time we note the recurrence of semi-anarchy in Ireland, and time after time do we resort to coercion to dispose of a storm, ever-brewing, which the world knows is the out- come of of injustice. This brings me to the Arrears of Rent Does it not occur to those who watch contemporary history, that the land question is gradually looming upon the country as an inevitable starting point Of a new departure in English. politics? There are men who believe, with whagebehef many sympathise, that a not far distant era will nee 'ssitate the passage of the millions of " broad acres," i new n the hands of our territorial lords, from their present possessors to State control. Whether this, if a fait aceornpli, would benefit our Empire, is not for the writer to say. It is an idea that has to bsem chronicled,an .LLiberal earndl ta in con junction t fearion withth e it, we may glean why o y operations of the Land League in Ireland. It is precisely on the same grounds as English churchmen feared the disestsb- lishment of the Irish Church; the one prophesied a similar fate to the other. Not a few of our popular politicians found their objections to the satisfying of Ireland's craving for Home Rule, to say nothing of Lend Leagueism, upon the approximate dang. er it represents to their own future as i land- owners. There is one thing, however, n the land question that creates more antipathies in Ireland than it does in either England or Scotland, and this is, that the owning by Eng- lishmen of Irish soil is nearly wholly due to wholesale con- fiscation in the past. Every reader of Irish history und. er- stands what this means ; and, perhaps, it is pardonable in a people so warm-blooded and impulsive as the Irish people are, if they think with abhorrence of the days when their laud was wrested from their forefathers; and, to speak frankly, it is provocative of anger to attach these facts to the grind- ing exactions made upon them by those who forget how ittle moral right they Lave to the soil upon which they

place such high premiums. Keeping to the main issue, however, we observe the growing influence of the land agitation, and our fear is lest the Government sacrifices its fealty to justice in its endeavour to circumvent the menace offered to a potent section of its party. If this fear is well based, which would seem to be the case, then our policy to- wards Ireland is to-day removed from that of the past in degree, not in kind, which simply implies, that Ireland has still to combat with political intrigue, which, if not so cruelly disposed, is not less selfishly so than that of the past. We regret this, if it be true, and earnestly hope Mr. Gladstone will end his grand career as a noble exemplar of determined unbias in the handling of the Irish question. It is a duty every man owes to his neighbour, to give him justice. Our public men should be tried on this principle, and confidence placed in them proportionally as they en- courage freedom and justice. As I have already trespassed sufficiently upon your space, I will reserve the conclush,n of my letter for your next issue.—Your a truly, Warrington, May 30th, 1082. BENJ. SAWDON.

div.head: WALKING DAY QUESTION.
div.p: THE WALKING DAY QUESTION.

MEETING OF SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS. THE MAYOR'S DECISION ACCEPTED. For this year the vexed question of Walking Day is at last definitely settled. At a meeting held in thq, Town Hall, on the 4th ult., it was decided to hold Walking Day on the Ist Friday in July, Lut subsequently the Mayor yielding to the representations of a deputation from a meetine, of work- ingmen, altered the day to the 23rd June, and the town was placarded to that effect. To consider this decision, on Tuesday evening a meeting of representatives from the various Sunday schools was held in the British Workman Public-house' Horsemarket-street. With the exception of about five ..schools two representatives were present from each school. Mr. Thomas Birchall was voted to the chair. After a conversation, conducted with calmness, it was de- cided without a ,iissentient voice to accept the Mayor's decision. A report of the proceedings wilr be found below. ' Mr. War. ROBERTS explained that as the secretary of the Nanconformist Sunday schools he had been requested to summon that meeting to consider the present condition of affairs relative to the vexed question of Walking Day. The Sunday schools of Warrington maintained that this was a question for them to decAe, and that they bad a perfect right to fix a day which, in their judgment, was most con- N enient for the Sunday schools, and which would not inter- fere with the general arrangements of manufacturers and shopkeepers in the town. He narrated what had already taken place with regard to the subject, and referring to the Mayor's announcement, said the Sunday school people felt that the Mayor had not acted quite fairly towards them. ( Hear, hear).' They had all the greatest respect for his Worship, and they would be extremely sorry to do anything which would interfere with the good feeling which existed in all their schools towards him. (Hear, hear). They thought, however, that he might at least have taken some of them into his confidence, and, before issuing his final decision, consulted with some representative of the Sunday schools. (Hear, hear.) The question that night was—Would it be wise for them, in the face of what had gone forth to the public, to create any further unpleasantness in the town by persisting in the resolution arrived at at the town's meeting? Or would it be better to accept, for this year, the Mayor's decision ; and for another year go in for having Walking Hay on Whit Tuesday? (Hear, hear.) He found there was an almost unanimous opinion in Warrington in favour of having Walking Day in Whit week, and if they could remove the strong objection they all felt about race day by adopting Whit Tuesday as Walking Day for the future, did not they think that would be the wisest course? He thought that would meet with the general approval of the town; for the shopkeekers he knew were at least ten to one in favour of Whit week, and they would be prepared to shut up their shops from Saturday to Wednesday to allow this to be done. He was sorry to say he had not been fairly treated the last day or two through that meeting having been called. It had not been his doing. He was the servant of the Nonconformist Sunday schools of Warrington, and he should never hesitate to do his duty when circum- stances required it; and at the dictation of their schools be _

bad called- that meeting. The CHAIRMAN said he had the greatest esteem and respect for the Mayor, but he thought the Sunday school teachers had not been anything like fairly dealt with in this matter—(bear, hear)—after theexpression of opinion given at the Town Hall, when there was not a single dissentient to the wishes expressed by the representatives of the Sunday and day schools. With reference to Mr. Roberts' suggestion , as to Whit week, there was one thing he could not overlook. Sunday schools did not need to add anything to their cost. They all no doubt found much difficulty in raising adequate funds for these sort of occasions, and having the school demonstration in Whit week meant more expense, because 1 the railway companies would not give them any advantages then, if they wished to go any distance. In his opinion that was an obstacle. Mr. WILLETT said he had there to express the opinion of the majority of teachers at Cockhedge school, that Walking Day should be on the 7th July. (Hear, hear.) They would not give way or be " bamboozled " out of that day, and the whole business ho thought had not been carried on very fairly, and was not very creditable to two or three gentlemen whom he did not wish to name. He could not see why a handful of 20 or 30 betting men should rule when the children's anniversary should be. There was no reason why they should deviate from the course they had already laid down, and he did not understand the Mayor changing his mind because waited upon by a deputation. The Mayor bad acted very indiscreetly in changing the day at all. (Hear, hear.) He concluded by moving that they adhere to July 7th, the day fixed at the meeting in the Town Hall. Mr. FRANK WILLIAMS, representing Bank Quay Mission, said they were in favotar of falling in with the Mayor's wishes for this year at least; and afterwards to adhere to the first Friday in July. This was also Mr. Crosfield's wish. _ _

Mr. JOHN TAYLOR said that how the Mayor could bow to the decision of the deputation which waited upon i him, he could not for the life of him see. He came to this meeting with rather strong feelings to enter his protest against the Mayor's decision in favour of Newton Race Friday. (Hear, hear.) He thought it a shame they should have been ignored in the way they had. The proper csurse would have been to have called another meeting, and let the matter be discussed again. He seconded the resolution that they adhere to the first Friday in July. Mr. WALLINGTON o'osereed that it was said the majority of the manufacturers were in favour of Race Friday. Mr. WILLETT said he had had an interview with Mr. Barlow, of Messrs. Rylands Bros., who stated tho firm would not stop on Newton Race Friday or Saturday, but on the 7th July, according to present arrangements. The CHAIRMAN remarked that they did not know who these manufacturers were; it was only a rumour. Mr. LAWLESS moved an amendment that Walking Day be held on Newton Race Friday for this year only. As the town had been placarded, the teachers of St. PAW'S schools thought this would be the best course. Mr. TAIIRANAO (Parish Church), in seconding the amend- ment, said that although the teachers of the Parish Church schools felt they had been hardly dealt with as a body—in fact, almost played with as children—they did not wish for this year to act contrarY to the Mayor's wishes. Before next year, however, they thought a meeting of those con- cerned shou'd be called to settle the question. His feelings were so strong with regard to the conduct of certain indi- viduals that he was afraid to give them utterance. The CHAIRMAN said that whatever decision they arrived at they all felt that they had not been treated exactly as they deserved, and he bad hastily drawn up a resolution somewhat expressive of this feeling. It would perhaps be as well to leave the motion and amendment in abeyance whilst they considered this resolution. It was as follows: "This meeting of Sunday school teachers deeply regret that the decision come to at the meeting, called by the Mayor on May 4th, and in favour of which representatives of Sunday- schools were entirely unanimous, should have been com- pletely ignored by his worship in deference to the clamour of a class of persons who had no practical connection or sympathy with Sunday schools, and without any consulta- tion with, or consideration for, the feelings or wishes of the workers in the said schools; and this meeting desires to ex- press its conviction that this opposition to the wishes of those most concerned, is unjustifiable and uncalled for, as the stoppage of work on the children's treat day has been considered by mann racturers generally as contributing to the convenience of Sunday schools and not as affording facili- ties for attendance at any local races." (Hear, hear.) Mr. COATES (Parish Church) thought the resolution could be altered, and he suggested a few amendments. He should not like to clash with the working men,—(hear,hear) —and he thought they would gain their point quite as well by agreeing with them a little. The Mayor had acted un- fairly indeed to the Sunday school teachers and man igers— (hear, hear),—and highly as he respected him, he thought he had made the greatest mistake lie had ever made during the whole of his mayoralty. (Hear, hear.) Mr. W. ROBERTS Said there was no doubt a tremendous amount of feeling on this question, and especially among the working men, and he should be sorry for anything to be done at that meeting which would increase the feeling. (Hear, hear.) Tha CHAIRMAN observed that they had duties to perform towards their setiools, and must not look merely to what outsiders thought. They clnsidered the interests of their schools paramount to any mere attendance at the races, —(hear, hear)—and conseqaently ought not to stint their mouth. Mr. JNO. HALL (Baptist) though they were treating the working men a little urljwely in having a day which would throw them out of employment. He did not think they ought to dictate te the working men on what day they should stop, and for this year he thought it would be better to fail in with the Mayor's arrangements. A Gentleman replied that by having Walking Day on the 7th July, they were really giving the men two days' work, as almost all the firms would be stocktaking. The CHAIRMAN: Mr. Hall is entirely under a misapprehen- sion. We should not stop on Newton Race Friday. Mr. WALLINGTON slid Wycliffe Sunday school was in favour of the 7th July, but their delegates had discretionary power, Rod would fall in with the majority. The reselat:on read by the Chairman, amended as follows, was flow moved by Mr. COATES, and carried unanimously:— This meeting f Sunday school teachers deeply regrets that the decision come to at the meeting called by the Mayer on. May 4th, and in favour of which the represen- tatives of Sunday schools were entirely unanimous, ehould have been so completely ignored by his pv,e nn odp.e practical reet ccael tcoo nt hn the ept iroens s ourr es yOmf ap act ilia; sw iot hf ue rnsdoanys wWl°lorshllai schools and without any consultation with, or consideration for the feelings or wishes of the said schools; and this meeting desires to express its conviction that this opposition

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 3, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 3, 1882.

to the wishes of those most concerned, is unjustifiable and uncalled for, as the stoppage of work on the children's treat day has been considered by the manufacturers generally, as contributing to the convenience of the Sunday schools only." Several representatives spoke of the advisability of now confoi ming- to the'decision of the Mayor for this year, and Mr. WM. ROBERTS said if they did so, it would be the means of settling the question afterwards, because he felt confident another year it would be held in Whit week. (Cries of "No.") The CHAIRMAN suggested that Mr. Willett 'should with- draw his resolution, but that gentleman said he should make I a breach of trust if he did so. _ .

_ Mr. TAYLOR saw the propriety of accepting the jMayor's decision, and withdrew from seconding the motion. The amendment was then read as follows, and put as a motion :—" That for this year we agree to support thedecision of the Mayor, fixing Walking Day on Newton Race Friday, but that a meeting of Sunday school teachers, manufacturers, add tradesmen be held to decide the day for future years." _ .
This was carried without dissent, and the meeting con- cluded with a vote of thanks to the Castnmarr, who promised to pay the expenses incurred in engaging the room.

Second heat: 1, T. Craddock, Warrington, 185 yards; 2, W. Aukland, Warrington, 200 yards, Third heat: 1, J. Ash- worth, Salford,loo yards; 2, W. Doming, junior, Widnes, 90 yards. In the finil heat they ran in the third lap, as they had started, in the following order—Aukland, Craddock, Overton, Parry, Ashworth, and Doming. When he had done about 30 yards of the next lap, Craddock by some means came to grief, and Aukland was overhauled soon afterwards by Overton and Parry, while Doming, the last man, bad suc- ceeded in passing Ashworth. In the fifth lap Overton led by a about a yard, and Parry and Ashworth, who had re- gained his lost ground, struggled for second place, closely fol- lowed by Doming, all having passed Aukland who then retired. Overton kept the lead in the sixth lap, but Ashworth was now sec,md, Parry third, and Doming last. In this order they passed on the next lap, and Overton won by about six yards, the earns distance separating Ashworth second, and Parry third. Doming, who rode most determinedly, was some half dozen yards behind the third man at the finish. TUG or WAR.—Four teams entered, but only two engaged in the contest, viz., Monks, Hall and Co.'s team, Captain T. Melia, cud Whitecross Wire and Iron Co.'s team, Captain C. Burton. This was a very exciting event, and, as previously stated, many of the spectators broke into the enclosure and surrounded the contestants, who struggled bravely for supremacy. In the first pull the Whiteeross team, who were on lower ground, won easily, but on changing places Monks, Hall, and Co.'s team did their utmost to turn the scale, and for several minutes neither side appeared to gain the slightest advantage. Ultimately the men from White- cross proved the strongest, and they were declared the winners.

440 YARDS FLAT RACE HANDTCAP.—First prize £3, se- cond £l, tnird 10s. Thera were 44 entries, and 30 competi- tors ran in three heats, which were won as follows :—First heat: 1, N. G. Woodyat, Liverpool, 30 yards; 2, E. W. Mercer, Prestwich, 21 yards; 3, D. Kershaw, Rochdale, 22 yards. Second heat: 1, J. H. Heys, Heywood, 38 yards; 2, W. Wareing, Widnes, 35 yards; 3, S. Boardman, Warring- ton, 22 yards. Third heat: 1, George Taylor. Manchester, 38 yards; 2, G. Bell, Manchester, 35 yards; 3, D. A. Hard- ing, Widnes, 35 yards. Final heat: 1, G. Bell; 2, J. H. Heys; 3, Geo. Taylor. Won easily. HALF %TILE FLAT RACE HANDICAP. First prize £3, second £l, third 10s. Thirty-five men turned out for this race, which was keenly contested. J. Wright, Widnes, 53 yards start, won the first heat, J. L. Neville, Man- chester, 45 yards, being second, and J. Smith, Widnes, 70 yards' third. The second heat was won by G. 11. Cross, Altrincham, 68 yards, W. Jeffrey, Stretford, 55 yards, second, and R. Harrison, Hor- wich, 38 yards, third. In the final heat Cross only just managed to win, he being closely pressed by Smith second, and Neville third.

pie if it was a sound one, as we think it was. A meeting was called on Monday evening at the Wesleyan school, and delegates appointed from the different Dissenting bodies in Earlestown and Newton met to deliberate as to what was to be done this year to stop the "unholy traffic," we fear with no better result than for the last 50 years, unless they can prevail upon their own people to set a good example of abstaining even from the appearance of evil. This same spirit of inquiry and demand for efficiency is seen in quite a different vocation in life. For Volunteers have now an opportunity of showing what mettle they are made of, mentally as well as physically, by undertaking an examination in military tactics, such as that which will be held in Warrington on Tuesday next, when officers from the rank of captain and upwards in this military division, will have an opportunity of competing for honours with officers of the line regiments, and of proving their fitness for superior command in case of emergency, when the Volun- teers and regulars may at any time be requested to coalesce, which we hope is a time far distant. There is no doubt that many of the Volunteer officers were, at the outset of the movement, more ornamental than useful to the several corps to which they belonged, and owed their military posi- tion often to their social position, which must necessarily have been subordinated if ever they had been called into the held. But the Volunteer movement, having attained its majority, has been looked upon with more favour by its elder brother of the line, and latterly better treated than when it was a 'prentice hand, having in the meantime developed some workmanlike qualities not to be despised. And now, to come to closer quarters, there is to be a sifting and winnowing, when, no doubt, many, from lack of time and opportunity, or perhaps from want of a real aptitude and genius for the art of war, will fail to find the much- desired letter (T) after their names on the army and navy list, where their names now appear, along with their brother officers of these services. We have good hope, and sincerely trust, that none of our local officers may fail, for it has involved severe study, intense application, and no little out- lay to win this much-desired and real honour. The examination of pupil teachers, preliminary to the examination of the schools in this district in June, was held on Saturday, in St. Peter's School, Newton, when 44 were examined, in subjects akin to those in which the scholars will be tested. As happens at each of these half-yearly ex- aminations, several of the pupil teachers hope to pass for a further course of education at the training colleges, the life at which, of itself, has an educational effect and is much valued as giving them position and status in their calling in after life, although it involves some self-abnegation for a couple Of years while attending the course of study there, and perhaps as many before; unless they happen to be well to do in their circumstances. A high standard of mental and moral excellence is thus attained which must be a life- long benefit to them and to those entrusted to their tuition. The exact degree of scholarship is not, however, to be con- fused with the collegiate training given at the colleges attached to our Universities. Even so, however, the stan- dards are being gradually raised to a height that might stagger some academicians of former years, who pride them- selves not a little upon their pass and class, when these were easier of attainment by reason of the smaller number who ventured up the steps of Parnassus there to inscribe heir initials.

div.head: DARESBITRY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: DARESBITRY PETTY SESSIONS.

TUESDA.Y.—Before Messrs. E. Greenall and R. Pierpoint. A NEGLIGENT FATHER.—Arab Chadwick, labourer, of Stockton Heath, was summoned by the attendance officer, Mr. De Prez, for neglecting to send his two children regularly to school. The defendant had been fined twice, and committed to goal once for this offence, but the children were running ANA the street and begging. A warrant was issued for the apprehension of the defendant, who did not

appear. A DEFAULTING FARM LABOURER. Mr. John Weir, farmer, Lower Walton, summoned Michael Varley for 12s. compensation by reason of his having neglected to fulfil his contract of service. When Mr. Weir was away at market, the defendant, who did rot appear, borrowed 3s. from Mrs. Weir, and left the farm. He did not return, and was now working at Dallam Forge.—The Bench made an order for 9s. as the claim included the sum borrowed. GAME TRESPASS.—SamueI Bailey and Joseph Proudlam, boatmen on the cabal, were charged with having, on the 28th April, at Moore, trespassed on land in the occupation of Thomas Percival, in search of game.—The gamekeeper gave evidence of the defendants sending a dog in chase of a hare.—Bailey was ordered to pay the costs, 9s. 61, but as there was a doubt in the case against Proudlam, it was dis- missed. PROSECUTIONS UNDER THE CANAL BOATS Ac r.—Richard Fox, owner of the canal boat "Havelock," and liviug at Whaley Bridge, was summoned by Mr. Farrington, inspector to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, for using his boat as a dwellinghouse without having it registered as required by Act of Parliament. Defendant was fined 103. and costs. —W. W. Lester and Sons. of Stoke-on-Trent, were summoned for a similar offence. On the 13th May, the inspector found the boat "Cupid," belonging to the defendants, being used as a dwellinghouse without being registered. It was shown that the boat had not been registered in consequence of the negligence of the inspector at Stoke-on-Trent, who, the gentleman representing the defendants said, was not a proper man for the post. The Bench under the circumstances, ordered the defendants to pay the costs. A HARDWORKED CARTER.—AIfred Barlow, a carter living at Warrington, was charged with being asleep whilst in charge of a horse and lurry at Stretton on the 21st April. The defendant said he had at that time not been in bed for four days.—He was ordered to pay costs ss. 6d. A WHITLEY SUPERIOR BEERSELLER CONVICTED.—Wm. Worrell, holder of an off license to sell beer, at Whitley Superior, was charged with selling beer to Thomas Towey, Michael Vasey, Michael Pyton, and Patrick Pyton, to be drunk on a field in his occupation. The four men were also charged with aiding and abetting. Mr. Moore defended Worrell and the Pvtons. Towev and Vasey had absconded. P.C. Speed said that on Sunday, the 7th May, whilst near the defendant's beerhouse, his attention was drawn to some men in a field behind. He went to the place, and there he found Michael and Patrick Pyton and Tovvey and Vasey sitting on a bench under a tree. Near them was a stone bottle containing about half a gallon of beer,a quart jug full of beer, and the men were drinking from four -1-pint cups. He asked them where they had got the beer, and they replied they had received the beer and utensils from Worrell's. The officer then questioned Worrell, who said he knew nothing about the men drinking in the field—" speak to his missus." Mrs. Worrell said she had served the men at 25 minutes past two, and she had supplied them with the cups, upon which they had paid 2d. each. The field was about 20 yards from the house of the defendant.—Mr. Moore sub- mitted there was no case made out under the section upon which the prosecution was taken. They had to prove that the land where the men were sitting was in the occupation of the defendant.—The magistrates' clerk ruled there was a pi.ima facie case.-1 he defendant was sworn, and stated the piece of ground upon which the men were sitting was only a few yards square, and was divided from the field for which he paid rent, by a brook.—The officer said the defendant's horse had grazed on the land many times.—Mrs. Worrell was called, and also stated the land was not under the defendant's control. There ran through it a footpath which led to Northwich The bench spoken of belonged to the defendant.—Mr. Pierpoint said either the land was under the control of the defendant or it was a highway. Mr. Moore could take his choice.—Mr. Moore addressed the Bench in extennation of the circum- stances, and said the defendants were not aware they were doing wrong.—The Superintendent said he had received many complaints, and the defendant Worral had been warned several times by the police.—Worral was fined 20s. and costs, but as this was his first appearance' his license would not be endorsed.—Michael and Patrick Pyton were each fined ss. and costs. INTERESTING TO FARMERS.—About twelve summonses had been issued against farmers in the district for attempt- ing to defraud the London and North-Western Railway Co. by sending a larger quantity of milk in their cans than they were registered to hold—Mr. Robert Davies, who appeared for the defendants, said he had bad a conference with the company's solicitor, Mr. Preston, and he asked with his per- mission, that the cases might be adjourned to next sessions. In the meantime a meeting of parties interested would be called to devise some means whereby these complaints might be avoided in the future. The cases were adjourned.

div.head: WARRINGTON ATHLETIC FESTIVAL-
div.p: WARRINGTON ATHLETIC FESTIVAL-

Athletic sports were held at Warrington on Saturday last, in the field opposite the Town Hall. Several hundred per- sons attended, and as it was arnounced the proceeds would be devoted to the Warrington Infirmary, a fair sum will doubt- less be handed over to the secretary of this deserving institution. The weather was showery, and the rain con- siderably interfered with the arrangements; but on the whole the festival passed off well. There were seven events, for which 263 competitors entered, and the close contests which took place proved Mr. J. B. Yeomans to be a most capable handicapper. The prizes consisted of cheques, which varied in amount from £5 to 53. Good arrangemerts had been made for the accommodation of the spectators, and there were the usual tents for the competitors, the secretary, and the sale of refreshments. With the exception of the occasion, during the tug of war, when the on-lookers broke into the middle of the field, the visitors were well behaved, although the shilling folks must have been annoyed by the cries of the numerous sporting men, whose offers to back the field" occasionally reached the grand stand. Sounds of merriment frequently came across the course from the part devoted to the sixpenny spectators, who varied the proceeds by indulging in the game well known by the name of "Whoa Emma," and when they showed a disposi- tion to take a little interest in the races, the ears of all present were assailed by the disagreeable whir of rattles, , which continued so long as to give one the impression that the stallholders had entered into a competition as to who could produce the most noise. Far more pleasant and enjoyable were the strains produced by St. Peter's school band, which, under the conductorship of Mr. Thomas Arm- strong, rendered a selection of music in good style. The officials were as follow :—Judges: Messrs. E. Ankland, J. Smethurst, Whitehead, J. H. Ardwick (Midland athlete), and P. Lawless; referee, Mr. Thomas Morris; clerks of the course, Messrs. C. Leigh and H. Eisen- heigh ; starter, Mr. R. Andrews; handicapper and hon. sec., Mr. J. B. Yeomans. The following is a list of the several events:—

300 YARDS FLAT RACE HANDICAP (YOUTHS UNDER 17). —First prize £5, second 155., third ss. Out of 49 competi- tors entered for this event 40 put in an appearance, and it was run in five heats, which resulted as follows :—First heat : 1 J. Warham, 2 J. H. Draper, 3 G. Grounds, War- rington. Second heat: 1 George Kyneston, Earlestown ; 2 R. Lewis, Earlestown ; 3 J. Rigby, Warrington. Third heat: 1 H. Jones, 2 J. Lawless, 3 J. Plunkett, Warrington. Fourth heat: 1 F. Thompson, Golborne ; 2 H. Green, Warrington ; 3J. McMahon, Farnworth. Fifth heat: IJ. Clarke, Wid- nes ; 2 G. F. Davies, Appleton; 3 S. Johnson, Salford. Final heat: 1 J. Clarke, 2 G. F. Davies, 3 J. Plunkett. Won easily. 120 YARDS FLAT RACE HANDICAP.—First prise £5, 2nd £1 10s., 3rd 103. For this race there were 62 entries, and only abmit a dozen failed to conic to the mark. The ten heats were won by the following :-Ist beat, N. G. Wood- yat, Liverpool, 20 yards; 2nd heat, J. J. Hartley, St. Helens, 19 yards; 3rd heat, F. Webster, Warrington', 24 yards; 4th heat, W. Raynor, Salford, 13 yards; sth heat, G. Ratcliffe, Warrington, 20 yards; 6th heat, R. Valentine. St. Helens, 17 yards; 7th heat, I'. Cunninghatn, Orford, 22 yardi ; Bth heat, W. Patten, Farnworth, 19- yards; 9th heat—dead heat—J. Kay, Salford, 15r- yards, ani J. Dom- bell, Warrington, 24 yards; tenth heat, R. Glossop, Moe- ton, 19A yards. Final heat, 1, R. Glossop; 2, N. G. Wood- Tat; 3,-J. Kay. Close finish. ONE MILE FLAT RACE HANDICAP.—First prize £4, 2nd £1 10s., 3rd 103. Thirty out of the thirty-four competitors who entered for this race put iii an appearance, and the event was most closely contested, R. Barlow, Radcliffe, 140 yards start, proved the winner, J. Wright, of Widnes, 100 "yards, being second; and W. W. Gibson, Crewe, Alexander C.C., 120 yards, third. Barloty took the lead soon after the start, and "maintained his position until he reached the straight in the last lap, when Wright forged ahead within about six yards of the tape. Barlow, however, kept close to Wright, and by a splendid spurt, when close on the tape, came in first. ONE MILE BICYCLE RACE HANDICAP.—First prize £3, sec,nd £l, third 103. Great interest centred in this event, which brought out 18 bicyclists who competed in three heats. The winner's were:—First heat : 1, T. H. Overton, Liver- pool, 150 yards start; 2, F. Parry, Shipbrook, 130 yards.

div.head: CO-OPERATIVE CONGRESS AT OXFORD.
div.p: CO-OPERATIVE CONGRESS AT OXFORD.

The Sheldonian Theatre, Oxford, was crowded on Mon- day on the occasion of the fourteenth annual co-operative congress of delegates from co-operative societies in Great Britain and Ireland. Lord Reay occupied the chair, and delegates attended from all parts of tl.ea United Kingdom.— In the coarse of his inaugural address, Lord Reay said it was impossible to overrate the influence of the co-operative movement. It had arisen among the working classes and had ascended into the highest regions, where it had obtained a firm footing English co-operators had never boasted that they were going to renovate English society, and the conse- quence was undoubtedly that by their aid English society had been spared a good deal of the friction which they saw elsewhere. Co-operation had been eminently fair in its com- petition, and had organised thrift on an irreproachable footing. Though a great deal more had to be done in that direction, co-operation had been the best friend of capital, and was therefore the strongest ally of the middle classes. He was sure that at the congress they would deride and scout the idea of annihilating the middle class. (Applause.) His lordship then referred at some length to the spread of the co-operative movement abroad. The question now arose whether English co-operation could not reach a higher de- velopment in the direction of productive co-operation. Could any better use be found for the profits which bad accrued and were accruing to distributive co-oporation The great difference between the productive associations and the distributive ones seemed to be this that the danger of capital being withdrawn and of membership being brought to a speedy conclusion in bad times was greater in the former than in the latter. These perils would have to be specially guarded against. Capital provided by the existing distributive associations could, however, be advanced in such a form as to exclude the possibility of its sudden withdrawal. On the other hand, the productive associations would have to submit to the supervision of tte distributive directors of the associations. The obvious advantages of this supervision were that it was received by those who were specially imbued with the spirit of co-operation, who were the best customers of the pro- ductive association, in that experience had given them a knowledge of the needs of the market. For the success of a practical co-operative association, a combination of circum- stances must arise which presupposed a rather high civilisa- tion and a number of virtues, such as perseverance, self- sacrifice, and discipline, in all its members. (Applause.) Co-operation was an immense step in advance; it was a great social revolution, and it had a great future before it. Revolutionary experiments were reforms, and co-operation was a great reform because it was a revolutionary experi- ment. (Applause.) The co-operative movement was dis- liked most by the revolutionary parties of all countries. Co-operation was one of the highest forms of intellectual democracy. The members of co-operative societies would bring to the solution of other questions minds well trained, accustomed to that sobriety of judgment and that self- discipline which excluded the possibility of lending a willing ear to chimerical schemes of nationalising capital and of equalising all incomes. (Applause.) The marvellous pros- perity of the cc-operative stores had been reached by a steady process of slow growth. It would be a fatal mistake to claim n for the co-operative movement the credit of being a panacea. There had been co-operative failures and there would be failures in the future. The annual meetings were intended to limit their number and to increase the success

of the movement by increasing the safeguards which ex- perience showed to be requisite. (Applause.) In closing, he cou!d not do better than ask them to pay a tribute to the memory of Lord Frederick Cavendish, whose cruel and un- timely death Englishmen in all parts of the world had deeply felt, btctuse his life was one of devotion to the performance of public duties, because he never shrank from giving to the country his best hours until he fell in its service. This noble examply of single-minded patriotism should encourage the humble co-operator to persevere, however difficult he mi,r,ht find the restraint wt.ich he had wisely imposed upon himself, without which neither co-operation nor any other human institution could reach its goal. (Applause.) The Congress resumed its sitting on Tuesday. The President congratulated the delegates upon the reception they had received from the University. Mr. A. H. D. Acland, of Christ Church, said that the University was now open to all creeds and to all classes, and hoped that the seed sown by the delegates would not be in vain. The Congress then considered the reports of the central board. The Congress also considered the reports of committees, and resolved— " That. the Insurance company be requested to reconsider the question of the distribution of the surplus profits; " "That the central board he instructed to form a special fund in aid of co-operative production;" That subscriptions be collected for a lifeboat to be presented to the National Society;" and "That the congress of 1883 be held at Ed i nbergh." _ _

The Congress concluded on Thursday, after papers had been read by Messrs. G. J. Holyoake, London, and J. Allan, CitaTow, on the revenue of the central board. The proceed- ings, which have been most successful throughout, were brought to a close with a series of votes of thanks to the Mayor and Corporation, and the university and college authorities, for the facilities which had been given to inspect the various buildings.

div.head: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
LOCAL NOTES.

The inhabitants of Earlestown have had female lecturers on temperance topics, but the appearance of a female preacher at the Welsh Congregational Chapel on Sunday drew such a goodly audience of Welsh-speaking people as might have made Bodicea feel happy. The Sunday school teachers in Eariestown are very much exercised just now I.y the thoughts of what will happen on Race Sunday—when the ownium gatherunt of the country side congregates on the common, converging from all points of the compass on the only public-house there, which, for- tunately for the teachers, and thanks to the landlord, is not permitted to open on that day. But the evil does not stop there, for it is said that illicit means of obtaining drink are known to the initiated. Worse, however, from this point of view is the fact that many Sunday school scholars find their way there, not from Newton and Earlestown only, but from miles around, for such is the mania for keeping this unholy appointment that they openly disregard the advice of both friends and teachers to go there—and to see what? Abso- lutely nothing but a crowd and to make one of it. Well, this state of thing has existed for more Man half a century, and all the schools have had ample experience of it since the institution of Sunday schools in Newton, just so long ago. All sorts of devices have been tried to wean the rising generation from this absurd habit; and cheap trips, when they really deserved that name, and excursions in abund- ance have been organised from time to time to win them away. but still the evil of the race week remains and will not diminish now that more racing is to be afforded the inhabitants of Newton, Earlestown, and the region round about. A couple of years or so ago, a committee of Sunday school teachers tried to ignore the existence of the races by putting off the excursions and "field day " during that week altogether. Each went his several way, and left the parents of the scholars to look after their children themselves, as indeed they ought to do, and thus stultified the well-considered action of their pre- decessors, because the good folks in Warrington had resolved to hold their Walking Day at a time more convenient to the majority there, forgetting that the evil was at their own door, and could not be ignored unless by giving up all they had ever contended for. Not that St. Peter's, St. Mary's, Or any other church calling itself after any saint ever paid the slightest attention to excursions, tea parties, picnics, or any- thing else during race week. They left all that to the Non- conformists, who might protest as much as they liked, for many of these were seen taking surreptitious walks on that. very day. And there was strong temptation to go to the races on the day when there was neither trip nor tea party. It was surely an error of judgment to give up their princi.

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.

On Whit Monday a gala, in aid of the funds of the Wigan Infirmary, was held in the Mesnes Park, Wigan, kindly lent for the occasion by the Corporation. The weather was gloriously fine, and there was a large attendance. In the evening there was a capital display of fireworks. THEFT OF A HonsE.—On Tuesday,. the Wigan borough magistrates committed for trial at the sessions a youth, aged 15, named William Harrop, of Manchester, on a charge of having stolen a horse at the last Wigan fair. The horse hard been sold by a person from Farnworth, and Harrop offered to hold it whilst the parties settled up. During their absence at a public-house the prisoner bolted with the horse, but he was subsequently apprehended in Manchester, having in the meantime exchanged the horse and sold the-other one. PUBLIC BATES FOR WWAN.—On Mond y, the Mayor if Wigan (Mr. Alderman Hopwood) opened the new public baths for the borough. which have been erected by the cor- poration on land in Millgate, adjoining the Free Public Library. To the late Mrs. Knowles, the wife of Mr. Thomas Knowles, M.P., must be given the credit for investing the movement with vitality, for it was ow'ng to a promise by that lady to contribute £l,OOO towards such an institution that the matter was taken up by the corporation. On the 27th October last the foundation-stone was laid by the then ' mayor (Mr. W. J. Lamb), in the absence, through ill health, of Mr. Knowles. Mr. Knowles's son, on the completion of the ceremony, handed over to the Mayor a cheque from his father for £l,OOO, the amount promised during her lifetime by Mrs. Knowles. Passing through the principal entrance, to the left is the ticket office, and opposite a waiting-room. Turning to the right, the gentlemen have a first-class plunge bath, 58 feet by 22 feet; and in the same corridor are four first-class slipper baths and Also a Roman bath. At the end of the main corridor is the second-class male plunge bath, 68ft. by 261 t. To the first-class plunge bath there are 22 dressing-rooms, and to the second-class 23. There is a separate entrance to the ladies' department, which has a plunge bath 23ft. by 16ft. The contoactor has been Mr. W. Winnard, of Wian, and the total cost, including the site, will be about £5,000. Monday's proceedings commenced with a procession through the principal streets of the town. On'arriving at the baths, the chairman of the Public Baths Committee (Mr. Park) handed to the mayor a gold key, with which his worship opened the front entrance and de- clared the building open. The mayor, ma the conclusion of the ceremony, entertained the corporation and invited guests to luncheon in the council chamber.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

LECTURE ON "THE PRESENT AGE," &C.—The Rev. W. I J. Hopper, of the Free Methodist Church, Winsford, de- I livered a lecture on "The present ago: its advantages and requirements," in the Free Methodist Chapel, Station-road, on Wednesday evening last. There was a fair attendance for Whit week, but far less than was hoped for by the friends and the Trust Fund intended t 3 be benefited. The lecturer dwelt on the gloomy side of the age but shortly, when he noticed the Sabbath breaking, avarice, and in fidelity, with forms of Fenianism, &c., which have appeared of late. The brighter aspect which he styled golden, had more attraction. Our literature and literary opportunities and advantages with our vast array of books, crowding like snow flakes in our way, not less than the spirit of invention, improvements, and developed resources, called forth some glowing remarks. He spoke of the scientific researches with the theological tendencies, our political and commercial relationships, and the passing away of the old world notions for far more liberal and broad opinions. He showed the future depending on this present, the kind of men we should cultivate now to secure a share in the grand results which would hereafter be. Many poetical passages illustrated the lecture, pointedly Wolsey's fall and speech to Cromwell. I Mr. Buckley, F.R.G.S. presided.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.—On Sunday last, two sermons were preached in the Congregational Chapel, Gol- borne, afternoon and evening, by the Rev. P. Webster, of Presall. In the morning a service of song was given, en- titled " Memories of Bible scenes." All the services were well attended, and the collections during the day amounted to £3O Os. 3d. Pupil'. TEACHERS' EXAMINATION.—On Saturday last, the pupil teachers of Golborne and district were examined in the Parkside Mills School, by Mr. Foyster. Several of the schools in Go'borne will be examined also during Whit- week. PROMISSORY NOTE DISPUTE —At the Leigh County Court, on Friday, Wm. Woodcock, late of Golborne, sued Joseph Bate for the recovery of 10 guineas lent on a pro- miesory note.—Plaintiff was represented by Mr. Taylor (Messrs. John Taylor and Sons), and defendant by Mr. Moore, of Warrington.—The money was leet to defendant and a man named Wm. Wright, who has since gone to America. The question was whether defendant signed the promissory note and knew its contents, and to prove this Elizabeth Woodcock, from whom the money was obtained, and her daughter, Elizabeth Pitman, were called. These persons could neither read nor write, but they said they saw the defendant write something, Wright having previously read it over. Oa being cross-cxamined by Mr. Moore, the first-named witness said the sum lent originally was £9, a further sum of £1 10s. being afterwards advanced, and the money was handed to Wright.—The defence was that Bate never signed the peper or authorised anyone else to do so for him.—Mr. Taylor having asked defendant to write his name, the signature was banded up to his Honour, who said this and the writing on the note were remarkably alike, and he must come to the conclusion that they were the same handwriting. He was unable to make out the exact mean- ing of the note owing to the peculiar phraseology adopted, but he held defendant to be liable for the £9 advanced on the first occasion, and for this sum he gave judgment. His Honour then directed the papers and signatures to be placed in charge of the registrar of the court. Addressing defend- ant, he said he had put himself in great danger of being prosecuted for perjury for sayieg he did not sign the note. —Defendant: I never did.—His Honour said he believed he did.

div.head: i4YMII.
div.p: i4YMII.
VAGBANCY.—For begging, at Lymm on the 29th May, Richard Hewitt, and John Griffiths, were each cornmitted to gaol for 14 days.
THE LYMNI SEWERAGE SCHEME.

For the purpose of considering the adoption of some ' scheme of sewage disposal, a special meeting of Lynam Local Board was held on Monday evening. Mr. Johnson, of the • firm of Messrs. Brockbank, Wilson, and Mulliner, was in attendance: At the call of the chairman, the clerk (Mr. Ridgway) read the plans of the various schemes, the cost of which are as follows :—A scheme £4010; B scheme, £4,436; C scheme, £3,933. The following correspondence had passed with reference to the subject :—" Local Govern- ment Board, Whitehall, S.W., 9th May, 1882. Sir,—' am :lirected by the Local Government Board to advert to your letter of the 23rd January last withl-eference to the sewerage of the district of the Lymm Local Board, and to enquire whether an amended scheme has been prepared, and con- sidered by the Local Board. If so, the Board would be glad to be informed of the result.—l am, sir, your obedient ser- vant, W. ROTTON, assistant secretary." " Warrington, 16th May, 1882. Mr. Ross and the Lytnm Sewerage.—Dear Sir, —We have been instructed to communicate with you again in reference to the abJve. Mr. Ross has been in hopes that before this time if commencement would have been ruMs)

with the works for abating the nuisance caused by the sewage flowing into his dam. This latterly has become so much worse that it is a serious injury to his property, and considering the sickness which is now prevalent in Lymn we must on his behalf urge the Board to press on the sewage scheme with all possible speed, so that the work may be commenced with as little delay as practicable. We have previously drawn attention to the matter, as you are aware ; but as the year is getting on, and we see no preparation for a commencement of the work, we feel compelled to add that unless the Board can give us a satisfactory undertaking that every effort will be made to clear the dam of sewage as speedily as possible, we shall have to consider the question of taking further action on our client's behalf, yours faith- fully, JouN WHITE, MCIVER and Co.—T. J. Ridgway, Esq, Clerk, Lymm Local Board." "Dane Bank, 19th May, 1892. To the Chairman, Lymm Local Board. Dear Sir,— In reply to your letter of the 17th ult. I am glad to have your assurance that the plan for the purifying of the Stretton brook and dam from sewage, is being hastened as much as possible. I feel that I have been over patient in the matter, as what was at first a nuisance is now developing into a source of great danger; and until the Pollution Act is in this case satisfactorily complied with, it will be my duty not to allow any false feeling of delicacy to influence my future conduct. With regard to your very natural suggestion of allowing the water from the mill to have free course through for a few days by letting off the dam, I would not venture upon my own responsibility to act upon it; at this season of the year the exhalations from the uncovered area would be a danger to which I would not expose my family or those residing in the village.—Yours faithfully, E. V. Ross." The letter from Mr. Ross is in reply to one from the Board informing him a scheme would be undertaken as quickly as possible, and asking it he would allow his dam to be drained off for a few days.—Mr. ROGERS thought the C scheme the most desirable one, and moved itsadoption.—Mr. DEWITCRST seconded the motion, which was carried.—lt was decided to bring the scheme before the inspector for approval in the usual way. This concluded the business.

div.head: MID-CHESHIRE ITEMS.
div.p: MID-CHESHIRE ITEMS.
Mr. S. H. Hobson has resigned his seat on the Nantwich Local Board.

The Nantwich Mill and Foundry, which cost some £50,009 or £60,000 for their erection, was sold the other day, at public auction, for £4,900. Forty-one deaths were recorded in the urban district of the Nantwich Local Board during the quarter ending 31st March last, being equivalent to a death-rata of 19.2 per 1,000.

The Primitive Methodists of the Nantwich circuit held their annual camp meeting at the Barony, on Sunday. WEAVER SAILING CLUB, NORTHWICH. The second match of this club took place on Saturday last, the entries being as follows:—Merlin, 2i tons, owned by Messrs. S. Burgess, D. Ashton, and A. Burgess; Ernest, 1 tons, owned by Mr. R. Hickson. A level start was effected, but Ernest went to the front at once, though the sailing was pretty close up to the top end of the Narrows, where Merlin got in difficulties and lost about four minutes. The first round ended as follows :—Ernest, 22min. 40secs.; Merlin, 25min. 15secs. The same order was maintained throughout the second round, which was concluded by Ernest in 24min. 22secs., and by Merlin in 25min. 15secs. Ernest thus won by 3min. 28secs. Mr. Joseph Barlow officiated as starter, and Mr. F. Willis as timekeeper. THE POACHING AFFRAY IN CllESHlRE.—lnvestigation was made on Friday into a desperate poaching affray which took place at Tarporlev, when five labourers named Thomas and Robert AstburY, Walker, Greaves' and Pettinger, were charged with night poaching, and with violence. The Earl ef Haddington's keepers, assisted by other watchers, came upon the prisoners on Mr. Tomkinson's preserves at Wil- lington Hall. There were seven in the gang. The poachers I rained showers of stones on the keepers, but ultimately ran away, leaving large quantities of netting, pegs, and numerous instrumEnts on the field. The keepers gave pur- suit, and one of them, namediEdvvin Jones, seized a poacher, when they rolled on the ground. The poacher called out, and another came to his assistance, and beat Jones about the head in a brutal manner, ultimately leaving him bleeding, and insensible. Walker and 'I homas Astbury were cap- tured, and the other men were subsequently arrested. The Magistrates committed the prisoners for trial at the Assizes on the full charge. THROWING A GAMFREEPER INTO A CANAL.—At the Middlewich Police Court, on Thursday. three canal boat- men—John Bowed, John Patin, and Arthur Palin—were charged with assaulting Jomes Higgins, a gamekeeper. Higgins and some others were playing cricket on the green in front of Lawton Hall on Whit-Monday, and observed the three prisoners picking rhododendrons in the garden. On being pursued they ran in the direction of the canal. Being overtaken near the bank, John Palin struck the _ _ _ _

keeper on the head with a stone, knocking him down. He got up again and closed with the defendant. Arthur Palin cried out to his brother to throw him into the canal, and Palin did so, but fell in also himself. The keeper managed to get out, but the effect of the severe blow on the head and the unexpected immersion rendered him half senseless. One of the defendants threatened to throw him in again, but he eluded him. The charge against Bowed was dismissed, but each of the Paling was fined 40s. and casts. THIRD ADMINSTRATITE BATTALION OF CHESHIRE RIFLES. —The eight companies representing the Third Administra- tive Battalion of Cheshire Rifle Volunteers marched into camp at Tatton Park, Knutsford, on Saturday, under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel Marshall, for eight

days' training. The battalion numbers 750 men of all ranks; the headquarters of the differer_t companies being at Northwich, Wineford, Altrincham, Sale, Cheadle, KnutsCotel, and Lymm. The Altrincham companies were under the command of Captain Joseph Holliday, Captain Butler, and Lieut. Jones; the Sale company, Captain Marsland ; Knuts- ford, Captain Davies and Lieutenant Roscoe; Northwich, Captain Cheshire ; Winsford, Captain Turner; Cheadle, Captain Howarth; Lymm, Captain Power. The other officers present were Major Fox, Captain and Adjutant Broddel I, Quartermaster Daggett, and Sergeant-Major Lind- say. The Northwich, Sale and Cheadle companies were conveyed by train to Knutsford, but the others marched to Knuts.ford from their respective quarters, the regimental band accompanying the Altrincham contingent, who mus- tered in strong force. The system of annual encampments seems to have had the effect of greatly popularising the service and acting beneficially on the physique of the men. Although the weather was very variable on Saturday, no serious discomfort arose from the showers which fell at in- tervals. The inspection took place yesterday, the volunteers returned to their homes to-day (Saturday.) DIE ELECTRIC LIGHT IN A ROCfi•SALT MINE.—The principal feature of interest to a visitor to the town of North- wich is undoubtedly the salt mines which exist in the neighbourhood. One of the largest of these, the Witten Hall Mine, situated on Warrington-road, has during the week been open for the inspection of visitors, and instead of be- ing lighted with candles, as has been the case in previous years, it was illuminated by the electric light, and presented a spectacle which amply repaid those who had nerves strong enough to endure the terror of the decent and ascent. Six- teen large lamps, each giving a light equal to 2,000 candles, placed in various parts of the mine' and particularly in the place where the men were at work, made the subterranean wall and and ceiling glisten like the spar rock in some of the Derbyshire mines. The lights had been supplied by the Hammond Electric Supply Company, of Dale-street, Liverpool, and the motive power for the dynamo machine was obtained by passing a band round part of the ordinary machinery belonging to the mine. One of the main features in connection with the lamps was that they were all supplied with the electricity necessary for them by one wire, and were all thus connected with each other. This, however, did not prevent their being worked separately, as each lamp could be taken down or put out without the other being touched. The mine could be seen to great advantage, and it presented, as we have said, altogether an exceedingly in and pretty spectacle.

div.head: ALARMING FIEE IN MANCHESTER.
div.p: ALARMING FIEE IN MANCHESTER.

About ten o'clock on Wednesday evening a fire broke out in premises in Mosley-street, Manchester, occupied by the Globe Parcel Express Company, and in a very short time the whole of the building was in flames, and property destroyed to a large amount. The whole of the fire brigade, under the com:nand of Assistant Superintendent Savage (Superintendent Tozer being indisposed) Were speedily in attendance with two steamers, but for a time their efforts seemed utterly futile. The flames rapidly spread from rcom to rooni—the Globe Parcel Express Company occupying the basement—and after the lapse of a few minutes they lourst through the topmost roof, lighting UP the city for a considerable distance around with alarming brilliance. By eleven o'clock the fire was at its fiercest. At that hour the sky was lit up over what seemed a vast extent, and from the lower end of Blackfriars-street the rising and failing sparks could be distinctly seen. The rush of people began early, and Market-street was soon half-filled with the mov- ing throng. The main body kept up the street to the corner of Piccadilly, but many seeing that the crush wa.s already beginning at the upper end of the main thorough- fare passed down Brown-street and other streets, and reached the scene of the fire by way of York-street. Sparks were falling thickly everywhere in this direction, and at one time there seemed no little danger that one of these falling tongues of flame would start a new conflagration in the neighbourhood. York-street was thickly lined with people, and as the corner was turned the spectacle, bath of the tire and the crowd, was one not to be forgotten. There was a , clear space for some 50 yards or so in front of the burning ' mass, but with this exception Mosley-street was packed from end to end, and it soonbecame impossible to make. way through the surging mass. The whole force of the brigade was on the spot, and eleven spouts were pouring simulta- neously upon the denies. These were shooting out of every window, but were kept down by the constant stream of the four powerful jets which were aimed so as rise above it and fall with great effect together. Jots were simultaneously being poured into the windows of the first and second floors, and by degrees some effect seemed to be produced upon the flaming mass. But for a long time the sky was still filled with the mass of sparks, rising and falling and eddying in every direction, fiery atoms in the void, which, if compar- ble to anything, were comparable to the meteoric shower in a famous November some 15 years ago. Much anxiety was felt as to the fate of the last houses of the block at the corner of Yolk-street, but nothing could stana the volumea 01. water incessantly poured into the building. The damage rill amount to many thousands.

IMPORTAN T TESTIMONIAL. 12, Hargreaves-street, Oldham, Nov. 17th, 1881. Dear Sir,—Ever since I was four yea, s of age, my parents in- form me that I have suffered from great weakness. At the present time, I am 21 years of age, and if the paeticulars of my case will be of any service to you, I snail be only too happy to give them to you. For a great many years I have been under different doctors, and the last doctor I visited told me he could do no more for me; so he sent me to the Soothport Hospital, but after remaining there some time without finding any benefit, I returned home. I have been treated as a consump- tive patient. I have earned very little money for my parents, seldom being able to work through being se weak, and most of the time I have been under the doctor's treatment. About three weeks ago I commenced wearing your" Afagnetaire," and in a week's time I felt so strong that I began work, and have never been off work one hour since. I assure you I should never have thought it possible that I should feel so strong as I d., now, and you may depend upon it both I and my parents shall always recommend your Appliances. 11, Broom-st,eet, Hanley, Jan. 4th, 1882. Dear Sir,—When I came to you four months ago, khad been paralysed in one leg for ten years, the limb being perfectly cold and stiffened. I also suffered from scrofula badly, and was troubled with a very severe cough. I have worn the belt and soles you recommended ever since' with the following result : I can now walk very well with the leg that was previously stiff and numb, and can bend the joints, the circulation too Is quite restored through my body, have lost the cough entirely and my face is very much better, the skin now being dry and much lighter in colour than before. We are all very highly satisfied with what your Appliances have done, and shall al- ways recommend them with confidence in any similar case. My spirits and appetite are also much better.—Yours truly, Mr. R. Lonsdale. JNO. GRIFFITHS.

Church Eaton, Stafford, December 26th. 1881 Sir,—ln behalf of my fellow-sufferers, and In justice to you, I give you my experience of your Magnetaire." Some seven years ago I had a severe pAralytic attack which had lett me with a stiff shoulder and arm, with little use in my hand. I used the electric remedies, then invented, for three years with benefit, and after that time, as I was convinced that I could not exoect any further relief from them at my age (now 76), I discontinued them. Hearing from Mr. Clendinnen of your Appliances (though without much faith in them). I purchased one of your Invigorators, and, to my surprise, in to, t days I found my arm much more supple and useful, but the benefit I have rectived is very marked, and I have but little doubt that my limb, though very weak, will continue to improve under your Appliances. I wish you to send me a Magnetaire Friction Glove, as I think friction will complete the cure.— Yours, &c., Mr. R. Lsnsdale. A. C. TALBOT.
