div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

SATLEDAY.—Before Mr. John Brock. THB BEGGING NUISANCE.—JOhn Birmingham, a tramp, who said be came from that town, was summoned for beg- ging in Victoriaroad.—Aa officer stated that about three &rock in the afternoon he saw the prisoner beggiug in Vic- toria-road. Prisoner went into several shops, and asked for bread and meat. On coming out of one place with meat and bread the officer asked him how he had got it, and he said he had paid for it. At the police station, meat, bread, tea, sugar, and is. sth in copper were found upon the pri- soner.—The magistrate said the prisoner was evidently an old hand, and he would be sent to gaol seven days, with hard labour.--Sarah Davies, a tramp, was charged with committing a similar offence in Victoria-road, on the pre- vious afternoon.—A policeman gave evidence in support of the case, and the prisoner was sent to gaol for seven days. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Brock (chairman) and Mr. W. L. Evans. AN AFTERNOON ADVENTURE ON RUNCORN BRIDGE.— Catherine Boden, a woman of ilbfame, was charged with stealing a sovereign belonging to John Grady.—The prose- cutor, who is a powerful young man, living at Alvanley, Cheshire, said that on the afternoon of the 29th ult. he was in Runcorn, somewhat under the influence of liquor, when he met the prisoner. They had some drink together, and then she asked him to walk over the railway foot-bridge to Widnes. He consented, and at that time he had a sovereign and some silver in his possessian, which he missed on getting to Widnes.—Michael Lee, a lad, of No. 115, Mid- Wood-street, said he was coming across the Runcorn foot- bridge on the afternoon of the 29th ult., about half-past five, when he saw the prosecutor and the woman together. Boden said the young man was her brother, and she had not seen seen him for eleven years. At the Widnes side the woman searched Grady's pockets for the tickets for taking them across the bridge, and remarked, "I think you have lost them." He saw the prisoner take a sovereign and sixpence from the prosecutor's watch pocket. She gave the sixpence to the man at the ticket box, and said it would pay for the tickets. However, before leaving the spot, the woman found the tickets, and the collector gave her the coin back again. He (witness) then asked her to give the stolen sovereign to Grady, but she merely answered, "It is a bad sovereign; he has tried to pass it at two or three places." In Church- street they met P.C. Timperley, who took the prisoner into custody on a charge of theft. On the way to the police station, the woman attempted to put the sovereign back in the prosecutor's pocket, but the officer prevented her.—A youth named McCullan, cf No: 54, Wellington-street, said ho was with the last witness on the bridge, and he cor- roborated the evidence given by him.—P.C. Timperlev pioved the apprehension of Boden, who, ire reply to the charge, said the prosecutor, whe was her cousin, had given her the money.—She now pleaded not guilty, and was com- mitted to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial. CAPTURE OF A COUPLE OF ALLEGED SHOP TIIIEVES.— Annie Elizabeth Thompson and Margaret Burns were charged with stealing, sometime between the 19th and 20th ult., a pair of boots, a pair of sheets, and a pair of trousers. the property of Mrs. Jamieson, pawnbroker, Anne-street West; also with stealing, on the 20th ult., a coat, value ss. 6c1., the property of Frederick Mean, pawnbroker, of the same street; and likewise a quantity of print belonging to Frederick Tebbutt, also of Anne-street West.—Mrs. Annie Jamieson, pawnbroker, Anne-street West, said the trousers, pair of boots, and pair of sheets now produced, which belonged to her, were worth about 17s. 6d. On the 19th ult. they were safe in her shop, and she missed them on the following day. She had not sold them to any one.—Sergeant Strich- land stated that on the 22nd ult., he searched the house of the prisoner Burns, who is a widow, in Victoria-street, and found the trousers, boots, and sheets. He took the two prisoners into custody. In reply to the charge, Thompson said she was guilty of stealing the things, but Burns knew nothing about them. Burns said "I am not guilty."—Mr. W. I'. Husband appeared for the defence of Barns, and said there was not a tittle of evidence against his client to justify the magistrates in committing her for trial.—Prisoners were next charged with stealing, between the 19th and 20th ult., a coat, value ss. 6d., the property of Frederick Meats, pawn- broker, Anne-street 'West; and also several yards of print, the property of Frederick Tebbutt, draper, of the same street, on the 20th nit. Mrs. Jamieson identified the trousers and boots as belonging to her. They were safe in her shop on the 19th ult., and on the 20th ult, she missed them. Neither of the prisoners had any right to take them from her shop. She was sure she hal not sold the articles to any one.—P.S. Strickland said that on Monday, the 22nd ult,, he searched Burns's house, and found the stolen things. —Mr. Husband contended the articles were lying quite openly in the house when discovered, and there was not a tittle of evidence to show that his client had either stolen or received thine—The second charge was then gone into.—John Dickson, assistant to Fredrick Mean, pawnbroker, Anne- street West, identified the coat produced as belonging to his master. It was worth ss. 6d. He missed the articles on the 28th ult. He had seen both the prisoners in his master's shop. Thompson paid a visit there on the 19th ult., and asked to see some boots, but they had none to fit her.—P.S. Strickland said he found the coat at Burns' house, where a man who co-habited with Thompson was wearing the article.—Mr. Husband argued that it was absurd to charge the prisoner with stealing and receiving the coat.—Evidence was next given in the third case against the prisoner.—Mr. Tebbutt, draper, also of Anne-street West, said he missed about 20 yards of print on the 20th ult., and the piece produced was similar to that he had lost. On the 20th ult, between ten and eleven at night, the prisoner Thompson came to ,his shop, and was wearing the facket produced, which was of exactly the same pattern and quality as the piece of print he had missed, which was worth Bd. per yard. As soon as he saw the jacket he gage information to the police.—Jane Burns said that about a month ago she went into the house of the prisoner Burns, and the woman Thompson was also there, making a jacket. Witness remarked that the staff was a very nice material, +an which Thompson said "Yes, a girl in Manchester wove it for me." She added that she had also a dress piece, which she intended either to sell or pawn. Witness after- wards pawned the dress piece at Mrs. Jamieson's, and beer, in which the three women shared, was purchased with the , proceeds.—Mrs. Jamieson stated that the print was pawned, at her shop by Mrs. Burns.—P.S. Strickland said be went to the house of the prisoner Burns, and found Thompson wearing the jacket. She stated she had obtained it from Liverpool. In the house he found the stolen dress and apron produced. He afterwards discovered a pawn ticket relating to the dress in the house, which showed the article had been pawned at Jamieson's.—After some observations from Mr. Husband, the Beach committed the prisoner Thompson to the next Liverpool Qnarter Sessions for trial On all three charges. They considered the first two charges against the prisoner Burns not made out, but they com- mitted her on the third charge, intimating that bail would be accepted. DRUNK AT THE STAR INN.—Edward Tallon was charged, on remand, with having been found drunk on the licensed premises known as the Star Inn, Elizabeth-street. Prisoner gave a false name and address. He was fined ss. and costs. TRAVELLING ON THE CHESHIRE LINES RAILWAY WITH- OUT A Trcemr"--Josepli Clarke was charged, on remand, visit!' travelling in a carriage belonging to the Cheshire Litnes Railway Company with the intention of avoiding payment of his fare. Inspector Simpson, from Liverpool, and Mr. Nutter, station master at Farnworth, gave evidence to the effect that on the 27th ult., upon the arrival of the 11-36 p.m. train from Farnworth, the prisoner was found lying ander one of the carriage seats. He went up to him, but on speaking to him he received no answer, as the man pre- tended to be drunk. Prisoner was got out of the carriage, and there put himself in a fighting attitude, and was only taken to the police station after considerable difficulty.— Clarke was fined 20s. and costs, and, in default of payment, ordered to be imprisoned one month RESISTING A POLICE OFFIeER.—A young man named James Douglas was fined 10e. and costs, or 14 days' im- prisonment, for having, on the night of the 19th ult., tried to rescue a prisoner from P.C. Snowdon, and struck the officer twice in the breast. lionELEss.—John Kennedy, a young man, was sent to prison 14 days, on the evidence of P.C. Pitt, for having been found the same morning in an empty luggage yen belonging to the London and North-Western Riilway, which he said he had been obliged to use as a sleeping place. ALLEGED DESERTION OF WIFE AND FAMILY BY A BLACK- SMITH.—Thomas Bette, a young man, was charged by Mr. Stewart, relieving officer, with having left his wife and family to be kept at the expense of the common fund of the Prescot Union whilst he was away at Nottingham.—Priloner tried to make the magistrates believe that his wife left him before he went away.—Mr. Evans appeared to think there might he something in the prisoner's story; and the Bench adjourned the further hearing of the case to the 6th inst., when the relieving officer said he should be able to prove that Betts was now living with another woman. HEAVY SENTENCE ON A WIFE BEATER.—John Barlow was charged with threatening to assault his wife.—Complainant said her husband had previously been sent to gaol six months for assaulting her, and a few days ago she heard him say under the window that the next time he suffered imprison- ment for her sake it would be thoreughly well merited, for he would most certainly take her life —Prisoner addressed the Bench at some length. He stated that he had served his Queen and country in the East, and the heat there had atiected his bead, so that when be was under the influence of a little drink, he, to a great extent, lost self-control. He added that he had never had a lucky day since he put foot in Preecot, and it the magistrates would discharge him he weem go to Ireland for good.—The Chairman said the police Peaks told too grave a story of the prisoner's conduct in the past to make it a virtue to exercise leniency to him ; and he would be sent to gaol six moeths, in default of finding sure- ties to keep the peace to his wife for the same period, himself in -e2O, and two sureties in £lO each, WARNING TO CORNER-MEN —William Bell was fined ss. and costs, on the evidence of P.C. Stacy, for obstructing the footpath in Widnes-road, on the 21st ult. STRIKING A WOMAN IN THE FACE.—Ellen Mulvey was charged with assaulting Mary Dolan, on the 28th ult.—lt appeared that the parties in the case bad not been on good terms for some time, and on the day in question Mulvey met Dolan, and after abusing her in very round terms, and using disgusting language, struck her in the face.—Defendant was fined IN. and costs. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun. SEarous CHARGE AGAINST A WIDNES JOlNER.—Thonias Sumner, a joiner, of Mill-brow, was charged, in Custody, with committing a criminal assiult on a girl aged five, !aimed Flizibeth Bennett, who lives in the, sime street.— '• The child stated that the offence was committed by the prieener whilst she was alone in the house.--Surnner W 39 trer_L27lded to the Petty Sessions on Wednesday.

Asiditi,nal loan required £so6 18 6 Total amount required £659 4 6 --- Clerk's Office, Frodsham, 27th May, 1882. Mr. Minwoon said the proposal for the sewerage was originally fixed at £2,879. The DEPUTY CLERK replied that the sum mentioned was merely that required for the buying of theland, dtc. Mr. MCINTYRE said that in order to get rid of this Frod- sham sewerage business, with which they had been so long troubled, he would move that the £6OO, which was necessary to pay the outstandingliabilities in connection with it, should be borrowed from the Board of iircirks' Commissioners, upon the same principle as former loans had been contracted. Mr. JOHN WEIR seconded tbe resolution, on the ground that the question had been on foot quite long enough. The motion was carried unanimously. ALLEGED NUISANCE AT HALTON COMMON.

The committee appointed to inspect and report a nuisance upon Halton Common' stated that they met at the place in question on the 26th ult. After making a minute inspection, the committee were unanimously of opinion that the nuisance arose from the sewage ic. emanating from the house occupied by Mr. Lee, together with a portion of the sewage and storm water from the village emptying upon the road at the lower side of the common, and forming a lodgment, owing to want of being carried under the road, and a proper and suf- ficient outlet, making it evident that the original, and also the natural drainage, has been cut off by the filling up of a ditch, and the erecting of a stone wall in its place. The only mode of improvement the committee could suggest, was that Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., should be requested to carry the sewage Jtc from Mr. Lee's house upon the adjoining land, and that he should be asked if he would allow the discharge from the town's drain to flow in the same course. The latter would add very little to the volume, except in the case of storms, as the sewage to a very great extent in other sorts of weather, is dealt with upon land situate higher up in the occupation of Mr. Nixon. The attention oE the committee vras also called to an open sewage -gutter, or sough, situate in a recess at the end of cottages belonging to the executors of Mr. Charles liazlehurst, and the conclusion arrived at ' was that it was a dangerous nuisance, and should be im- proved immediately; and that if the lead pipes laid in such sough, and covered over with liquid sewage, be water pipes, the Sanitary Authority should insist upon their im- mediate removal, as much evil might result if the water became contaminated. The state of a pee which receives a large amount of sewage from property be- longing to Mr. Hazlehurst and others, and is situate in a field belonging to the Marquis of Cholmondley, and near to residences on the south side of the village, was brought under the notice of the committee, and it was decided that the pool should be emptied and filled up with soil to the ground level, and pipes laid so as to carry the sewage dic. upon the land at a further distance from the dwellinghouses. The drainage to farm and cottage premises belonging to the Marquis of Cholmendley, was also examined, and considered to be much in need of improvement. At the conclusion of the inspections, strong feelings were expressed that the Sanitary Anthorily should issue notices for the abatement of various nuisances, and that if such notices were not com- plied with within reasonable time, proceedings should be taken to compel such compliance. A brief conversation followed, in the course of which Mr. SMITH said the sewer was in a most disgraceful state. The Rev. J. Locxwoon moved the adoption of the re- port, which was seconded by Mr. J. WEIR, and agreed to, without dissent.
The DEPUTY CLERK: Proceedings will follow in due course.
PRESTON 'BROOK WATER SUPPLY.

The Local Government Boat tl wrote stating that they had considered the annual report of the medical officer for 1881, and adverting to the statement which it containei as to the water supply of Preston Brook, they wished to en- quire what steps the authority proposed to take for provid- ing that place with a wholesome supply. Mr. Farrington (the inspector) presented a report giving a number of details as to what had been done for the pur- pose of supplying the township with water since 1880. He added that the total number of houses yet without a supply within a reasonable distance was 31, of which 11 belonged to the Preston Brook estate; 13 to the Bridge- water Navigation Co.; five to the London and North- Western Railway Co., one to the North Staffordshire Rail- way and Canal Co., and one to the trustees of the Wesleyan chapel. In reply to questions, Mr. FARRINGTON remarked that if three new wells were made, the difficulties under which the township laboured would probably be met. This concluded the business.

div.head: WAERINGTON POLICE COURT.
div.p: WAERINGTON POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pict mere) and Councillor Fairclough. MISCELLANEOUS.—Thomas Hamilton, for being drunk and disorderly on Saturday night was fined 103. and costs, with the alternative ef 14 days' imprisonment—John Clayton was mulcted in the sum of 53. for being helplessly drunk in Cockhedge-lane ; and a fine of ss. and costs was inflicted upon George Gerrard for drunkenness and disorderly be- haviour in the market on Saturday.—Ss a suspicious character John Shields was committed to prison for a month on the evidence of P.C.Taylor, of Dalian Forge.—For sleeping out on Sunday night, Thomas Wilson was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. •

div.head: TuEsuAY.—Before Councillors Monks and Broadbent.
div.p: TuEsuAY.—Before Councillors Monks and Broadbent.

DRUNK AND DISOIIDERLY.—A. man named John Bohan, of 14. Dolman's-lane, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Dial-street, on Monday afternoon. This was his 69th appearance. Councillor Monks, in fining defendant 23. 61 including costs, said that he hoped by letting him off so easily he would try and become a better man.— Michael Galvin, who resided at 9, Farrell-street, was also fined 23. 6,1. including costs for being drunk on Monday after- noon, in Fennel-street.—A fine of 53, including costs was imposed upon Peter IVlelior, of 7, Ship-yard, fora like offence, in Winwick-street, the previoUs night. WEDNESDAL—Before Alderman Burgess and Councillor Fairclough. DRGNIC AND DISORDERLY.—James Connolly, of 33, Bos- tock-street, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Sankey-street, on Tuesday afternoon, and was fined 53. and costs with the alternative of seven days hard labour.—A man named Charles Gerrard, a labourer, and late of Manchester, was fined ss.and costs for being drunk in Napier-street, on Tuesday afternoon.—A married woman named Margaret Jackson, alias Riley, who resided at Atherton-street, for a similar offecce in Mersey-street, on the same day, was ordered to pay ss. and costs, or in default to undergo seven days' im- prisonment. —Patrick Carroll was charged, under a warrant, with being drunk and disorderly in Cheapside, on the Bth of February last. Fined ss. and costs, or in default, seven days bard laboni.—Mark Casey was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Dolman's-lane that morning. —A tramp named Ann Welsh, hailing from Knntsford, Ives charged with being drunk and behaving in a disotderly manner whilst being admitted as a casual inmate to the wards of the Warrington workhouse. It appeared from the evidence cf James Curry, porter at the workhouse, that he had left the gate at nine o'clock on Tuesday in charge of one of the inmates for a period of abaut five minutes, giving him instructions not to admit anyone until he returned. I When Curry returned to take charge of the gate he found

the defendant in a very drunketrstate waiting to be admitted. Defendant said she had been waiting at the gate three- quarters of an hour,land used, on being admitted, language of a most vile and filthy character. She was sent to gaol for seven days with hard labour. A RUNAWAY FATHER SENT TO GAOL.—A man named Peter Swift, who had lately been employed as a fitter at Bedford Leigh, was charged with running away from the Borough of Warrington, on the 19th of April last, and leav- ing his son chargeable to the Union —Defendant said he went to Bedferd Leigh to obtain employment as a fitter, and he had been receiving wages to the amount of 325. per week. He had not paid the bill for the maintenance of his child in the workhouse during his absence, which Mr. Garnett said was 273.—He was committed for three months with hard labour. ASSAULT WITH A PoKElL—Daniel Dodd, residing at 19,1 Stamford-street was charged with violently assaulting his lodger, Thomas O'Brien, by striking him on the head with a poker at five p.m. on the 30th instant.—The prosecutor declined to give evidence, not wishing to press the case.— Defendant said that O'Brien came home for his dinner some- what the worse for drink, and when he had finished it he asked defendant to lend him a shilling, a request which he acceded to. He then left the house and returned again shortly afterwards to ask defendant to lend him some more money. .Upon defendant refusing to accede to his request, prosecutor commenced to quarrel with the defendant, and a scale ensued. Dodd, in defending himself, used the poker freely, dealing O'Brien several blows on the head.—The Bench fined defend.int ss. and costs, or in default 7 days imprisonment with hard labour. THURSDAY.—Before Captain Litton (chairman) and Alderman Webster.

A DISHONEST LODGER.—An old woman, named Bridget Kelly, styling herself as a hawker, last from Knutsford, was charged with stealing a twill sheet, of the value of 2s. 61, the property of Patrick Farrell. The prosecutor keeps a common lodging house in Cloth Hall yard, and on Tuesday afternoon the prisoner went there, staying all night. Next morning, whilst Mrs. Farrell was busily engaged, the prisoner left the house, returning in about two hours. Then, ex- amining the bed upon which the prisoner had slept, Mrs. Farrell discovered a quilt had disappeared. Under the threat of "sending for a policeman," the prisoner produced a pawn ticket, which showed she had pledged the sheet for Is., at Morton's pawnshop, Winwick-street.—The prisoner was sentenced to a month's imprisonment with hard labour. FRlDAY—Before Messrs. Ziba Armitage and John White. A FATHER ROBBED BY HIS SoN.—A young mara, named Charles Maxwell, aged 18, but who looked considerably younger, was charged with stealing from the house of Robert Maxwell (his father), in 17, Tilley-street, on the 31st May I last, one piece of corduroy, one piece of calico, and one handkerchief.—lt appeared that the father left home on the 30th tilt., for a short holiday, leaving the house in charge of woman named Mary Ann Tickle. When she went into the house on the following morning, she found that the door had been forced open, evidently by an iron bar, which was lying close by. Information was given to P.C. Maclean, who, about nine o'clock, apprehended prisoner with the articles in his possessioa. Prisoner has been convicted on previous occasions for similar offences, and has served three years in an industrial school.—The father said that prisoner was unmanageable.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for three months, with hard labour. IMPUDENT THEFT or TOBACCO.—DanieI May, a labourer, and last of Runcorn, was fined ss. for stealing one ounce of twist tobacco, the _property of John Stirrup, tobacconist,
THE CORN HILL.

The CLERK, in answer to an enquiry made by the Rev. 'l'. Chambers at the last meeting, said the number of vagrants grinding corn was 100. At present there were 25 packs ground of the value of £2O 16s. The value of the corn un- ground was unknown. In a day or two the Guardians would be able to do away with the ground corn to one firm. Rev. T. CHAMBERS : Then they have been enjoyed in accordance with the determination of the Guardians when the mills were put down. The CLERK: Yes. We have been labouring under disad- vantages recently. There has been a great deal of building going on at the Rainhill Asylum, and there has been a great deal of work in the laying of the pipes in the Vyrnwy water scheme. People have come here in the hope of obtaining wore, but finding they could obtain none, they have taken advantage of our tramp wards. Rev. T. CHAMBERS: There is no reason for saying that the mill is not answering. The CLERK : No; I think it will be a grand thing. PAYMENT or PAUPER CHILDREN'S SCHOOL FEES. The CLERK stated that the Special Committee appointed to consider the auditor's suggestion had had a meeting, but there had not been any attempt to prepare the report in- tended to be sent to the Local Government Board. In the meantime he wanted the Guardians to adopt one suggestion at once with respect to the payment of school fees for pauper children. When the auditor was over he suggested that paupers' children's pence should not be paid by and through the relieving officer, but that every child should take its own money. Suppose there were 35-0 children went to the school, 200 of that number paid their school pence, while the 150 had to say " Oh, my father and mother gets relief." The auditor wished the Guardians to pay the money in the first place to the parent, and then let the parents produce a ticket to the relieving officer that their children were regularly attending. If the children were not atterding school regularly, the whole of the relief to the parent would he discontinued. It was required by law that if the children were not attending school the relief must be stopped, and to obviate this the children were required to go to school eight times a week. A card must be initiated by the teacher to that effect. Rev. J . BARNACLE : You see you cannot touch them if they go no more than eight times. Would that satisfy? Would it he wise for that to go forth to them? The CLERK: They are entitled to know that, if they don't know. The Revs. T. HEAVY PENALTY FOR EXPOSING DISEASED MEAT.— Frank Connolly was charged with having in his possession, in a certain stall in the Market Hall, a portion of a heifer unfit for human food.—Mr. Whittle (deputy town clerk) ap- peared to prosecute on behalf of the Corporation, and Mr. Moore appeared for the defendant.—lnspoctor Norman said that on Saturday. the 20th May, his attention was called to . _ _
seme meat which was hanging -up in the defendant's stall, and also to sofne meat which was lying in a basket covered

over with a quantity of bones. He examined the meat, and found that each piece (there were 90 in all) was unwhole- some, unsound, and totally unfit for the food of man. He seized the meat and had it sent to the offices at the Town Hall, where it was examined by Mr. Gornall (the medical officer of health) and Mr. Robinson (veterinary surgeon).— Mr. Gornall said he examined the meat and found about 90 pieces, varying in weight from one eunce to one pound, in an advancing state of decomposition. The general charac- ter of the meat was, that the muscular tissues were in an undeveloped state. The animal was completely devoid of fat.—Mr. Robinson, veterin ry surgeon, gave similar evidence Edward Richardson said that on the 17th May, he went to Bank Qmay station for the carcase of the heifer which had been slaughtered in Frodsham, and was wrapped in two pieces of cloth. He brought it to Mr. Preston's slaughter house in Bank-street, where he left it until Friday night, when he conveyed it to the shop of the defendant in the market and hung it up. When he brought it to Mr. Pres- ton's slaughter house on the Wednesday, Inspector Norman came in, examined the heifer, and gave instructions for it to be sold immediately before it went bad. The meat which was hung up for sale on the Saturday was that which Mr. Norman pronounced to be fit for human food, and was in his opinion perfectly sound.—John Hatton, and Wm. Carlile gave corroborative evidence, but the Bench considered the case proved and tined the defendant and costs.

THE EX kMINEE SATURDAY, JUNE 3, 1882. 9 pointing 7th June as the nomination day, and 16th June WARRINGTON BOARD OF as the day for the special election of a Uruardian for the ! township of Little Woolton. 'The CLERK stated that steerage tickets for the passage of five children, named McNelly, to America, where their rela- tives reside, had been sent for. Some of the children were in Kirkdale schools and some of them out. Possibly the auditor might surcharge them in the amount. The Cluardiaus expressed their approval of the course taken with regard to the children. THE WHISTON ASSISTANT OVERSEER.—WHO, IS TO BE BELIEVED? The CLERK read the following letter from Mr. E. Range, assistant overseer for Whiston :—" Buxton, 25th May.—l am in receipt of Mr. Hartley's letter asking me either to resume duties at once or resign. Now, gentlemen, I pre- sume that letter was written through the statement made by the overseers for my township, which statement was un- true. I never yet said I would not pay anyone to collect, but the reverse. Smith, the overseer, called upon me many times during my confinement to the house, and after I was able to go out a little, I told him every time I saw him that could they find anyone to do my work until I was well. I tried all my friends, but none of them would undertake the job. Now, gentlemen, I leave my case in your hands and if you think I ought to resign I will do so, as it will be fully a month before I can resume duties; but should you choose to appoint some one in my place until I am well, I shall be glad for them to receive my salary for the time they do the work. I am sure gentlemen, when I was in health I did my duty, as the remarks made by Smith, at the election of overseers, will prove." Rev. T. CHAMBERS 'Slid there was a great discrepancy between the statements of the assistant overseer and the two overseers. The CLERK : He does not seem to hold his overseers in very high estimation. The CHAIRMAN: We have the means of payment if any man will undertake the duties. Mr. LEATHERBARROW said there was £3OO owing on the March rate. The CLERK said that £17,000 was the rateable value. . Mr. LEATHERBARROW ; And the rate is 3s. 6d. in the pound. The CLERK: The highway rate is rather heavy-9d. or 10d. The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said that as Mr. Range was sick he (Mr. Chambers) was unwilling that he should resign, but he had shown very scant courtesy to the overseers, and he ought to be taught civility. If he understood right, the overseers did not know who to appoint. The CtterumAx : They are responsible for the money; I do not think our clerk ought to find a man. The CLERK: I do not mean to; if you appoint Mr. Makin my impression is that he would undertake the work. If a stranger was got there would be very little done in a month. And then he would have to order a separate bond for the performance of his duties; and it would take a month to get that bond. In the Whiston township there are valuable railway and colliery assessments. Mr. PARIS: I beg to move that Mr. Makin be asked to undertake his duties. Rev. T. CHAMBERS: I second that. This was carried.
THE NEW SCHOOLS: FINANCIAL STATEMENT.

GUARDIANS. Mr. Blackhurst presided at the meeting held at the Work- house on Wednesday. The other members present were the Rev. Jobs Yonge, Major Certwright, Messrs. Woolfall, Burn, Bonnel, Appleton, Derbyshire, Caldwell, Longshaw, Hunt, Brown, Greenall, Houghton, Kilshall, Cooper, Marsh, Garnett, Taylor; and J. C. Sutton (clerk.)
THE ATTENDANCE OF THE HOUSE COMMITTEE. During a conversation in reference to the quality of the flour supplied to the house, in which it was suggested the

matter should be left to the House Committee. Mr. LONGSHAW asked if the committee consisted of a number of members—[The CHAIRMAN : Nineteen]—because there seemed to be only two members, ad to leave these disputes in the hands of two persons he thought wsa hardly the thing. (Laughter.) Mr. WOOLFALL asked the chairman how many members attended the committee the previous Friday. He was stir- __•
prised at Mr..Longshaw saying what he did when he knew

nothing about it. Major CARTWRIGHT :I am not at all surprised. Why does he not come himself? (Hear, hear.) He is one of the 19 no doubt, and every member of this Board has been invited over and over again. We never have heard of any- one going through the place, and if he has any fault to find, let him come and find it.
Mr. DARBYSIIIIIE.: Mr. Longsbaw is not on the com-

mittee. (Laughter,) Major CAirrwitlGHT : Is not he? He ought to be than! TIIE STATE OF THE HOUSE. The MASTER reported that there were 501 inmates as apinst 477 in the oorresponding week of last year, and that during the week 174 men, 27 women and 5 children vagrants had been relieved. The visitor's book cantained the following entry by Mr. Henry Stevens, sub-inspector, dated 26th • May ;—" I have visited the workhouse to-day, and shall report to Mr. Cane upon it. I recommend the adoption of some means to prevent vagrants from delaying, after obtaining their orders, to present themselves for ad- mission until late at night. There is not a continuous supply of water for the hespital w.c., and a few more fire buckets are desirable."

THE SCHOOLS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee, which were as follows, ' were adopted on the proposition of the Rev. J. YONGE, seconded by Mr. APPLETON. Resolved that the Clerk be directed to apply to the Local Government Board to issue orders and regulations applicable to the new schools and children's homes at Padgate (Poulton-with-Fearnhead), and to request the Local Government Board to submit the draft for consideration of the Guardians prior to approval thereof ; that the officers of the institution consist et superintendent and matron, two schoolmistresses, schoolmaster, and the following industrial trainers :—At lodge, out-door superin- tendent of labour, and wife; No 1 home, tailor ; No. 2 home, shoemaker; No. 1 home, mother; No. 2 home, mother; No. 3 home, female industrial trainer; No. 4 home, sewing mistress.

The CLERIC said he had written to the Local Government Board as follows :—" My Lords and gentlemen,—The new schools at Poulton-with-Fearnhead. By orders enabling them in that behalf, the Guardians borrowed £1,710, and therewith paid for land •/1,650, and tenants compensation £6O. They further borrowed £8,290, and thereout have paid contracts £7,550. and architect £450, leaving a balance in hand of £290. The amount of present contract is £8,690, and architect's commission, .1543 2s. Gd. ; total, £9,233 2s. 6d. leaving a balance of £943 2e. 6d. unprovided for. I enclose a notice sent to every Guardian oefore the lag Board meeting, at which meeting it was unani- mously resolved to borrow an additional sum of £4,000. £943 2s. Gil. of the loan is necessary to complete present contract, £125 18s. 4d. for strip of land, say £BOO for furni- ture, £2,130 198. 21 balance for day rooms, washhouse, laundry, general storeroom, committee room, office, and suitable boundary wall, and the necessary expenses and con- tingencies. I enclose a statement of the figures on a separate sheet, and an estimate of the probable further outlay. The supplemental or new plans will be prepared and submitted to your honour- able Board without delay. The Guardians are, however, in immediate want of money to enable them to meet present demands; and, as it is to the advantage of the Union to in- clude the £4.000 in one loan, they desire me to request your honourable Board to furnish them at once with the neces- ssry form required to be signed by a majority of Guardians, that the order of your honourable Board may be issued at the earliest date practicable."—The statement was as fol- lows:—" Re new schools at Poulton-with-Fearnhead.— Financial account.-11th December, 1879, &et order,ll,7lo. Cash paid for land £1,650, ditto tenants' compensation £6O: £1,710. 4th May, 1880, second order, £8.290. Cash paid on account of building contract (£8,690), '£7,550 ; ditto on account of architect's fees k£543 21. 6d.), £450: balance, £290—£8,290. To contract, £8,690; to architect, £543 , 2e. 6d.—£9,233 2s. 61 By builder, £7,550; by architect, 1£450; cash in hand, £290; balance required, £942 2s. 6d.- 1, £9,233 2s. 6d. May, 1882, lean now required; to balance required to complete, £943 2s. 61; to additional land, £125 18s. 4d.; to furniture, £800; day rooms, etc., and con- tingencies, £2,130 19s. 2d.—£4,000." The minutes of the School Building Committee stated : A meeting of this committee was held on the 30th May, when the architect submitted sketches of proposed stores, office, committee room wash-house, drying and ironing- room, &c., and of the play sheds contemplated at the new schools, and houses for the children. Proposed by Mr. Blackhurst, seconded by Mr. Humphreys, and resolved with one dissentient, that the sketches submitted be new approved and recommended to the Guardians for approval, and that the necessary detailed plans be prepared for sub- mission to the Local Government Board, but that no steps be taken towards the erection of the additional buildings until the present contract is completed. The committee regret that the work of the contractor is still but slowly proceeded with, and instruct the architect to communicate this opinion to him, and that penalties will be enforced if more satisfactory progress is not immediately reported by the architect. It was moved by Major Cartwright, seconded by Mr. Wallington. and resolved that unless the contract be fin:shed by June 21st, the committee will, under the terms of the agreement, take the work out of the hands of Mr. Napier, and give the same into other hands; and that the forfeitures stipulated by the contract will be enforced, and the unpaid balance of contract applied to the cost. Mr. DARBYSHIRE moved the confirmation of the minutes, and said every member of the Board knew as well as he did what the circumstances were. A fortnight ago the Board unanimously consented to an application to the Local Government Board for £4,000 to conclude the present con- tract. and also to erect other buildings which were neces- sary, but which were not in the original plans. The Board directed that plans and sketches of the new buildings intended to be put up should be produced at that meeting, and be expected the architect had brought them with him to show to the Board. He wished it thoroughly to be under- stood by every member of the Board that none of the work would be commenced, and nothing would be done beyond obtaining the rough sketch, before the present contract was entirely completed, and then it would be for the Board to say even who should be the architect of the new building, and who should' be the contractor. (Hear, bear.) He hoped when the old contract was finished the schools and , homes would be in such a condition that the children would be moved from the barracks to the schools before the build- ings which they proposed to erect werA erected. He thought , there would be sufficient accommodation for the children ' without waiting for the completion of the proposed new I buildings. Mr. BROWN seconded the motion, and asked on what date the present contract should have been executed. Mr. DAREYSHIRE said the first date was the 31st December, 1881, but there was a clause giving an extension of time to cover strikes and bad weather, which brought up the time to the 31st March, 1882, and he believed that was the time the schools should have been completed. Mr. APPLETON: What is the penalty for neglect? Mr. DATiBYSiIIEE said if the Board wished to impose the penalty, he believed it was £lO a week, though he had not seen the agreement for 12 months. The CHAIRMAN said unless the schools were completed by the 21st June the committee would impose the penalty. Mr. GARNETT : Has the builder bad notice of this? The CHAIRMAN : He will have notice this afternoon. Major CARTWRIGHT remarked that the Board a fortnight ago resolved, he supposed unanimously, to apply to the Local Government Board for £4,000 more, and it was then said by one member that they had very nearly spent the £lO,OOO which was borrowed. Now, if he had said the Board had spent nearly or wholly £ll,OOO he would have been near the mark; and it appeared to him (the Major) the £4,000 the Board had decided to apply for would not be sufficient. It was well known by the members of the Board, so far back as June, 1879, wkat the Board was led into by the then chairman as the requirements for the building of these schools. Mr. Winstanley said that all they would re- quire would cost about £5,000 for the accommodation of 200 children. That was what he led the Board to believe the scheme would cost, and he was supported by the then Board to a very great extent, but opposed by him (Major Cart- wrioht). Mr. Garnett then said "there is the question of land." But the who:e buildings and everything was to cost £5,000. That was the starting point ; there was dust thrown in the Board's eyes to say all they required they could get for £5,000. It was costing £l4,ooo,—and he said: £14,000 for the completion of these plans was not sufficient —and for how many children? Two hundred children; they could not put another child in. When they went upon the ground again they would have to apply for £4,000 more to build four more houses. He had told the Beard over and over again what the cost of the scheme would be and be told them by goim.r, in for £4.000 they would very soon see I where they would be. They would be as they were that day I —the clerk would want money, for this reason : £l,BOO had already gone, and £BOO was wanted for furniture. The Board would be in this dilemma very shortly; they would have to apply for £4,000 more. 'lt was coming to what he said at the beginning of 1879, for if anybody would take the trouble to read the reports they would find that he then said it would come to £16,000 before the schools were completed. The Board were in a dilemma, and their only course was to get out of it, and when they were once out to keep out. Mr. Garteemer agreed with Major Cartwright that the Board were in a dilemma, but he thought it was a little un- gracious to bring up something whick, took place two years ago, as the then chairman was dead. At that time he, with Major Cartwright, thought that the matter was not put fairly before them, but he was not at all deceived or disan- Pointed at the cost. Howeree, the Board went into the scheme with their eyes opeta, and Major Cartwright, who , was the one wise man in the lot, protested. The Board had got the buildings up so feae he %new very credit Ably, but

they had further" expenses to incur, and the qnslttion now simply was as to whether the efforts they had made to reduce the cost were sufficient. He thought in this matter they were bound to be governed by what Mr. Pierpoiut had submitted, and that it might fairly be assumel that some- thing like £4,000 more or less would meet the case. He would'go in for getting the schools into their own hands as soon as possible, and would impose the penalty. The builder had had everything in his favour, and if he had had, sufficient men he thought Mr. Pierpoint would tell the Board Mr. Napier might have completed the work months ago. Mr. COOPER after stating that when the matter was first brought forward it was negatived by 11 to 9, remarked that he thought the scheme had gone so far that the Board were bound to carry it out to the end. He thought it was only fair to the ratepayers to know that when they saw the Cleric half yearly bringing in his increased estimates, they were not going to have the rate put upon pauperism, because in the country board room they had not had a single applica- tion for out-door relief, and it should go hafore the public what the money was for.
The Rev J. iTONGE said against Mr. Cooper's statement :he number of paupers in the house was 60 above that of Last year.

The CHAIRMAN said they had not less than 550 inmatp., and when the children were forced out there were only 350. If the premises were not sufficient for 350 then he did not know how anybody could hold up for them. Major CARTWRIGHT : There were considerably more in the house when the first complaint was made. The CLERK said during the winter the Board had bad in the house 550 inmates, whereas before they proceedPd to build the schools or do anything in that direction they were advised that the house according to the legal mode of measuring the space would only accommodate 350; so that the Board had really had chargeable this winter indoor 200 morer persons than they could accommodate legally in the house. The question was: If this course had not been taken what course would the Guardians have taken?

The CHAIRMAN: Exactly. The Board must have adopted some course it was quite clear. He did not think any gentleman need be under any apprehension in regard to the £4,000. The question had been discussed by the committee and Mr. Pier- point, and they were satisfied .£4,000 would be quite suffi- cient. It would be time to go into the question of extra houses when they were required. They were not required at the present time. Mr. DARBYSIIIRE was surprised that a gentleman like Mr. Cooper, and possessing the intelligence he did, should state that pauperism was lessening, when he heard that morning it had increased by 50 over the corresponding week of last year. If Mr. Cooper could devise some means by which the current of pauperism could be stopped, and to make poor people more provident and spend their money in a more wise way than they were spending it—(laughter; and Major Cartwright: A teetotal lecturel—then they would not be compelled to provide for pauperism. But as long as pauperism forced itself upon the Guardians they should provide for it. The Building Committee would only be too glad to pull down the schools, but when they had an increase of 50 one year over another, what were they to do? No one would rejoice more than he to see pauperism lessened, but notwithstand- ing what Mr. Cooper said it was increasing. . _ _

'Mr. GARNETT asked whether the 21st June would allow the contractor sufficient time to complete the schools. Mr. PIERPOINT (architect) considered the time sufficiently long if the builder placed more men on the work. If Mr. Napier did not finish in three weeks, which it was within his power to do, he could not tell when he would finish. The minutes were then passed.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
Mr. Trevelyan, the Irish Secretary, arrived in London i‘onl Dublin yesterday.
The Marquis of Conyingham died yesterday afternoon at his London residence.
Mr. John C. F. S. Day, Q.C., has been appointed judge in .be place of Load Justice Bowen.
Mr. Thomas Brennan, secretary to the late Land League, was released unconditionally from Kilkenny gaol yesterday morning.
Mr. Mundella, who is at present in Dublin on a visit to the Lord-Lientenantp.is expected to resume his parliamen- tary duties on Monday.
On Thursday evening a portien of the hut encampment ot Pembroke dock, the quarters of the 23rd Royal Welsh Fusiliers were destroyed by fire.

The St. Petersburg Official Messenyv publishes an Imperial order abolishing the present West Siberian Government and establishing a Government of the Steppes. Cardinal Manning has, the Press Association learns, directed petitions to be signed protesting against Roman Catholics being tamed for the support of board schools, of which they cannot consistently avail themselves. At Corfe Castle yesterday, Joseph Kingsford was com- mitted for trial for the murder of his companion, Thomas Rigby, a pedlar, by smashing his head with a stone, on Whit-Monday.
A meeting of the Irish Parliamentary party was held yesterday, Mr. Parnell presiding, at which, after discussing the Coercion Bill, it was decided to propose further amend- ments to that measure.

A serious poaching affray took place on Thursday.night in the woods on Lord Kestevens estate at Irfford. A keeper named Syford, while out on duty, met three poachers and demanded from them their game, etc. A serious conflict ensued, in which Lyford was seriously injured. Two of his assailants have since been arrested.

Many of the leading Liberals of the country have decided in celebrate in a few weeks Mr. Bright's 25th year of representing Birmingham. The exact nature of the care- mony has not yet been agreed upon,. but will be settled at a special meeting os the executive committee of the Birming- ham Liberal Association on Wednesday next.

The Press Association learns that arrangements are being made by the London and Counties Liberal Union for a great political demonstration, to b 3 held at the Crystal Palace, in celebration of the jubilee of the passing of the Reformation Act. No date has yet been fixed, but the middle of August is regarded as probable. In the First Division of the Edinburgh Court of Session yesterday, judgment was given in an action at the instance of Miss Josephine Hubert, an actress,. against Mr. W. Bent- ley, a well-known actor, for the paternity of a child, born in 1876. Their lordships sustained the judgment of the lower court, finding that the pursuer had failed to prove her case, and dwelt strongly on "the disgraceful nature of the case, and falsehood shown oi . both sides."

An unprecedented cricket performance took place at Lords yesterday, when Barnes and Midwinter—playing in the match Marylebone Cricket Club V. Leicestershire—put on no less than 454 runs while they were in together. At the luncheon interval Barnes was not out, 264, and Midwin- ter, not out, 186. On resuming the former only added two, and the latter one, and the innings closed for 546 runs. THE EGYPTIAN QUESTION.

A Constantinople telegram dated Thursday evening says: The Council of Ministers has not yet replied to the last joint verbal communication of Lord Dufferin and the Mar- quis de Noailles on the Egyptian question. Contradiction is given to the statement that Edhem Pacha had been sum- moned to Constantinople with a view to his undertaking an important diplomatic mission. A Cairo telegram in the second edition of the Daily News. says :—The Khedive has had a long interview with Kaghib, Hafiz, Ahmed, Rachid, and Cadri Pachas, but did not ask them to form a new Ministryomerely consulting them as men of experience. The explanation given of this is that the Khedive had received a telegram from the Porte reassuring him on the situation, adding that a Commissioner would positively leave Stamboul on Friday. The Central News is enabled to state that the Turkish Commissioner appointed to investigate the state of affairs in Egypt, left yesterday for Cairo. Neither the French nor EnOish Governments had, up to a late hour yesterday, re- ceived news of his departure, but the information is accepted as accurate in official circles.

div.head: NORTH WALES COLLIERS' STRIKE.
div.p: THE NORTH WALES COLLIERS' STRIKE.

The men resumed work yesterday morning at Wrexham and Acton and other collieries on terms amicably. arranged between masters and men. It is expected that there will be a general resumption of work on Monday morning nt. Over a dozen collieries are now working, and the district is resuming its wonted aspect. Of course there la still much &stress among the families of the miners, and: this will be the c4se for some time.

div.head: ALLEGED ROBBERIES BY A SALVATIONIST.
div.p: ALLEGED ROBBERIES BY A SALVATIONIST.

At ll,desowen, yesterday, Mary Williams, 17, a prominent member of the Salvation Army, was charged. with stealing a watch and a quAntity of valuable. god s belonging to her father. It was stated that since the prisoner had been a member of the Salvation Army she had- robbed her father four times, and bad pledged the stolen goods to provide her with money to go to the "barracks." The accused was apprehended, when leaving the "barracks," and a dis- tut bine() took place. The prisoner was remanded, and bail refused.

div.head: T 11E, ODDFELLOWS' MEETING AT CARDIFF.
div.p: T 11E, ODDFELLOWS' MEETING AT CARDIFF.

Too- Oddfellows' Annual Movable Committee continued 1 their meeting at Cardift on Wednesday. The Sub, Committee appointed to exatnine the Proceedings of the Court of Directors during the past year in their report expressed some concern at the increasing heavy expertliture ; connected with the general management of the tinity, ;especially as connected with deputations. The M.C. of the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows at Car. cliff on Thursday morning after adopting the auditor's re- port-proceeded. to discuss the proposed alterations in the rules. A proposition from South London adding to the objects of the society as described in rule I section 5, that of insuring a sum of money to be paid at the death of a mem- ber's child was carried by a large mAjority. The following town Ive.re COMinated for the hrAtlng of the next A,M.C.
